Nitin Kumar, Nicholas Jerla, John Ponis, Sarbajit Banerjee, and G Sambandamurthy study a layered crystal with a mouthful of a name, beta sodium vanadium oxide, prized for switching its electrical resistance. They track how charge order, a patterned arrangement of electrons, shows up in transport and in low-frequency resistance noise as the crystal cools through two transitions.

Above the transitions, noise behavior points to electrons hopping between near neighbors. Below the sodium-ordering transition, sodium ions settle into a zig-zag pattern that reshapes the electronic state. Below the charge-ordering transition, noise drops sharply, a sign of correlated electron motion. A strong electric field can break the ordered state and flip the crystal into a conducting state, with switching across a wide cold range driven by electronics, not heating. Stable, quiet states hint at uses in cryogenic memory.
arxiv-2511-00476:
Ghazal Kalhor and Afra Mashhadi test whether large language models remember scholarship fairly. As these models move into search and discovery tools, they increasingly answer questions about who worked with whom. The authors ask three prominent models to reconstruct coauthor lists for researchers, then compare the output against bibliographic reference data across disciplines and world regions.

A systematic pattern emerged: highly cited researchers were recalled far better, so memorization favors scholars who are already visible. The tilt was not uniform, though. Clinical medicine and parts of Africa showed more balanced reconstruction than the global trend. The findings warn that discovery tools built on model memory can quietly amplify existing inequalities, and they argue for careful auditing of memorization-driven bias before such systems are trusted.
arxiv-2511-00676:
Easton Huch, Fred Feinberg, and Walter Dempsey build a Bayesian approach for causal effects that leans on randomization itself for strength. Instead of modeling how outcomes arise in a whole population, they fix the observed potential outcomes. The likelihood is built from the randomization distribution of a statistic, the distribution created by the experiment's own assignment lottery. A treatment effect model is still needed, but marginal outcome distributions often are not.

The weaker assumptions buy provable strength: a Bernstein-von Mises theorem and large-sample behavior for posterior means are proved. The posterior mean matches classical Hodges-Lehmann estimators in the large-sample limit, bridging to weighted estimators of the inverse-probability and Hájek kinds. Posterior randomization tests allow model checking in the same language. A nutrition case finds strong effect variation that moderation checks had missed.
arxiv-2511-01176:
Wenqing Zhu and colleagues test how well large language models detect code clones, duplicated code fragments that maintenance tools need to find. Earlier studies reported strong results, but left open whether performance holds across data sets and whether the models answer the same question the same way twice.

They built seven clone data sets from the CodeNet and BigCloneBench collections, sampling code pairs by their text similarity, and evaluated five language models under four published prompts. Models did well on CodeNet derived sets, with one reaching a high F1 score, but performance fell greatly on BigCloneBench derived sets. Consistency was a bright spot: over ninety percent of judgments stayed the same across repeated submissions, and score fluctuations from inconsistency were tiny.
arxiv-2511-01276:
Yiyao Ma, Kai Chen, Kexin Zheng, and Qi Dou generate dexterous robot grasps by transfer. A multi fingered hand must grasp stably and adapt to the task, yet analytical methods are slow and generative methods, trained on limited data, generalize poorly to new objects and tasks.

Their idea is to transfer a high quality grasp from a shape template to a new object in the same category. That is reformulated as generating the object's contact map. A conditional diffusion model does the work, seeing shape similarity and task requirements. A dual mapping mechanism handles complex shape differences, and two extra maps encode contact parts and directions for stability. A cascaded diffusion framework transfers all three maps consistently, and a recovery step picks reliable contact points and optimizes the final grasp.
arxiv-2511-01876:
Peter Ván writes a short note on Korteweg-type fluids. These are fluids whose stress depends on density gradients. They serve to model capillarity and phase interfaces. Two schools build their theory in unlike ways. One, from Dunn and Serrin, rests on the entropy principle and one line of argument about objectivity. A newer school uses weakly nonlocal thermodynamics.

Ván compares the two schools head-on. Their unlike objectivity arguments, he finds, lead to the same constitutive functions. So the seeming clash is not there. The real split lies in the pressure tensors each school allows for perfect Korteweg fluids. That split traces back to unlike symmetry demands made along the way. The note sorts what is mere convention from what is physics.
arxiv-2511-01976:
Yifan Zhang and Sarang Gopalakrishnan ask whether ordered phases of matter survive when a system is lightly disturbed by noise. Their setting is quantum and classical matter in thermal balance, described by Gibbs states, and the disturbance is weak local decoherence, which scrambles nearby information. The question matters near phase transitions, where correlations stretch over long distances.

The pair prove that, below a certain noise strength, the damage can be undone by local operations they call decoders. One consequence is that heat-stable quantum memories keep a working threshold even close to the critical temperature. A parallel result points to fast local denoisers in the late stages of diffusion models.
arxiv-2511-02076:
Carlos Lopetegui-González, Massimo Frigerio, and Mattia Walschaers develop a geometric way to describe entanglement in states of light that go beyond the familiar Gaussian family. Their objects are bosonic states of finite stellar rank, a measure of how non-Gaussian a state is. The framework breaks the state's stellar polynomial into atomic pieces and draws a structural graph from those pieces.

The graph's connected parts reveal the state's mode-by-mode entanglement and every way it could be split apart by passive optical operations. A key notion, essential variables, counts the minimal effective modes in a core state. From this the authors derive complete separability tests for two-mode states and for rank-two states across any number of modes, and they show how the method measures preparation difficulty on examples.
arxiv-2511-02376:
Aashray Reddy, Andrew Zagula, and Nicholas Saban automate the kind of patient, multi-turn manipulation that coaxes harmful answers out of language models. Most safety evaluations test one prompt at a time, but real attacks unfold over a conversation, adapting to each refusal. Their training-free framework, AutoAdv, runs such attacks automatically, combining three adaptive mechanisms that learn as the conversation proceeds.

A pattern manager reuses tricks from successful attacks, a temperature manager adjusts randomness in response to failure modes. A two-phase rewriting strategy first disguises the harmful request, then refines the disguise turn by turn. The system reached attack success rates up to ninety-five percent against one open model within six turns, a large gain over single-turn baselines. Tests across commercial and open models found multi-turn attacks consistently stronger, which the authors frame as an urgent case for conversation-aware defences.
arxiv-2511-02976:
Leopoldo Diaz, Harold Hjalmarson, Jesse Lutz, and Peter Schultz present AIDE, a method that feeds atomic-level defect data into device models of semiconductors. Radiation-born defects shorten device life, but their chemistry runs too fast and too dilute for direct measurement. Their 2025 case study uses silicon-doped gallium arsenide as the test material.

The model tracks the Fermi level and its electron and hole parts as charges settle, using an arsenic vacancy as the worked example. It settles at a Fermi level near 1.32 electron volts, where the triply negative vacancy is the most common charge state, as expected. It then follows a diffusion-driven reaction in which a gallium interstitial and the vacancy, pulled together by charge, form a gallium antisite. The method reaches regimes experiments cannot.
arxiv-2511-03076:
Jungjun Choi and Ming Yuan build a framework for pricing errors in asset markets, where a factor model says what returns should be. Their model mixes hidden latent factors with firm traits, and splits mispricing into two parts. Inside alpha is explained by firm traits but runs against factor exposures. Outside alpha stands apart from both. Their 2025 paper generalizes two recent approaches and fixes their orthogonality and scaling issues.

Estimation uses low-rank methods with explicit debiasing and closed-form answers, backed by inference theory that allows many firm traits. On United States stock returns from 2000 to 2019, they find strong signs of both alphas. Inside alpha moved by industry, while outside alpha looked like firm-specific shocks beyond the listed fundamentals.
arxiv-2511-03276:
Jinjie Ni and colleagues report a surprise lead for diffusion language models when training text is scarce. Models that write one token at a time usually dominate, but diffusion models build text by cleaning noise step by step. Under matched training, the diffusion models pulled ahead once the same small data set was read many times over.

Three traits drive the edge: reading in any order, heavy compute from two-way cleaning passes, and a built-in form of data variety. Adding noise helped the usual models yet never closed the gap. At larger scale, a diffusion coder passed its matched rival on a fixed budget drawn from ten billion fresh code tokens. The finding hints that scarce, high-grade data may favor diffusion designs.
arxiv-2511-03976:
Xu Zou, writing alone, introduces PETRA, a pretrained evolutionary transformer for predicting future mutations of SARS-CoV-2, the virus whose rapid, uneven evolution keeps challenging public health and vaccine design. Raw genomic sequences are noisy, so PETRA trains instead on evolutionary trajectories drawn from phylogenetic trees.

Tree-based training captures the hierarchy of viral change and reduces sequencing noise, while weighted training counters geographic and temporal imbalance in global data. Recall scores for nucleotide and spike amino-acid mutations far exceeded the best baseline reported. PETRA also helped track major recent clades in real time. Code was released openly for others to test and extend.
arxiv-2511-04076:
Hao Li, Haotian Chen, Ruoyuan Gong, Juanjuan Wang, and Hao Jiang propose Agentmandering, a game-theoretic approach to fair electoral redistricting that uses language model agents. Ensemble methods generate many lawful maps but ignore the strategic selection step, letting partisan actors cherry-pick a compliant map that still favours them.

Two agents for opposing interests negotiate in turns under a Choose-and-Freeze protocol, alternately selecting and freezing districts from a small candidate set. Choices stay constrained and interpretable as the state is partitioned step by step. Tests on post-2020 census data across all states showed significantly reduced partisan bias and unfairness in the abstract's reporting, treating selection itself as part of fairness.
arxiv-2511-04576:
Zhuo Zhang leads five authors reviewing neural methods for parametric partial differential equations. Such equations pervade science, and their solutions shift with physical properties, boundaries, and shape. Classic solvers must rerun for every new parameter set, which blocks wide exploration.

Two paradigms are compared in depth. Physics-informed networks embed the laws as soft constraints and suit inverse problems with sparse data. Neural operators, like DeepONet and Fourier operators, learn maps between function spaces directly. The review weighs where each approach wins, giving practitioners a map for choosing tools in parametric studies.
arxiv-2511-04676:
Ahmad Nouri-Zonoz and three colleagues present KGB-evolution, a simulation code for kinetic gravity braiding. The code extends an existing relativistic N-body tool with an effective field theory description. K-essence models appear inside it as a limiting case.

This first step implements the linearized dark energy stress-energy and scalar field equations. Power spectra match the hi_class linear predictions closely on large scales. Agreement holds at low redshift there and across all scales at high redshift. The runs also show small-scale growth pushing the dark energy field into nonlinear clustering, groundwork for a fuller Horndeski extension.
arxiv-2511-04876:
Catrin Harris leads four authors measuring how flow rate changes capillary trapping of a stored non-wetting fluid. Heterogeneity trapping isolates fluid upstream of rock contrasts, beyond ordinary pore-scale trapping. The setting matters for carbon dioxide storage underground.

Residual trapping barely responds to flow regime, but theory says heterogeneity trapping should. Steady drainage and imbibition runs at varied rates test that claim on layered Bentheimer sandstone. Medical X-ray scanning watches the fluid in place during each run. An analytic model accompanies the data, giving storage planners a rate-aware view of how much carbon dioxide stays put.
arxiv-2511-04976:
Xin Nie and co-authors report iFlyBot-VLM, a vision and language model built for robots that must see a scene and then act in it. Its aim is to close the gap between rich sight of the world and low-level motion control.

The model turns sight and space facts into a shared action language that is not tied to one robot body. It is built for four skills: grasp of space and size, finding named targets, turning acts into control values, and planning task steps. Tests on ten current embodied tests check how far this one model can stretch.
arxiv-2511-05076:
Raju Biswas and a co-author define pre-Schwarzian and Schwarzian derivatives for log-harmonic mappings that are locally one-to-one on the unit disk. These maps extend classic analytic ones, and their derivatives gauge how far a map bends from simple forms.

The authors study traits and uses of the new derivatives in geometric function theory. They give an exact test for when a non-vanishing log-harmonic map has a finite pre-Schwarzian norm. They also link that norm to the norm of a linked analytic function, which ties the new theory back to known results.
arxiv-2511-05176:
Soham Chatterjee and co-authors give a deterministic method to list-decode Reed-Solomon codes over any finite field. Past landmark methods were either random in their runs, or fixed but with cost tied to the field's characteristic, which can be huge.

Their method decodes from a set level of agreement in time that grows in a tame way with code length and field size. Reed-Solomon codes guard data in many systems, and list decoding can fix more errors than unique decoding. A fixed method with clean bounds makes that power safe to rely on.
arxiv-2511-05976:
Seyit Okan Kara completes a model with a new force that acts only on leptons, fixing a consistency flaw in earlier versions. The added symmetry charges all leptons equally and leaves quarks neutral. Such a symmetry normally breaks gauge consistency through anomalies, unless extra particles cancel them.

Kara adds one vector-like lepton family and singlet scalar fields. Their vacuum values break the symmetry and give mass to the new boson and the heavy leptons. He derives compact anomaly conditions, the boson's couplings and decay widths, and shows a trace condition suppresses mixing with ordinary forces. The setup also fits a standard neutrino mass mechanism and offers a stable dark matter candidate. Constraints from colliders are worked out across the parameter space.
arxiv-2511-06076:
P Michel and co-authors make lenses and gratings out of gas itself, using a pattern of entropy rather than sound. Gas optics can steer intense laser light that would damage solid optics. Older designs paired a standing sound wave with an entropy mode to carve periodic structures, but the sound wave limited lifetime and steering angles.

Dropping the acoustic mode entirely frees the design. Lifetime and time profile become controllable, and arbitrary patterns become possible, including chirped gratings and lenses with stronger contrast. The wider operating range covers larger diffraction angles. It also fits laser pulses from femtoseconds to microseconds. The authors present entropy-mode optics as a flexible new class of diffractive elements for high-power laser work.
arxiv-2511-06276:
Fernando Rodriguez Avellaneda and Paula Moraga sharpen estimates of aerosol optical depth, a measure of particles in the air tied to climate and health. Satellites report this quantity only at coarse scales in space and time. Finer maps would let officials target air quality policy and health interventions far more precisely.

Their Bayesian model treats the true field as a smooth process in space and time seen only through averaged readings. Covariances come from a diffusion-based partial differential equation, and fast approximate inference keeps the computation practical. In an India case study, the method tripled spatial detail and cut the time step from three hours to one.
arxiv-2511-06376:
Qian Ma, Ruoxiang Xu, and Yongqiang Cai examine what positional encoding really buys a transformer during in-context learning. In practice, context arrives as tokens from a finite vocabulary rather than as smooth control signals. The question is whether a single-layer transformer can still approximate any target function from such token context.

Without positional encoding, the authors show, vocabulary in-context learning lacks the universal approximation property. Adding positional encoding restores it, and they give several sufficient conditions that a positional encoding can satisfy to do the job. The findings explain, from approximation theory, why a component often treated as bookkeeping is actually load-bearing for in-context learning.
arxiv-2511-06476:
Mulan Wu, Mengyu Xu, and Dongyun Kim improve confidence intervals for clinical studies that can only enroll few patients. Small samples arise from tight budgets, scarce volunteers, and rare conditions. The usual normal approximation then gives intervals that miss their stated coverage, which can mislead treatment decisions.

Their method builds intervals from a quadratic-form statistic tied to a modified chi-squared distribution, yielding tighter accuracy for small samples and proportions. The authors recommend which sample sizes and proportions suit the method in practice. Worked examples use real clinical trial data, showing how the intervals behave where the standard approximation struggles most.
arxiv-2511-06676:
Subhojit Ghimire measures dialect bias in a popular toxicity filter and builds a teaching tool that makes the bias tangible. Automated moderation now scans everyday speech, and a post flagged as toxic may simply be written in a dialect the model misunderstands. The study compares scores for African-American English against Standard American English.

On average the model rated the African-American English text about one point eight times more toxic and nearly nine times higher for identity hate, a systematic skew. The interactive tool lets users drag a sensitivity threshold and see the real lever of harm. The harm is not just biased scores, but the neutral-looking policy cutoff a human sets, which turns skew into silencing.
arxiv-2511-07076:
Leander Grech and six co-authors use reinforcement learning to design the control pulses behind perfect entangling gates, the two-qubit operations at the heart of universal quantum computation. Shaping electromagnetic pulses by quantum optimal control can push gates toward their theoretical limits, but calibration is laborious and fragile under noise. The team instead trained a collection of reinforcement learning agents inside simulation settings built to be robust.

The agents discovered near-optimal pulse shapes that realize perfect entangling gates even under noisy conditions. Chosen agents were then validated on higher-fidelity simulations, confirming the plans were not artifacts of the training setting. Because the approach makes no assumption about the underlying hardware, it could transfer across quantum computing platforms while reducing the calibration overhead that optimal control demands.
arxiv-2511-07276:
Salem AlMarri and five co-authors confront a useful weakness of multimodal anomaly detection: the real world's inputs arrive corrupted. Systems that fuse video and audio beat video-only models in the lab, but environmental distortions can damage one or both modalities after deployment, and nobody had systematically measured the damage. The team built RobustA, a curated evaluation dataset that applies controlled audio and visual corruptions so the effects on detection can be observed.

They also propose a detection method built for this reality. It learns a shared representation space across modalities and, at inference time, dynamically weights each modality according to its estimated corruption level, leaning on whichever channel is cleaner. The dataset, with its extracted features, will be public, and the method showed notable resilience against corrupted inputs.
arxiv-2511-07376:
Jiewei Feng, Ken R Duffy, and Muriel Médard squeeze more accuracy out of a guessing-based error correction decoder by feeding it correlated noise patterns. Modern guessing decoders can decode almost any code structure, and one variant, ORBGRAND-AI, already exploits channel dependencies that other decoders ignore. This paper integrates that decoder as the pattern generator inside Guessing Codeword Decoding, a related universal decoding scheme.

A direct integration slightly worsened the block error rate while reducing the number of patterns queried. A more nuanced approach that leverages total correlation in the noise did better on both axes: it improved the block error rate by about 0.75 decibels while keeping the reduced query count. The work shows correlation in channel noise is a resource that universal decoders can spend for accuracy and speed at once.
arxiv-2511-07576:
James Miley, Grant Kennedy, and Alvaro Ribas resolve a giant dust belt around the star HD 126062. Intermediate-mass stars host bright debris discs and, unusually often, leftover gas long after planet-forming discs fade. Such systems are prime places to watch discs and planets interact.

First ALMA observations at millimeter wavelengths image the thermal glow of the belt in detail. Nearby extended gas emission also comes into view. Measuring the belt size and structure tests how planets or collisions maintain it. The system joins a small set where dust, gas, and possible planets can be studied together around an A-type star.
arxiv-2511-07676:
Ziqing Guo, Jan Balewski, and Wenshuo Hu present a quantum algorithm for learning patterns hidden in classical data. Trigonometric encodings map data into quantum circuits, but variational training by blind gradient search offers no guarantees about what the measured outputs mean. Existing methods stall on that gap.

Their quantum oracle stays traceable to the classical data, with circuit depth growing only linearly in qubit count. Approximate result patterns become learnable with structure intact. The Quantum Approximate Walk Algorithm aims to keep the link between data and quantum outcome auditable. Such traceability matters if quantum learning is to be trusted on real datasets rather than demos.
arxiv-2511-07776:
Gina Sohn, Genghan Zhang, and Konstantin Hossfeld give spatial dataflow accelerators a language for programs that change shape at run time. Machine learning models increasingly use data-dependent tensor sizes and control flow. Older abstractions for these chips force dynamic behavior into static, unoptimized molds.

Streaming Tensor Programs introduce flexible routing operators, an explicit memory hierarchy, and symbolic-shape semantics. Dynamic data rates and dimensions become visible to the compiler instead of hidden. Programs can then adapt tile sizes and flows as data demands. Efficient dynamic execution could let accelerators serve modern models without falling back to general processors for every irregular step.
arxiv-2511-07976:
Seyedehanita Madani and Vishal Patel address misaligned satellite image pairs used to spot land changes over time. Change detection compares images taken months or years apart, but seasons and shifts can break exact alignment. Many joint registration methods need retraining and transfer poorly to new places.

Their modular pipeline leaves existing detection networks untouched. A diffusion module creates in-between morphing frames, dense registration links those frames step by step, and a small U-Net refines the combined flow. On three public data sets, the method improves both registration accuracy and later change detection across several model types.
arxiv-2511-08076:
Yoshihito Kuno and Ikuo Ichinose map the mixed state phases of gauge Higgs subsystem codes under decoherence that preserves logical information. Some lattice gauge models double as quantum error correcting codes, with logical qubits stored apart from gauge degrees of freedom. Local decoherence respecting gauge symmetry can still disturb the stored information in subtle ways.

The authors clarify the full phase diagram and find an unusual critical mixed state where logic survives while the rest turns critical. Mapping to a decohered toric code helps explain the behavior. Tests with specific unitary couplings between logical and gauge qubits show robustness depends strongly on the starting mixed state.
arxiv-2511-08376:
Ozay Ezerceli and co-authors introduce TurkEmbed, a Turkish language embedding model built to beat current options on inference and similarity tasks. Turkish models often train on machine translated data sets, which can blunt accuracy and semantic depth. TurkEmbed instead combines diverse data sources with advanced training methods, including matryoshka representation learning, which packs useful information into embeddings of several sizes for resource limited settings.

On the Turkish semantic similarity benchmark, correlation scores improve clearly over prior models. The model also passes the previous state of the art system, Emrecan, on Turkish natural language inference and similarity sets, with gains of one to four percent. Faster coding adds practical value for downstream Turkish applications.
arxiv-2511-08476:
Hadi Ghaemi, Lauren Snyder, and Markus Stocker present ORKG reborn, a digital library built for machine readable research knowledge rather than papers alone. Leading archives organize story papers, so reusing a given finding still needs manual pulling and sorting by a reader. ORKG reborn instead publishes fine grained, reproducible knowledge expressions that link research statements to their supporting data and code evidence, inside papers designed from birth for reuse.

Retrieval can then run by statistical method, software package, variable, or data constraints, which document search cannot offer. Demonstrations with published papers from computer science to soil science show practical viability against state of the art archives. The work argues research knowledge databases carry enormous untapped potential.
arxiv-2511-08676:
Dusmanta Patra, Gopal-Krishna, and Ravi Joshi report fresh evidence that old radio galaxy lobes can re-energize their own particles. Their sample holds forty X-shaped radio galaxies, sources whose two pairs of lobes form an X, including fifteen newly reported from the LOFAR survey data.

Spectral maps combine low-frequency LOFAR images with higher-frequency FIRST data for sixty-eight well-resolved wings. In eleven wings the spectrum stops steepening along the lobe, or even flattens, exactly the signature of particles gaining energy in place rather than only aging. The change mostly begins where the lobe stream bends into the wing. The authors expect the enlarged set of examples to spur follow-up observations, theory, and simulations of this acceleration clue.
arxiv-2511-09176:
Arvid Siqveland extends the language of schemes, a central tool of algebraic geometry, from commutative rings to associative ones. Building on his earlier preprint, he defines how simple modules over one ring contract to another. He collects them into a space he calls the associative spectrum. For commutative rings this space matches the usual prime spectrum.

Siqveland puts a topology on the new spectrum that reduces to the Zariski topology in the commutative case. He then restricts the structure sheaf of rings to any subset of the space. One payoff is practical: complex varieties can be used inside real algebraic geometry by restricting along the inclusion of real numbers into complex ones.
arxiv-2511-09276:
Sarvenaz Babakhani, David Remy, and Alina Roitberg estimate human metabolic rate from body-worn signals using deep learning. Estimating energy expenditure from heart rate, breathing, or motion data has mostly relied on classical regression. Earlier neural studies rarely separated the effect of the architecture from the effect of the chosen signals.

The authors compare classical baselines with newer neural models across single signals, pairs, and grouped inputs. Minute ventilation proves the most predictive single signal, and a transformer achieves the lowest overall error in their tests. Grouped signals from a five-signal smart shirt work well with faster convolutional models. Results vary strongly between people, which the authors say calls for adaptive, personalized modeling.
arxiv-2511-09376:
Alexander Nadel and Ron Wettenstein speed up SHAP, the popular method for explaining tree ensemble predictions feature by feature. Two families of SHAP computation exist: a fast path-dependent version using tree structure, and background SHAP, which needs a background dataset. Their algorithm, WOODELF, unifies trees, game theory, and Boolean logic.

For each customer, WOODELF builds a pseudo-Boolean formula. It encodes their features, the ensemble, and the background data, then computes background SHAP values in linear time. It also yields path-dependent SHAP, interaction values, and Banzhaf values. On a three-million-row test, it finished in minutes on CPU and seconds on GPU. The best earlier method needed most of an hour, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-09476:
Klaus Mattis and Swann Tubach settle questions about a special element, called eta, inside étale motivic spectra. That subject is an algebraic cousin of stable homotopy theory. They show every object of the stable étale motivic homotopy category, over any scheme, is complete with respect to eta. Completeness here means the object is fully determined by its eta-power approximations.

In some cases the fourth power of eta actually vanishes, while the third power never does, mirroring classical topology. They also prove an étale version of May's nilpotence conjecture about detecting when ring spectra vanish. From that they derive a version of Nishida's nilpotence theorem: any positive-degree self-map of the unit is nilpotent in this setting.
arxiv-2511-10076:
Xiangyue Zhang, Jianfang Li, Jianqiang Ren, and Jiaxu Zhang generate gestures that move along with speech, over long stretches, without falling apart. Most generators work with local joint rotations defined through the skeleton's hierarchy, so small errors stack up along each limb and end effectors drift into implausible poses. Their framework, GlobalDiff, runs diffusion directly in the space of global joint rotations instead.

Working globally decouples each joint from upstream mistakes, but it removes the skeleton's built-in structural guidance. Three constraint levels restore it: virtual anchors around joints for fine orientation, angular consistency across bones for integrity, and a multi-scale temporal encoder for rhythm. On standard co-speech benchmarks the system improved performance by about forty-six percent over the previous best across several speakers.
arxiv-2511-10276:
Konstantin Soshin and six co-authors introduce RoboBenchMart, a simulated benchmark that moves robot manipulation out of the kitchen and into a retail dark store. A mobile manipulator must handle varied grocery items packed densely at different heights and depths, a geometry and workflow unlike tabletop benchmarks. The suite includes a procedural store layout generator, trajectory generation, evaluation tools, and fine-tuned baselines, all open source.

The authors model a realistic fine-tuning setup for current generalist vision-language-action models and evaluate several leading systems. Even on common retail tasks the models struggled, suggesting their household success does not yet transfer across domains. The benchmark targets a setting with strong near-term automation potential and gives researchers shared ground to improve on.
arxiv-2511-10476:
Moncef Derouich and Saleh Qutub study how collisions and magnetic fields shape the polarization of the solar oxygen infrared triplet, a set of spectral lines near 777 nanometers. Light from these lines carries clues about conditions in the Sun's atmosphere, but reading those clues requires knowing how often oxygen atoms collide with neutral hydrogen.

The authors compute, for the first time, a full set of collisional depolarization and polarization transfer rates for the relevant oxygen energy levels. Feeding those rates into a multi-level atomic model, they find that collisions and turbulent fields stronger than about 20 gauss erase most atomic alignment deep in the photosphere. Higher up, in the thinner chromosphere, the polarization survives. The results support a chromospheric origin for the observed linear polarization signals.
arxiv-2511-10776:
Yuta Kawakami and Jin Tian refine how counterfactual choices should be compared when outcomes are uncertain. A decision maker weighing several actions usually ranks their expected potential outcomes, but an average can hide which action is most likely to deliver the best result for a particular individual.

The authors introduce two metrics. The probability of potential outcome ranking gives the most probable ordering of outcomes for an individual. The probability of achieving the best potential outcome singles out the action likeliest to land the top-ranked result. They prove identification theorems for both quantities, derive bounds for when exact values cannot be pinned down, and present ways to estimate them. Computer experiments check the estimators' behavior, and a use on a real-world dataset shows the machinery at work.
arxiv-2511-11076:
Andrey Pilipenko and Vadym Tkachenko study birth-and-death random walks that run in continuous time without the usual memory-free rule. Such walks step up or down by one and wait random times between steps, which models queues, populations, and spread. Two edge questions matter: can the walk blow up to infinity in finite time, and can it enter from infinity?

The authors give exact conditions for both outcomes, stated through a scale function and a speed measure built from step chances and waiting-time transforms. The tests closely mirror classic tests for smooth diffusion and for memory-free walks. They then work out plain conditions for semi-Markov cases with tame and heavy-tailed waits.
arxiv-2511-11276:
Haoyi Wang addresses segmentation of volumetric medical scans, where a model must label each region in a 3D image despite scarce hand labels. Neighboring slices are anatomically alike in graded ways, but recent contrast methods use hard cutoffs that throw away that graded signal. They also ignore the global direction of anatomical change across a body, which warps the learned feature space.

Wang's CORAL method adds two objectives. A contrastive ranking loss makes feature gaps between slices track their anatomical distance, and an ordinal loss enforces the shared direction of anatomical progression across patients. Learning slice relations this way yields features that carry anatomical information more faithfully.
arxiv-2511-11476:
Angela Lopez-Cardona, Mireia Masias Bruns, and their colleagues present Symbiotik, a dashboard system that adapts its visualizations to the viewer's mental workload in real time. Dashboards support critical decisions, but they almost never adjust when the user is overloaded or under-engaged. Symbiotik reads neurophysiological signals to estimate workload and uses reinforcement learning to reshape the display on the fly.

A user study with one hundred twenty participants across three visualization types shows the approach improves task performance and engagement. The authors offer the system as a scalable real-time architecture and a validated method for neuroadaptive interfaces, where the interface tunes itself to the mind using it.
arxiv-2511-11576:
WenZhuo Zhu and four co-authors introduce DAOpt, a framework for testing whether large language models can build optimization models when the numbers are uncertain. Most earlier work gave models tidy problems with known parameters, while real decisions, from supply chains to staffing, must survive unknown demand and costs.

DAOpt combines a new dataset called OptU, a multi-agent decision module, and a simulation environment that scores models on out-of-sample feasibility and robustness. Few-shot examples drawn from stochastic and robust optimization sharpen the models further. The benchmark gives researchers a harder, more realistic measure of automated modeling skill under uncertainty.
arxiv-2511-11676:
Hanchen David Wang, Siwoo Bae, Zirong Chen, and Meiyi Ma name a hard learning setting. They call it continual multitask learning. One model must learn new tasks over time from the same input stream. It must not lose the skills it learned first. A driving system may learn traffic signs first, then traffic lights.

Old methods often grow split, task-specific features. Those features clash with each other. The team's framework, Learning with Preserving, guards shared structure as new tasks arrive. Safety-critical fields need this kind of growth without silent forgetting. Driving and medical imaging are the clear cases. A system that forgets quietly is a risk, not a tool.
arxiv-2511-12276:
L. Thomas van Binsbergen, Christopher A. Esterhuyse and Tim Müller reflect on eFLINT, a language built for writing legal and regulatory rules in a form software can reason with. Checking whether software complies with laws and contracts is growing in cost as digital services spread. Automating that check is hard because legal work involves interpretation that changes over time.

The language was developed as an experiment in syntax and semantics that can handle different kinds of norms and revision. The authors review its design, applications and implementations, and the cross-disciplinary work it requires from legal and software experts. Their aim is adaptable compliance practice for governments and firms facing frequent new rules.
arxiv-2511-12576:
Mohammad Meymani and four co-authors compare small and large generative language models on understanding application behavior, with malware detection as the test task. Large models analyze and generate code well, enabling code summaries, behavior analysis and malware hunting. The question is how much of that ability survives in far cheaper small models.

Across accuracy, precision, recall and combined scores, larger models win overall, but small models stay competitive on precision and recall in their experiments. Small models also bring faster inference and lower cost, which matters in resource-limited settings. The authors conclude small models can complement large ones, giving a practical balance between detection strength and operational feasibility.
arxiv-2511-12976:
Yoonjae Seo, Ermal Elbasani, and Jaehong Lee quantize object detectors unevenly, spending bits only where the picture is complicated. Standard quantization compresses every region of an image to the same precision, wasting accuracy on busy textures and wasting bits on blank sky. MCAQ-YOLO measures morphological complexity tile by tile, using fractal dimension, texture entropy, gradient variance, edge density. Contour complexity, and treats that score as a predictor of how much damage quantization will do there. Complex tiles keep more bits; simple tiles get fewer.

The allocation is computed at calibration time and adds almost no inference overhead, keeping throughput at one hundred fifty-one frames per second. A curriculum that raises quantization difficulty gradually steadies training. On a construction safety dataset it reached strong accuracy at about four bits per weight on average, beating uniform four-bit quantization, with gains also on COCO and Pascal VOC.
arxiv-2511-13076:
Yu-Peng Ma, Ming-Jian Gao, and Jun-Hong An extend topological physics into systems that are both nonlinear and non-Hermitian. Topological phases are prized because bulk invariants guarantee states at the boundary, a rule called bulk-boundary correspondence. Non-Hermitian systems, which gain or lose energy, break that rule in its usual form, and adding nonlinearity made the theory murkier still. The authors introduce an auxiliary system and apply the generalized Brillouin zone idea there, restoring a complete correspondence for a class of nonlinear-eigenvalue systems.

Along the way they find a novelty: the interplay of non-Hermiticity and nonlinearity creates an exotic complex-band topological phase alongside the usual real-band phase. Its results enrich the family of nonlinear topological phases and give metamaterial designers a firmer footing, since engineered materials are where gain, loss, and nonlinear response can be dialed in.
arxiv-2511-13376:
Sebastian Kebrich and 3 co-authors assess how stratospheric aerosol injection would affect renewable energy systems. The idea, which would spray particles high in the sky to cool the planet, draws interest as emission cuts lag behind climate goals. Less sunlight could also cut solar power output, so the energy side needs careful study.

Their method models a yearly injection case aimed at a two-degree cooling and tracks effects on sunlight, solar potential, and full energy systems. Solar potential fell by a fraction of a percent on average, with larger summer drops in northern Europe. Modeled systems mostly absorbed the loss with small capacity shifts, thanks to built-in flexibility.
arxiv-2511-13576:
Anhao Xiang, Weiping Pei, and Chuan Yue test how well Google Play's three privacy channels help users judge an app before installing it. Rules under laws such as GDPR and CCPA push the store to surface data safety labels, privacy policies, and permission manifests. Whether shoppers actually use those channels well was untested.

One hundred ninety participants worked with simulated versions of the channels and answered five sets of questions. Data safety labels offered the clearest interface, privacy policies proved most informative and effective overall, and permission manifests raised the strongest concern about overall risk. The channels complement each other, the authors conclude, and each still needs improvement.
arxiv-2511-13676:
Hyunwoo Oh and 9 co-authors present T-SAR, a full-stack design that runs ternary language models on CPUs alone at the edge. Ternary quantization shrinks models greatly, but CPU tools leaned on memory lookup tables that capped scaling, and separate accelerators are impractical for many edge devices. Their fix moves the lookup work inside the processor's vector registers.

By reorganizing the SIMD arithmetic units to build lookup tables in-register, T-SAR removes the memory bottleneck and raises parallel work. Reported gains span several-fold to very large multiples on core matrix operations, with only small power and area costs. Energy efficiency beat a leading edge GPU board by a clear multiple in their tests.
arxiv-2511-13876:
Xiaoyang Wei, Camille Kurtz, and Florence Cloppet address a size limit that hampers medical image AI. The popular CLIP framework pairs images with text, but its text reader caps out at 77 tokens, far too short for full radiology reports. Even medical text encoders stop near 512 tokens and grasp meaning only shallowly.

Their system, QwenCLIP, swaps in a large language model embedding module with a much longer input window and adds learnable prompts to sharpen image-text matching. The change lets the model take in long clinical reports in full. The authors report better alignment and stronger results on radiology benchmarks, and they release the code publicly.
arxiv-2511-13976:
David Baraglia and Joshua Tomlin study exotic symmetries of four-dimensional shapes. For a smooth four-manifold, the Torelli group collects deformations that can be continuously undone but perhaps not smoothly, a gap that makes four dimensions special. The authors look at connected sums of complex projective planes and their mirror versions.

For each count of ten or more mirror summands, they prove the Torelli group maps onto an infinite-rank integer lattice, so it is enormously large. They also show one such mapping class group is not finitely generated. The proofs use Seiberg-Witten invariants for families of manifolds, with care for the chamber structure that appears when the positive Betti number equals two.
arxiv-2511-14176:
Seunghun Lee and Eran Nevo settle an extension question for simplicial complexes whose vertices sit on the moment curve. Given a finite geometric complex in low dimensions, can it always be completed to a triangulation of the cyclic polytope on the same vertices? The answer depends sharply on dimension.

For dimensions two through four the extension always exists. From dimension five upward the authors construct, for every allowed vertex count, complexes that admit no such triangulation. The four-dimensional case carries an algebraic payoff through a known correspondence. Every maximal rigid object in a certain higher cluster category is cluster tilting. That is a structural result about Auslander algebras of type A.
arxiv-2511-14276:
Frederik Hoppe, Lars Kleinemeier, Astrid Franz, and one co-author ask if big table models give good reusable data codes. New table models score well by reading the task in context, but they fuse code-making and task work in one heavy net. This study pulls the two apart. It takes codes from three such models and tests them on tasks they were not built for.

The codes were judged on spotting outliers and on plain learning tasks. Plain hand-built features did as well as, or better than, the codes from the big models, and they cost far less compute. The team says the pricey codes may not earn their cost when the goal is a code that can move from task to task.
arxiv-2511-14376:
Alfonso Pedro Ridao measures whether a portrait subject's shoulders are square to the camera, as biometric document standards require. Automated quality tools for identity photos rarely quantify this specific pose attribute. His shoulder presentation evaluation algorithm needs only the three-dimensional coordinates of the two shoulder landmarks that common pose estimation frameworks already output.

From those coordinates it computes shoulder yaw and roll scores. On a data set of one hundred twenty-one portraits, the scores correlated strongly with human-assigned labels, at about zero point eight. An error-versus-discard analysis confirmed the metric flags non-compliant photos usefully. Ridao offers the method as a lightweight compliance check for enrolment systems.
arxiv-2511-14476:
Dalia Ali and three co-authors study what happens when language model training reflects diverse human values. Most alignment work uses feedback that can hide differences between social groups. The team collect ratings from more than one thousand people in the United States and Germany. Raters scored model replies for toxicity, bias, helpfulness, and related traits.

Ratings differed clearly by gender, politics, and race on some traits. Models trained on one group's tastes behaved in distinct ways. Keeping rater disagreement worked better than majority vote for cutting toxicity. Finer rating scales also helped more than simple yes or no choices.
arxiv-2511-14776:
Kenji Sahay, Snigdha Pandya, and five co-authors introduce COMPASS, a control system that helps language models stick to the evidence in front of them. Models often state false claims with fluent ease, even when the needed facts sit in the prompt. The cause is poor balance between attention to the given context and attention to stored knowledge.

COMPASS scores how much the model relies on context, then uses a feedback controller borrowed from engineering to adjust attention heads during generation. The goal is steady factual grounding without retraining or extra passes. The framework is light and readable, which makes it useful both for safer deployment and for studying how models work inside.
arxiv-2511-14876:
Henry Wong and five co-authors evaluate adversarial attacks against full autonomous driving agents, not just isolated vision models. Prior work showed crafted inputs can fool driving perception models. Whether those tricks cause harmful driving actions across agents and scenes was unclear. The team use a city driving simulator linked to a public leaderboard of top agents.

Adversarial patches designed to stop or steer agents are streamed into the simulator at runtime. Agents are tested across varied environments and scenarios. The holistic setup reveals which attacks transfer to real driving behavior. Results inform risk assessment for deployed systems. Defenses must be judged at agent level, the authors argue, not only at model level.
arxiv-2511-15376:
Shuolei Wang, Zimeng Xiao, and four co-authors present QSentry, a detector for backdoor attacks hidden inside quantum neural networks. A backdoored network behaves normally until a secret trigger appears, then it answers as the attacker wishes. Quantum networks inherit that vulnerability from their classical cousins, and quantum-specific defenses are only now appearing.

QSentry clusters the measurement outputs of the network and hunts for the statistical oddity that poisoned examples leave behind. Silhouette scores and relative cluster sizes help isolate the suspicious group precisely. In tests it catches attacks even when only one in a hundred training samples is poisoned, and its scores climb steeply as poisoning grows. Early defenses like this shape how quantum learning can be trusted.
arxiv-2511-15576:
Halima Giovanna Ahmad, Gianluca Esposito, and ten co-authors report the first measurement of non-local magic on real quantum hardware. Magic is a resource that lets quantum devices do tasks beyond a classically easy set, and non-local magic is the part no local operation can erase. It captures how entanglement and magic act together to give quantum advantage.

Using a superconducting processor, the team measured it two independent ways and got matching results that also fit theory. A noise model with no free parameters pinpointed readout error and one gate channel as the main error sources. They also erased local magic on the device while keeping the non-local part, suggesting a sharper benchmark for near-term machines.
arxiv-2511-15676:
Jing Qian, George X. Wang, and six co-authors introduce DuoZone, a window manager for mixed reality headsets that mixes user control with guidance from a large language model. Virtual windows floating in three-dimensional space are powerful, but placing and resizing many apps by hand burdens users and slows work. DuoZone splits management into two complementary zones designed to reduce that load.

A recommendation zone offers layout templates and suggests apps based on tasks and goals stated by voice or text. An arrangement zone then lets users fine-tune windows by dragging, resizing, and snapping. In a user study against a manual baseline, DuoZone sped up tasks, lowered mental effort, and increased users sense of control.
arxiv-2511-16276:
Bernhard Heim and Johann Stumpenhusen work on a number theory problem tied to the Lehmer conjecture. The conjecture says that the Fourier coefficients of the 24th power of the Dedekind eta function never vanish. The coefficients are values of the D'Arcais polynomials, so the question becomes where those polynomials have roots.

A recent approach used the Dedekind-Kummer theorem, a tool from algebraic number theory, to rule out roots of unity as roots of certain eta powers. Heim and Stumpenhusen extend that method and widen the set of points proven not to be roots of the D'Arcais polynomials. Each new non-root is a small step toward the non-vanishing statement behind the conjecture, reached with elementary and checkable arguments.
arxiv-2511-16576:
Alima Subedi, Sankalpa Pokharel, and Satish Puri present PolyMinHash, a system for approximate similarity search over polygons in spatial databases. Exact nearest neighbor search becomes infeasible as polygon collections grow. Text, image, and trajectory search have approximate methods, but polygons lacked them. Their scheme adapts MinHashing to two dimensional area based similarity.

Random points are sampled until one lands inside the polygon. The count needed forms a hash value that preserves area based Jaccard similarity between polygons. Short signatures then support fast approximate search. Trade offs between accuracy and runtime are presented in detail. Geographic information systems could query similar land parcels or building footprints far faster with such signatures.
arxiv-2511-16676:
Juan Carlos Najera-Tinoco and three co-authors solve fractional growth models with fractional neural networks. Growth models include exponential and logistic forms, plus regular harvesting variants. Fractional versions use a Caputo derivative to capture memory effects in growth. Splitting that derivative yields a trainable network design coded in stats software.

Cases compare analytical solutions with network approximations directly. Agreement tests whether the fractional network reproduces known motion accurately. Such solvers could handle models where closed forms are unavailable. Fractional growth arises in populations, epidemics, and resource systems with memory. A neural solver tied to the fractional operator itself, rather than generic curve fitting, keeps the mathematics visible in the method.
arxiv-2511-16776:
Jonathan M. O. Massey, Joseph C. Klewicki, and Beverley J. McKeon explain where the logarithmic growth of wall-pressure variance in turbulent boundary layers comes from. At high Reynolds number the inner-scaled variance grows with the logarithm of the friction Reynolds number, and the pressure itself obeys a Poisson equation with two sources.

The authors posit that the linear, rapid source, tied to mean shear, contributes a Reynolds-number-independent offset, while the nonlinear, slow source supplies the logarithmic coefficient. The linear part lives mostly in the buffer layer and maps onto the near-wall cycle. The nonlinear part concentrates in the vortical fissures between uniform momentum zones in the inertial layer. Those fissures hold a growing share of strain and vorticity as Reynolds number rises, tying their changing statistics to the observed logarithmic growth.
arxiv-2511-17276:
Julien Merand, Boris Meden, and Mathieu Grossard estimate the joint angles of a multi-fingered robot hand from a point cloud of the hand itself. Knowing the configuration matters for grasp planning, but classic inverse kinematics works from fingertip positions and then needs extra decisions about the intermediate joints, or slow numerical solvers for complex hands. Their method learns the mapping directly with machine learning.

A conditional variational auto-encoder takes point clouds of the hand's key structural elements as input and reconstructs the joint configuration that produced them. Validated on the MultiDex grasping dataset with the Allegro Hand, the method answered in a twentieth of a millisecond with accuracy comparable to leading approaches. The speed makes it attractive inside grasp planning loops that must test many candidate configurations.
arxiv-2511-17476:
Himadri Halder studies how fragile quantum many-body scars are when their host system is perturbed. Scars are exceptional energy states that refuse to thermalize while surrounded by ordinary thermal states, showing low entanglement and periodic revivals. The spin-1 XY chain hosts a family of such states built from long-lived quasiparticles. Halder adds a typical symmetry-preserving perturbation and asks whether the scars survive in large systems.

Perturbation theory describes the deformed scars at small sizes, but finite-size scaling of the perturbation's matrix elements indicates the scars ultimately thermalize as chains grow. The long-range order tied to the scars decays under the perturbation, and the relaxation time of the oscillatory dynamics scales as the inverse square of the perturbation strength. The paper draws a sober conclusion: these scars are a finite-size reprieve, not a permanent violation of thermalization.
arxiv-2511-17576:
Rayan Aldajani tests whether body fat share can be estimated cheaply from front body photos and simple body measures. Standard scans that measure fat directly are accurate but costly and out of reach for most people, yet fat share is a key number for managing weight. Since no public data set existed for photo-based fat estimation, Aldajani built one for this study from measured cases and web posts with self-reported values.

Two routes are tried: image models based on a standard vision network, and regression models using measures such as weight, height, and neck, ankle, and wrist size. A combined model that merges both routes is sketched for later work. The study is a feasibility check, and its mixed data sources mean the findings should be read as early evidence.
arxiv-2511-17776:
Melika Shirian, Kianoosh Vadaei, Kian Majlessi, Audrina Ebrahimi, Peyman Adibi, and Hossein Karshenas present PrismSSL, a Python library that gathers self supervised learning methods in one place. Such methods train models from unlabeled data, but tools are scattered across sound, images, graphs, and mixed data types.

PrismSSL offers one modular interface for setting up and running training in a few lines of code, plus small benchmarks for checking results. It connects with common model hubs and adds distributed training, tuning search, logging, and a web dashboard. The library is free under a permissive license for reuse and extension.
arxiv-2511-17876:
Mukul Singh, Ananya Singha, Aishni Parab, Pronita Mehrotra, and Sumit Gulwani test whether training for associative thinking makes language models more creative. Associative thinking links distant ideas, and it underlies much human creativity and problem solving. Their method fine-tunes a base model with reinforcement learning, rewarding outputs that connect concepts more widely, scored by a prompt-based judge using established measures from creativity research.

Models trained this way not only write more original and coherent stories, the team reports, but also show better abstraction and flexibility on programming and chart-making tasks. That spread is notable: a reward aimed at one human trait appears to lift performance across unlike generative jobs, hinting that creative habits may transfer inside a model.
arxiv-2511-18176:
Felipe Lara, Rishabh Pandey, and Vinay Singh study a multiobjective bilevel optimization problem, where an upper level decision constrains a lower level one and each objective is a ratio of two functions. Such fractional bilevel problems arise when output measures are tuned inside a hierarchy of decisions.

By reformulating the problem as a single level one, they establish refined necessary and sufficient tests for optimality, using nonsmooth constraint rules and convexity notions built from directional convexificators. They also prove weak and strong duality results for a Mond Weir type dual problem in the same language. Examples illustrate the advantages of their approach over earlier treatments.
arxiv-2511-18676:
Yongcheng Yao and five co-authors present MedVision, a large benchmark for quantitative medical image analysis with vision language models. Clinical work often needs numbers, a tumor's size or a joint's angle, while current medical models mostly answer categories or write descriptions.

The benchmark gathers many public data sets across anatomies and imaging types, with millions of annotated slices, and focuses on detection, tumor size estimation, and angle or distance measurement. Off the shelf models perform poorly, but supervised and reinforcement fine tuning on MedVision improves all three tasks strongly, yielding a solid open baseline.
arxiv-2511-18776:
Jun Kimura reviews icy worlds, the moons and dwarf planets of the outer solar system where water ice dominates and solid bodies behave very differently from the rocky inner planets. Spacecraft have found subsurface oceans, cryovolcanic activity, and thin but lasting atmospheres on some of these bodies, showing they are active and evolving.

Kimura surveys current knowledge of their surfaces, interiors, and atmospheres from spacecraft data, telescopes, laboratory work, and theory. Recent results from several missions and observatories sharpen that picture. Upcoming missions to the Jupiter and Saturn systems and to Uranus should advance the field and help judge habitability.
arxiv-2511-19076:
Matjaž Konvalinka and T. Kyle Petersen revisit the Eulerian numbers, a triangle of counts with many uses in combinatorics and probability. These numbers have been studied from many angles, and several formulas describe them. The authors focus on two formulas whose terms alternate in sign, which makes them harder to prove directly.

Both formulas are proved with a sign-reversing involution method that Benjamin and Quinn call D I E. The idea pairs up terms so that unwanted parts cancel and only the wanted count remains. Each proof then extends to a wider setting, so the arguments reach other parts of mathematics beyond the Eulerian numbers themselves.
arxiv-2511-19676:
Parsa Madinei and five co-authors prune whole layers from large vision-language models without the usual steep quality loss. Earlier layer pruning hurts these models badly. Their method, INTERLACE, studies layers in consecutive triplets to find local waste.

Within each triplet, the most redundant of the first two layers is removed. The remaining one is fine-tuned to recover lost capacity, while the third stays frozen as a stable anchor. Fine-tuning uses just one percent of a data set for one epoch. Even so, the pruned model keeps nearly ninety percent of its average performance. That is after dropping a quarter of the network, a leading result.
arxiv-2511-20376:
Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller recover hidden cliques from messy random graphs. Their 2025 paper studies random intersection graphs, a network model. Many cliques of roughly size k are planted at random. Each vertex joins each clique independently with some probability. Vertices can belong to polynomially many cliques at once. That overlap defeats simple and even spectral methods.

The authors give the first efficient recovery algorithms here. Both exact and approximate recovery are achieved. The methods tolerate noise and monotone adversaries. They even survive an optimal number of corrupted edges. Recovery works once cliques exceed roughly the square root threshold. The proofs-to-algorithms route runs through sum-of-squares optimization. Certificates must prove no large clique hides outside the truth. Modified biclique certificates supply that ingredient. A sharp concentration property keeps false positives away. The same ideas certify that the recovered clustering is optimal.
arxiv-2511-20576:
Lin, Anand, and Brown cut the measurement rounds quantum error correction needs. Their 2025 paper introduces local single-shot checks for toric codes. Syndrome measurements detect errors but are themselves noisy. Standard schemes repeat them many times per decoding round. That repetition costs heavy time overhead in fault-tolerant machines.

Single-shot correction uses one round, but usually needs heavy checks. Heavy checks wreck circuit-level performance in practice. The new checks cap their weight by acting on small lattice patches. A dynamic measurement scheme rotates which checks run when. Required rounds shrink by a factor tied to patch size. Simulations used sliding-window decoding under circuit-level noise. Local checks beat conventional ones at reduced window sizes. Fixed-width checks preserve the effective circuit distance with bare qubits. Variable-width checks won under phenomenological noise instead, with higher thresholds.
arxiv-2511-20776:
Hiroyuki Yamase and colleagues build in 2025 a strong-coupling theory of plasmons, collective charge oscillations, in bilayer materials like the cuprate superconductors. A bilayer supports two plasmon modes where a single layer has one, and earlier work described them only in the weak-coupling regime, ignoring the fierce electron correlations that define cuprates. The team's t-J-V model, with no double occupancy and a long-range Coulomb term, treats them head-on.

The two modes survive, resembling their weak-coupling counterparts. One twist: particle-hole excitations are noticeably suppressed, so the plasmon modes stay sharp across a wider range of momenta. Superconductivity in these materials emerges near 5 percent hole doping and peaks around 16 percent. The authors propose that plasmon signals in yttrium-based cuprates correspond to the lower of the two modes, and call for experiments to test the claim.
arxiv-2511-21076:
Aaditya L. Kachhadiya introduces in 2025 the Deceptron, a learned module that helps solve physics inverse problems, where the unknown input must be recovered from measured output. Such problems are ill-conditioned: plain gradient steps crawl and depend touchily on step size. The Deceptron learns a local inverse of a forward model. Training adds a supervised fit, forward-reverse consistency, and a Jacobian composition penalty. That penalty pushes the product of the two Jacobians toward the identity.

At solve time, its D-IPG algorithm steps downhill in output space, pulls the step back through the learned inverse, and projects, under the same safeguards as baselines. On recovering the initial condition of a one-dimensional heat problem, it hit the target tolerance in about 20 times fewer iterations than projected gradient. A damped oscillator problem needed 2 to 3 times fewer, rivalling Gauss-Newton in cost. A 2D variant, DeceptronNet, previews image-space corrections.
arxiv-2511-21176:
Retractions were once rare embarrassments; lately they arrive by the ten thousand as paper mills and sloppy work flood journals. Zhengyi Zhou, Ying Lou, Zhesi Shen, and Menghui Li study global retractions in 2025 through a topic lens, asking which subjects, not just which fields, carry the problem. They assign topics to roughly 46,000 of some 55,000 retracted papers and pair them with Web of Science publication counts from 2000 to 2024. A relative retraction rate then compares each topic against the global background.

Retracted papers grew from 140 in 2000 to over 11,000 by 2022, far outpacing overall publication growth from 785,000 to about 2.8 million papers a year. The year 2023 set a record with over 14,000 retraction notices. Electrical engineering and computer science alone account for more than 9,700 retractions, about 31 per 10,000 papers. Some low-rate fields hide badly hit topics, and some topics show suspicious publication surges alongside high retraction rates, flags the authors offer for targeted integrity checks.
arxiv-2511-21276:
Sutirtha Biswas and Kshitij Kumar Yadav blend physical law with deep learning to predict how buildings shake in earthquakes, in 2025. The standard finite element method is accurate but too slow for large-scale or real-time seismic analysis. Purely data-driven networks are fast, yet they often fail on new shaking patterns because nothing forces them to respect mechanics.

Biswas and Yadav propose PhyULSTM, a physics-informed network marrying a U-Net, which reads patterns across scales, with LSTM layers that track sequences over time. Governing physical laws are written into the training loss, curbing overfitting and improving generalization when data are scarce. The model beats earlier seismic predictors such as PhyCNN on the authors' tests. It can even run without explicit physical constraints, extending it to structures whose material behavior is only partly known.
arxiv-2511-21376:
Lukas Pin, Stef Baas, Gianmarco Caruso, David Robertson, and Sofía Villar bring system to a guesswork corner of clinical trial design in 2025. Response-adaptive randomization shifts enrollment toward treatments that look better as results accumulate, benefiting patients. Trials first need a burn-in, an opening phase of plain equal randomization that stabilizes estimates; 88 percent of such trials use one. Picking its length, though, has been improvised, with no guideline.

Pin and his coauthors build the first systematic framework for that choice. Their formula blends total sample size, problem difficulty, and two new metrics, reactivity plus the expected error in final allocation, into one principled rule. Simulations grounded in real trial designs show the formula finds a sweet spot. Type-I error inflation and estimation error stay controlled, while the power and patient-benefit advantages of adaptation survive, replacing rule-of-thumb choices with a defensible calculation.
arxiv-2511-21476:
Filippo Stocco, Michele Garibbo, and Noelia Ferruz survey how to steer protein-generating AI toward rare but valuable designs, in a 2025 review. Generative models have produced working binders, receptors, and new enzymes, but they imitate their training data, so they mostly sample the most probable proteins. The unusual regions of protein space, where novel functions hide, stay underexplored.

Stocco and his coauthors organize the steering toolbox into two camps. One camp changes the model itself, through reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning toward target properties. The other leaves the model frozen and guides sampling instead: conditional generation, retrieval-augmented prompting, Bayesian guidance, and tailored sampling schemes. Their taxonomy maps which knobs suit which constraints. The review closes on an open tension: natural protein fitness is fluid and context-dependent, so no single score defines the design goal.
arxiv-2511-21576:
Ridha Horchani imagines a force of nature that only quantum objects can feel, in a 2025 theoretical proposal. His Quantum Latent Gauge framework adds a hidden gauge interaction, a cousin of electromagnetism, that couples exclusively to quantum coherence. The trick is a coherence current built by coarse-graining the ordinary mass current: it vanishes for classical matter but switches on for superpositions and entangled states.

The theory keeps gauge invariance, causality, and healthy time evolution while staying invisible to every classical fifth-force search. It predicts three distinctive signatures. Interferometers should see phase shifts growing in step with fringe visibility. Decoherence rates should grow with the square of mass in a pattern unlike collapse models. Distant entangled masses should feel selective forces. Horchani works out a benchmark version in detail. Current atom interferometers and levitated nanoparticles can already place the first constraints, opening a new window on the quantum-classical border.
arxiv-2511-21976:
Thomas and colleagues compute how shear Alfvén waves, ripples along magnetic field lines, behave when the field becomes chaotic. Perturbation coils in tokamaks, added to tame edge instabilities, break field symmetry and create chaotic trajectories that may change Alfvén instabilities; analyses had assumed the waves stay unchanged.

The team built special pseudo straight field-line coordinates for chaotic regions using quadratic flux-minimized surfaces, which survive where ordinary flux surfaces do not. With those coordinates they turned the reduced magnetohydrodynamic equations into an eigenvalue problem and solved it numerically at several perturbation strengths, watching flux surfaces break as the perturbation grew stronger. Wave solutions on a flux surface stay relatively unchanged while it survives, and retain some original features even when it is destroyed. This gives a firmer basis for judging whether coils suppress or amplify Alfvén activity.
arxiv-2511-22376:
Andrews and San Mauro analyse argumentation frameworks, diagrams of arguments linked by attacks that mark conflicts between them. The grounded extension collects the conclusions even a maximally sceptical reasoner must accept, built by repeatedly applying a defence rule until nothing changes. For finite frameworks this settles quickly. The authors ask what happens when the framework is infinite, so the process may need infinitely many rounds.

Using computability theory and set theory, they pin down exactly how long the process can run: the number of rounds reaches the first non-computable ordinal, the standard ceiling for such constructions. They also show that deciding whether an argument is grounded-accepted is complete for a very high complexity class, making it maximally hard in a precise sense. That contrasts sharply with finite frameworks, where the same question is answerable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2511-22476:
Lin and colleagues improve the starting point for a family of quantum chemistry circuits. The unitary cluster Jastrow ansatz and its local variant are promising trial wavefunctions for variational quantum algorithms, normally initialised from a classical coupled-cluster calculation. Cutting the circuit down to fit real hardware, with fewer repetitions and dropped interactions the processor cannot connect, degrades that starting point and the final energy accuracy.

The team offers two fixes. Compressed double factorisation rebuilds a better approximation of the classical amplitudes within the truncated circuit, helping both expectation-value and sampling-based algorithms. For sampling-based methods, tensor network simulation further tunes parameters so the circuit produces better samples. Tests on exact simulators with up to 52 qubits and on superconducting processors with up to 65 qubits showed improvements. In one sampling method, the compressed start even beat the untruncated ansatz because its samples were more diverse.
arxiv-2511-22576:
Kapuriya, Hatami, and Buitelaar test whether text-to-image story generators respect the cultures they depict. Story visualisation turns story lines into matching pictures, and models have grown consistent, but cultural fidelity is rarely checked. The authors propose a Progressive Multicultural Evaluation Framework with five new metrics: cultural appropriateness, visual aesthetics, cohesion, semantic consistency, and object presence. The authors automate scoring with a jury of multimodal language models, checked against human evaluations.

The results expose a Western tilt. Models produced more coherent, appealing, culturally appropriate stories for real-world datasets than animated ones, aligning most strongly with English-speaking cultures on nearly every metric. Chinese scored in the middle, even beating English on cohesion, while Hindi ranked lowest on all metrics except visual aesthetics. Supplying cultural focus points helped judging in English but barely in Chinese or Hindi. The framework is offered as a foundation for more faithful story generators.
arxiv-2511-22876:
Nakayashiki takes a classical identity of integrable systems to a degenerate limit, harvesting new formulas. Tau functions of the KP hierarchy, a universal system encoding many soliton equations, satisfy addition formulas; the determinant form expresses shifted tau functions through other tau functions. Taking a careful limit of that formula, Nakayashiki obtains a degenerate addition formula expressing tau function shifts through Wronskian determinants of wave functions.

The formula settles a visible puzzle: vertex operators and Darboux transformations both manufacture new KP solutions from old. On quasi-periodic backgrounds their outputs looked alike, in genus one nearly identical, without proof. The degenerate formula clarifies the exact relation between the two constructions. Applied to theta function solutions, the machinery also yields a new addition formula for Riemann theta functions, differing from every formula in Fay's standard reference. Soliton techniques and theta function theory end up bound into one identity.
arxiv-2511-22976:
Ruibal Ortigueira and colleagues connect two ways of measuring how different two probability descriptions are, one classical and one quantum. In quantum physics, an open system's evolution is often unraveled into random paths of pure states, described by the stochastic Schrödinger equation. So a quantum state becomes a classical distribution over pure states. The team asks how to define relative entropy, a measure of dissimilarity, directly on those distributions.

They show the smallest classical divergence between two such distributions is reached exactly when both are written on a shared, possibly non-orthogonal basis of the two quantum states. They give a constructive algorithm for finding that basis. The resulting entropy turns out to equal the known Belavkin-Staszewski quantum relative entropy. And the shared basis yields a new proof that relative entropy shrinks under Lindblad evolution, the standard equation for open quantum systems.
arxiv-2511-23076:
García-Consuegra and Rajantie compare two definitions of the effective potential, the quantum-corrected energy landscape that decides a scalar field's vacuum state, in de Sitter spacetime. De Sitter spacetime is the expanding geometry that approximates the universe during inflation. The two definitions agree in flat spacetime but diverge in de Sitter, and the authors compute both explicitly at one-loop order, the first level of quantum correction.

For light fields, the standard textbook potential is wrecked by infrared contributions, very long wavelength fluctuations. Its perturbative calculation fails to converge. The constraint potential proposed in 1986 stays free of that problem and can be computed reliably. The authors also give evidence for an earlier conjecture that the constraint potential is the one that belongs in the Starobinsky-Yokoyama stochastic theory of inflation. At one loop it reproduces the field's probability distribution, its long-distance correlations, and the vacuum lifetime.
arxiv-2511-23376:
Li Siyan and colleagues ask whether an AI assistant should adapt its answers to the skill of each user. Novices tend to want clear steps in plain words, while experts want short answers in terms they know. The team built this quiet tailoring into an assistant on a customer data platform.
