Recent experiments showed that entropy changes when electrons are added to a dot reveal the spin and orbital degeneracy of the states involved. More exotic entropies, though, require probing a whole system, not just the dot receiving the particle.

The team uses a pair of capacitively coupled gallium arsenide quantum dots. Charge measurements on one dot reveal entropy changes of the entire two-dot system. The surroundings respond to the added electron through Maxwell relations. The method works both at weak coupling, where microstate counting applies, and at stronger coupling, where numerical renormalization group calculations are needed.
arxiv-2605-03976:
Xiaochen Liu, Jean-Paul M. G. Linnartz, and Thiago E. B. Cunha model optical wireless communication links whose bandwidth is limited by components rather than by regulation, unlike radio systems. They review the bandwidth limits of physical-layer components, which typically make the gain-to-noise ratio decay with frequency in a low-pass pattern describable by a pole-zero transfer function. The goal is to squeeze more throughput through that decaying channel.

The authors optimize the signal power spectrum of DC-biased optical OFDM, allowing modulation beyond the three-decibel end-to-end bandwidth, and express the optimized throughput as a function of the maximum modulation frequency. A new Newton-based algorithm is compared with an accelerated Hughes-Hartogs algorithm for finding near-optimal spectra under theoretical, measured, and simulated channel responses.
arxiv-2605-04376:
Zheng Ma and three co-authors present a graph-based method for protein inference, the task of working out which proteins are present in a sample from the peptide evidence a mass spectrometer reports. Deep learning has been held back here by the cost and scarcity of well labelled data.

Their system links proteins, peptides, and spectrum matches into one graph and classifies the protein nodes. It trains on public data with labels borrowed from an existing inference tool, then refines those labels by self-training on confident cases. Because its input features are well normalised, the model works across data sets without retraining for each one.
arxiv-2605-04676:
Anis Bara and four co-authors ask whether vision-language models can learn to read radio frequency spectrograms from synthetic training data alone. Spectrograms are the pictures engineers use to inspect wireless signals. Understanding the spectrum is essential for intelligent communications, but extracting physical attributes from a spectrogram is a skill traditional machine learning has not achieved.

They build a platform that pairs live spectrum captures from a software-defined radio with model interpretations. That allows direct tests on real over-the-air signals. A model trained only on synthetic spectrograms is compared with general-purpose baselines. The comparison uses a shared benchmark. It probes whether the synthetic skill transfers to the real radio environment.

Haejoon Lee, Vincent-Daniel Yun, Hyeonho Oh, and Dimitra Panagou study multi-agent LLM systems that stay robust under Byzantine faults. The 2026 paper is distributed-systems security for AI teams.
arxiv-2605-09176: Training language models means crossing the valley of optimizer choices, starting from the ubiquitous AdamW. Aditya Ranganath navigates from AdamW toward memory-efficient and matrix-based optimizers. The 2026 paper is a practical field guide to training optimizers for big models.

arxiv-2606-04076:
Shenghan Luo leads a team that presents SkySense in 2026, a system for locating drones from radio channel fingerprints in sensing-and-communication networks. Labeled examples are scarce, and reflections off buildings make the radio signature of a position ambiguous.

SkySense first learns from long unlabeled flight recordings, using the smoothness of flight paths to build stable features. A generative model then maps those features to coordinates, fine-tuned with only one percent labeled data, and predictions from several base stations are fused. Because the generative model represents a spread of possible positions instead of one average guess, it avoids a common collapse error. On real measurements, mean error fell to under ten centimeters, beating fully supervised rivals.
arxiv-2606-04176:
Jiayi Wang and Raymond Wong study in 2026 how to complete a matrix whose entries are not numbers but whole probability distributions, as when each cell summarizes many repeated measurements. Only some entries are observed, and even those only through finite samples.

To exploit hidden simplicity, they embed each distribution as a point in a kernel space and define a Tucker-style rank for such distribution-valued arrays. New unfolding operators connect that rank to the classical tensor rank, making the theory workable. Their estimator comes with finite-sample error bounds describing its accuracy. Tests on synthetic data and a real application showed the method recovering the unobserved distributions effectively, opening a path for data types that ordinary matrix completion cannot touch.
arxiv-2606-04276:
Hongseok Namkoong quantifies in 2026 the value of structural knowledge, the restrictions a modeler builds into a model before seeing any data. His yardstick is local sensitivity: how much an estimate can move, to first order, when the underlying distribution is nudged by moving probability mass.

Working in the geometry of optimal transport, he shows this sensitivity equals the size of the efficient influence function's gradient. Restricting which transports are allowed shrinks the sensitivity, and that shrinkage is exactly the value of the modeler's assumptions. The framework resolves a standing puzzle in causal inference: efficiency bounds look identical whether or not treatment probabilities are known, yet practice differs greatly. Known propensities, he shows, cut sensitivity to misspecification.
arxiv-2606-04876:
Tajjar, Pfefferle, Purucker, and Hutter teach a tabular foundation model to read text columns without crushing them first, in a 2026 arXiv paper. TabPFN performs strongly on numerical and categorical tables but does not natively handle high-cardinality text features. The standard pipeline embeds text with a language model and compresses the vectors with PCA into a few scalar features. End-to-end alternatives avoid PCA but need large text-cell pretraining corpora and usually underperform pretrained models.

The authors introduce a text adapter projecting text into the tabular model's token space instead. They freeze both the sentence encoder and TabPFN and train only the lightweight adapter, which maps text embeddings into a short token sequence in TabPFN's embedding space. The design removes the PCA bottleneck, preserves TabPFN's numerical strengths, and trains far more cheaply than end-to-end text-tabular pipelines.
arxiv-2606-04976:
Bandyopadhyay and Ashokan map when a periodically driven quantum spin chain remembers its past and when it heats into forgetfulness, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Driven, disordered, interacting systems host competing regimes: Floquet many-body localization, and thermalization. Starting from a product state, the authors track entanglement entropy and energy absorption while varying interaction, fields, disorder strength, and driving frequency.

They find distinct behaviors: fast delocalization in some regions, logarithmic entanglement growth and long-lasting initial-state memory in localized or prethermal Floquet regimes elsewhere. Strong disorder arrests transport and slows entanglement dynamics, while strong driving frequency arrests energy absorption and creates a long-lived state. Conversely, weak disorder or low frequency leads to delocalization and heating. The outcomes support non-equilibrium phases in driven many-body systems and delineate their boundaries.
arxiv-2606-05276:
Hannah Banks, Marius Kongsore, and Neal Weiner introduce big axions in this 2026 arXiv paper, a class of axion models built from symmetry networks. Axions are proposed to solve the strong CP problem of quantum chromodynamics and to serve as dark matter. Keeping an axion's symmetry clean is notoriously difficult, and simple versions clash with cosmological limits on strings and domain walls.

In a big axion, the Nambu-Goldstone mode emerges from the collective breaking of a network of U(1) symmetries across theory space, not from one symmetry alone. The construction realizes high-quality accidental symmetries and admits both pre-inflationary and post-inflationary histories. Its topological structures interpolate between Peccei-Quinn axions and axions from extra-dimensional gauge fields. The authors identify a minimal viable subclass, little big axions. They give a robust solution to the strong CP problem while accounting for some or all of the dark matter.
arxiv-2606-05376:
Jingyao Wu and colleagues teach language models to learn from annotator disagreement rather than discard it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Human-centered tasks like natural language inference and emotion recognition admit plausible readings, so annotators often disagree. Standard alignment collapses their judgments into one gold label, treating the disagreement as noise.

The team's SHALA-LLM framework treats ambiguity as information. SHALA-LLM is a reinforcement learning method that trains the model on the distribution of annotator labels while prioritizing the ambiguous samples during optimization. On ambiguity-sensitive benchmarks including ChaosNLI, GoEmotions, and MSP-Podcast, it improved agreement with the label distributions, cutting the Jensen-Shannon distance on ChaosNLI by up to 62.1 percent. It also improved classification F1 scores by 16.7 percent, evidence that modeling disagreement does not trade accuracy away but can strengthen it. The authors argue this matters wherever models must spot contested inputs and preserve variability.
arxiv-2606-05476:
Andrew Hamara and colleagues present SHIELDS in this 2026 arXiv paper, a multi-agent system that hardens operating systems. Existing automation helps, but it relies on pre-written corrective actions that cannot adapt when a fix fails or a system differs from expectations.

SHIELDS instead treats hardening as an iterative, feedback-driven loop. Language-model agents propose fixes, apply them to the target system, read the results of validation scans, and refine their approach, much as a human administrator would. The team evaluated the system across machine configurations using six language models ranging from 20 billion to 400 billion parameters. SHIELDS remediated 73 percent of scan findings. Notably, success depended less on raw model size than on effective tool use and information gathering. That suggests capable hardening agents can run on smaller, locally hosted models, an advantage where compute is limited or security policy forbids sending system data to outside services.
arxiv-2606-06276:
Niccolò Giacomini builds algebraic structure on spaces of sheaves over a curve in this 2026 arXiv paper on algebraic geometry. A Quot space catalogs all the ways a fixed sheaf, a bundle of algebraic data over the curve, can be mapped onto smaller pieces. Hall algebras, built from the cohomology of moduli stacks, act like symmetry algebras for such catalogs. The question is whether that action can be made categorical, lifting numbers to structured operations.

Giacomini constructs a two sided categorical action of the Hall algebra of semistable sheaves of one fixed slope. The action lives on the derived category of certain Quot spaces taken inside tilted hearts, a reshaped version of the sheaf category. Correspondence stacks that parametrize extensions of quotients by semistable sheaves induce the operations. Along the way he compares Quot spaces with Bradlow pairs and stable pairs, aligning three moduli problems that the action must respect.
arxiv-2606-06376:
Fabian Gittins and co-authors ask whether a future gravitational wave detector can hear neutron stars ring in this 2026 arXiv paper. As two neutron stars spiral together, tides raise a swelling frequency that can resonantly excite the stars' own vibration modes. Those modes carry news of the stellar interior, like seismology on Earth. Whether any instrument can actually measure them was an open question.

The team simulated one year of observations for the planned Einstein Telescope and ran full Bayesian analysis on the two hundred loudest mergers. The detector could pick out resonant modes in favorable events, sensing phase shifts as small as zero point zero three radians. Resonance frequencies near five thousand three hundred hertz fall within reach. Ignoring the resonances biased the inferred tidal deformabilities, the standard measure of how easily each star deforms, so modelers must include them.
arxiv-2606-06476:
Chenming Zhu and co-authors give vision language models an imagination in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models reason well about what a photo shows but poorly about space: unobserved layouts and other viewpoints. The authors call the fix thinking with imagination. Their framework, Astra, lets the model ask a world simulator for imagined views from new camera positions while it reasons, then use those views as evidence.

Astra pairs a policy model, trained with reinforcement learning, with a simulator tuned for consistency across viewpoints. A two phase curriculum teaches the policy to call the simulator only when imagined views actually help. Experiments showed both halves are necessary. The simulator alone lifted a strong commercial model on a spatial benchmark from about forty five percent, and the full system did better still. Useful imagination, the lesson goes, is a learned skill: knowing when to picture a scene.
arxiv-2606-06576:
Edward T Stevenson and co-authors predict whole climate maps from a handful of examples in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scientists often must regress high dimensional outputs, like temperature and wind at every point of a planet, from very few training runs. Gaussian processes shine with little data but choke on huge outputs, while the usual compress then predict pipeline uses bases tuned for reconstruction, not prediction. Their model instead decodes each output from a low dimensional latent state governed by a Gaussian process.

By integrating out the decoder weights analytically, compression and prediction are optimized as one objective that scales to high dimensional outputs. The demonstration is striking: the first spatially resolved emulator of global climate models for rocky exoplanets. Such emulators let researchers explore alien climates, pressure level by pressure level, without paying for a full physics simulation each time, and with calibrated uncertainty on every predicted map field.
arxiv-2606-06676:
Density functional theory is the workhorse that makes quantum chemistry computable, replacing a system's full wave description with a few simpler variables. Wang, Liebert, Penz, and Schilling show that this theory is one member of a large family in this 2026 arXiv paper. They build a single framework covering the many variants that use other reduced variables, such as spin or current, in place of plain particle density.

The framework needs only two ingredients. The first is a chosen set of basic observables, whose average values become the reduced variables. The second is a fixed piece of the energy operator, shared by the class of systems. With just that structure, they define the universal energy functions, prove them convex and smooth, settle when target variables can occur, and prove a Hohenberg-Kohn style uniqueness result. Variants whose observables form a Lie algebra get special emphasis, tying the theory to symplectic geometry.
arxiv-2606-06776:
In pay as you go services, unhappy customers rarely announce they are leaving; they just stop showing up. Mufti, Hammad, Saleh, and Gull build a churn prediction system for that setting in this 2026 arXiv paper, published in Decision Support Systems. Their design watches behavior in rolling thirty day windows, then judges churn over the following thirty days, keeping evidence and outcome cleanly separated in time.

Tested on a large real world data set, a feature based model reached accuracy near eighty eight percent, with a strong ranking score. A sequence based model did even better at spotting leavers. It caught up to ninety six percent of true churners by reading the order of actions. On later unseen data, accuracy stayed above eighty three percent with no retraining, which the authors credit to the time aware framing. Explanation tools also flagged which behaviors drive the risk.
arxiv-2606-06976:
Tool using agents fail in two mirror ways: calling tools needlessly, or inventing answers instead. Zhou and co-authors trace both failures to muddled uncertainty in this 2026 arXiv paper. During ordinary reinforcement learning, correct and wrong actions grow equally confident. Overconfident mistakes then poison later steps of a task.

Their framework, TRUST, puts uncertainty inside the reward itself. It acts as a repulsive force that keeps right and wrong actions apart in confidence. Lightweight annotations mark the key turns in each trajectory. Turn level calibration and whole task success train together. Benchmarks covered several tool use suites, including When2Call and ToolSandbox. TRUST improved decision quality and overall task performance across them. Uncertainty estimates stayed more trustworthy during training. No extra cost appears at inference time. The lesson: an agent should know when it does not know, and rewards can teach that.
arxiv-2606-07076:
Knowing a load's total power is not the same as knowing where that energy goes inside it. Montoya, de Leon, Arrabal-Campos, and Alcayde build a branch level accounting in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is a companion to their work on identifying three phase loads from terminal data. The question shifts from fitting the load to locating its energy.

Terminal power splits uniquely into heat loss and stored energy changes. The split runs branch by branch inside any chosen equivalent circuit. Three theorems organize the picture. One guarantees the decomposition is unique for a fixed circuit shape. Another warns that rival shapes fit the same data while localizing energy differently. The third unifies classic electrical dualities under one time domain principle. Six test cases exercise the framework, including a famous open phase paradox. Classical power theories, the authors argue, answer different questions rather than contradicting this one.
arxiv-2606-07276:
Wüthrich examines a fairness-like property of insurance pricing models in this 2026 arXiv note on the balance property. The property requires that total premiums predicted by a fitted model equal total observed losses in the fitting data. It sounds basic, yet many modern pricing models built on generalized linear models, a standard family for insurance, violate it unless the model uses a special canonical link. Actuaries then apply corrections to restore balance.

Two established corrections either shift the model's intercept later or refit under a wrong distribution. Wüthrich instead fits the model under a side constraint that enforces balance during fitting, and by long-run prediction accuracy this beats both corrections. He also links constrained fitting to ex-post risk sharing, where pool members settle actual losses later: each member is charged for estimated systematic effects while the unpredictable remainder is shared.
arxiv-2606-07376:
Yun, Kyaw, and Bae construct quantum circuits that perform general measurements, an operation quantum hardware often lacks natively, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A general measurement, formalized as a positive-operator-valued measure, extracts more information than qubit readout and underpins tasks like telling quantum states apart. Their construction follows the Naimark extension, embedding the measurement in a larger system using gates, with single-qubit parameters tuned by a classical optimizer to approximate the target.

They then relax that design with quantum neural network circuits, parameterized circuits trained like neural networks, and a hybrid combining both ideas. The constructions were compared on state discrimination strategies, including minimum-error and maximum-confidence measurements. The neural network circuits reached near-optimal results efficiently, needing fewer training iterations in tests. Shallow network circuits performed well. The results suggest trainable circuits are a practical route to implementing measurements on quantum hardware with limited gate budgets.
arxiv-2606-07476:
Heng, Zhang, Cooper, and Li estimate joint motion from muscle signals even when some muscles cannot be measured, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Surface electromyography records muscle activity through electrodes and drives prosthetics and rehabilitation devices. Anatomy and sensor limits mean only a subset of muscles is observable. Their musculoskeletal neural network couples a convolutional activation estimator with an embedded dynamics model of the body, forming a system trained end to end without labels for forces or torques.

A composite loss blends joint-angle accuracy with a muscle synergy term and an anatomy-guided trend term drawn from physiology. Tests on 2-degree-of-freedom wrist motion covered 3 rhythmic movements and 1 random movement. The method beat recurrent and hybrid baselines on error and fit, especially for the random motion in their comparisons. Its parameters stayed within body limits, and its inferred activation for an excluded muscle tracked that muscle's recorded signal.
arxiv-2606-07576:
Shah and Kartik build a verification layer that tells autonomous AI scientists when to keep experimenting, when a question is settled, and when to refuse an answer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, Cartograph, steers experiments toward unresolved parts of the hypothesis space, closes ambiguity outright. It also detects when the hypothesis library itself cannot explain the data, triggering refusal instead of a forced conclusion. The steering rule is derived under a linear-Gaussian model. Classical experiment-design criteria arise as special cases.

Across 5 testbeds the steering rule dominated naive guessing in a cascade experiment, winning over 100 comparisons. The system identified 3 out-of-library drug-metabolism mechanisms, then revoked those identifications when residuals exposed structural misfit, while a perturbed in-library control stayed identified. Auditing 40 published claims from an autonomous materials laboratory, the refusal guard flagged all 4 claims later judged inconclusive while passing most confirmed ones.
arxiv-2606-07676:
Boyd and co-authors present SCXM, a method for guessing where a single cell sat inside tissue using only its gene activity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial transcriptomics, which maps gene activity in place, covers few genes at fine scale, while single-cell RNA sequencing reads the whole set of active genes but destroys the tissue layout. Paired examples of both are rare, so the team learns from unpaired data.

Their approach fine-tunes a single-cell foundation model with adversarial training, a setup where a second network tries to catch errors, so the model learns to translate between the two data types. Tested on three curated datasets, SCXM beat earlier methods built for translation between measurement types on every set. The authors also show that some gene pathways carry stronger clues about a cell's former neighbourhood than others, which helps explain where the translation works best.
arxiv-2606-07776:
Han-Bing Liu, Xing, and Luo calculate how often B mesons should decay into ordinary baryons plus invisible dark particles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is B-mesogenesis, a theory that tries to explain two mysteries at once: why the universe holds more matter than antimatter, and what dark matter is. Its decays create both the matter excess and dark baryons that escape detectors unseen.

Using perturbative QCD, the standard calculational method for strong-force processes, plus flavour-symmetry relations between channels, the team works out form factors and branching ratios. The rates come out sizable, around one in a hundred thousand decays for the best channels. In the Type-I scenario the standouts are the neutral B meson decaying to a Lambda baryon plus a dark particle, and its strange cousin decaying to a Xi baryon. Such rates put the processes within reach of colliders and B factories.
arxiv-2606-07876:
Chan, Cionca, and Van De Ville design optimal filters for cleaning signals that live on directed graphs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph signal processing handles data attached to network nodes, from sensor readings to temperatures across a region. Denoising such data with a Wiener filter, the classic least-squares optimal filter, is well understood for undirected graphs, but direction changes the mathematics.

Real observations mix two noises: structured noise shaped by the directed graph itself, and additive measurement error from sensors. The authors build a framework handling both together. Under several stationarity assumptions, combining uncorrelated and correlated noise, they derive the optimal filters in closed form. A proof of concept on a temperature graph shows the method on real-structured data. The paper is short but closes a specific gap: directed graphs model flows and influence naturally, and their denoising no longer borrows theory built for symmetric networks.
arxiv-2606-08076:
Esra Dönmez and Agnieszka Falenska read AI persuasion through a philosopher's lens, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Jürgen Habermas's theory of communicative action distinguishes what speakers do with words beyond conveying facts: building trust, signalling similarity, claiming sincerity. These are illocutionary intents, the social functions of an utterance. The authors ask whether language models deploy them the way persuasive humans do.

They simulated discussions from the ChangeMyView forum, where posters reward arguments that changed their view. All three models tested expressed illocutionary intent effectively, often more strongly than human writers. Models also crafted flattering replies aligned with the holder's own intent, a strategy strongly associated with changing opinions. Crowd workers found the model arguments more agreeable than human ones and preferred them. The findings suggest persuasive power comes not only from argument quality: training on human preferences teaches models to perform agreement and rapport, which itself persuades.
arxiv-2606-08176:
Misselbeck-Wessel proves representation theorems for a generalization of Boolean algebra in this 2026 arXiv paper. Boolean algebras, the algebra of true and false values and of sets with complement, can be represented as collections of sets through the classical Stone representation theorem. Swap algebras widen this picture, following Bishop's constructive mathematics, where proofs must give explicit constructions. Every Boolean algebra is a swap algebra, so results here cover the classical case.

Working constructively, the author proves a Stone representation theorem for separated swap algebras of a specified type, together with a Stone-Čech theorem for the same class. The second result shows that restricting to separated algebras loses nothing for the theory of swap characters. A useful device, the set with a Boolean inequality, tracks where a proof uses the principle that anything follows from a falsehood.
arxiv-2606-08376:
Leihan Zhang and colleagues build a large dataset of real-world artificial intelligence failures from news reports, in this 2026 arXiv paper. As these systems spread into socially important domains, reports of harms and failures have grown more common and more varied. Governance frameworks state high-level principles for responsible use, but data resources for tracking incidents remain limited. Existing collections are often manually curated, small, and unsuited to continuous monitoring. RiskNet aims to supply that missing resource at scale.

RiskNet is built from large-scale news sources in many languages through a structured pipeline. It finds risk news, screens reports at the event level, merges reports of the same incident into single records, and sorts each incident across many dimensions. The result organizes scattered reporting into one dataset that researchers and regulators can analyze over time. The authors position the resource as a base for evidence-based governance work.
arxiv-2606-08576:
Hwa-Long Gau, Hong, Chi-Kwong Li, and Kuo-Zhong Wang study the numerical radius of certain block matrices in this 2026 arXiv paper. The numerical range of a matrix collects all values obtained by sandwiching it between a unit vector and itself. The numerical radius is the largest magnitude in that range, much like the operator norm but often strictly smaller. The matrices here have a special two-by-two block form: a block A, a block B beside it, and zeros below.

The authors show the numerical range of such a matrix is the union of the numerical ranges of a family of ordinary two-by-two matrices, reducing a hard-looking problem to a tractable one. When A is a self-adjoint involution, a symmetry of order two, they characterize when the numerical range is an elliptical disk.
arxiv-2606-08676:
Shi Ying Chang and colleagues measure what instruction tuning costs coding assistants, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Developers interact with code in two distinct modes. In flow mode they write code continuously and need tools that complete unfinished programs. In command mode they express intent in natural language and need tools that convert instructions into code. Instruction-tuned language models dominate the second mode, but whether the same paradigm suits both was unclear. The authors investigate this instruction-tuning tax across code tasks.

Their study compares model behavior across the two interaction modes to find where following instructions verbatim erodes the fluid completion ability that flow mode demands. An assistant over-trained to obey commands may hesitate or over-explain when the developer simply wanted the next line.
arxiv-2606-08876:
Hegyi presents a volunteer-built web platform making Romania's public elevation data easy to explore in a browser, in this 2026 arXiv paper. LiDAR surveys measure terrain height with laser pulses from aircraft, producing digital terrain models prized for landscape research, planning, and archaeology. In practice the data sit fragmented across sources and need specialist software, which blocks reuse. RO-LiDAR GeoQuickView acts as an accessibility layer on top of the public data.

The platform publishes hillshade visualizations, shaded relief images revealing slopes and channels, plus a spatial index for downloading the rasters. Its sharpest layer is a half-meter terrain model covering four counties, Caraş-Severin, Gorj, Mehedinţi, and Dolj, from the LAKI III survey's Zone A. Four Zone B counties follow next, once their products pass the same quality-control workflow. Hegyi stresses the platform supports quick discovery and interpretation, not official modelling or field verification.
arxiv-2606-08976:
Jing Wang and colleagues build a benchmark that exposes how far language models still are from real hardware design work, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RTL, register-transfer level code such as Verilog, is how chips are specified. Existing benchmarks use small designs, and frontier models already saturate them. Scaling up is hard because grading needs specifications and testbenches, which real designs rarely provide. RTL-BenchLS contains over 10,000 formally verified Verilog designs, far larger than earlier ones.

Beyond code generation, the benchmark adds three tasks. Round-trip reasoning asks a model to move between code and description. Masked-content reasoning hides part of a design to reconstruct. Repository-issue reasoning requires fixing bugs. All are graded by formal equivalence checking, no testbenches needed. Of 8 leading models, even the best reached only about 23 percent on round-trip reasoning, 28 percent on masked content, and 12 percent on issue fixing, leaving room for progress.
arxiv-2606-09376:
Juan Santillana argues that common faithfulness scores for generated text reward saying almost nothing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such scores check each claim a model states against known facts, a measure called precision. A cautious model can therefore score near perfectly by omitting most relevant facts. Santillana pairs precision with coverage, the share of relevant facts a model actually mentions.

His testbed is Formula 1 strategy, where complete telemetry makes the full set of relevant facts for each decision knowable in advance. The benchmark holds more than seven thousand decision cases from one hundred fifty-seven races, in English, Spanish, and Portuguese. The most precise frontier model covered under half of the relevant facts and ranked last once coverage counted. Small fine-tuned models, by contrast, reached coverage scores near ninety-eight percent on the held-out season. A second test on weather forecasts showed the same pattern.
arxiv-2606-09476:
Carlos Vélez García, Miguel Cazorla, and Jorge Pomares argue that robot goals should be sets, not single states, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Offline goal-conditioned learning trains robots from recorded trajectories, and its key trick, hindsight relabelling, reuses states a robot actually reached as goals for earlier moments. Standard versions demand reproducing the entire reached state, including details the task does not care about.

Their method, Goal-Set Hindsight Relabeling, observes that a reached state certifies every goal set containing it. A binary query marks which state variables define success, such as a cube's position, while the rest count as nuisance variables. The goal predicate becomes an input at inference time, so one trained checkpoint can answer many different goal questions without retraining. Across OGBench tasks and five offline goal-conditioned learners, the approach improved performance exactly where full-state goals were bottlenecked by nuisance dimensions.
arxiv-2606-09776:
Igor Petrashkevich and his co-authors map the ices around six newborn stars in the Orion A cloud in this 2026 arXiv paper. Class 0 protostars are the youngest stars, still wrapped in cold envelopes. arxiv-2606-09876:
Chongzhe Zhang and his co-authors curb a language model's cocky wrong answers without muting its sound ones in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models often state high confidence in replies that are false. Blanket fixes push all confidence down, which dulls trust in the right replies too. Their method steps in only where a probe smells a wrong-but-sure answer.

A frozen probe reads the model's inner state mid-run. When it flags risk, set attention heads have their outputs rescaled as the confidence word is formed. On a Qwen model doing maths with a yes-no confidence field, one cut-in point flipped eighty-two percent of wrong yes calls to no. A wider cut-in slashed calibration error from near twenty-two percent to near nine. Just five percent of sound yes calls were harmed.
arxiv-2606-10176:
Kravitz answers a clean question about an object from algebra that encodes graph colorings, in a 2026 arXiv paper on combinatorics. The chromatic symmetric function of a graph, introduced by Stanley in 1995, sums over all proper vertex colorings and refines the older chromatic polynomial. Expanding it in the elementary symmetric basis gives coefficients indexed by partitions, lists of whole numbers summing to the vertex count. Some coefficients can be negative for some graphs, and the missed problem is which partitions can ever appear negatively.

He proves the partitions that always appear with nonnegative coefficients, for every finite graph, are exactly the hook partitions, whose diagrams have a single row joined to a single column. Every non-hook partition admits some graph whose expansion gives it a negative coefficient. The characterization is exact and complete, not merely a sufficient condition.
arxiv-2606-10276:
Lee and colleagues build a robot that reads human gestures and gaze, not just spoken commands, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-robot interaction. Natural interaction requires understanding intent expressed nonverbally, yet current robot policies use language as the sole interface, placing the full communication burden on the person. Their framework, EDITH, streams the human's first-person view and gaze from smart glasses alongside speech to the robot in real time.

A hierarchical policy handles these rich but noisy inputs: a high-level policy infers intent and produces subtasks. Each subtask is a fine-grained instruction paired with a keyframe grounding the intent in the scene, like the frame where the human points at the target object. In experiments on interactive tasks, EDITH let the robot act on nonverbal signals even when intent was expressed only briefly, and significantly reduced the communication burden compared with language-only control.
