The picture is of stable communities absorbing a modest flow of newcomers while exchange networks carried goods much farther than most people traveled.
plos-pone-0357776:
Haiyan Feng led a team of eight authors speeding up cancer gene sequencing prep, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Before DNA can be sequenced, labs must build libraries from samples, a slow and fiddly process. The team introduced a one-step method, called OS-MPCR, based on multiplex PCR, to prepare libraries for cancer sequencing.

Feng's method folds several steps into one, cutting time and cost in the pipeline. Faster prep means oncologists get results sooner, which can matter when treatment choices wait on gene findings. Lower cost also widens access for labs with small budgets. Methods papers like this rarely make headlines, but they are the kind of quiet advance that clinical sequencing depends on.
plos-pone-0357976:
Yen Hai Le and coauthors published a 2026 environmental health study in PLOS ONE tracking a mercury-resistance gene through people, food, and water in three countries. Bacteria carrying the merA gene can detoxify mercury, so its abundance fingerprints mercury pressure in an environment. The team built a precise gene test and screened human stool, retail chicken, and water samples from the environment in Japan, Vietnam, and Ghana.

The contrast was stark: the gene appeared in a small share of Japanese stool samples, most Vietnamese samples, and nearly every Ghanaian one; chicken showed the same ladder. Water carried the gene almost everywhere, more abundantly in Vietnam and Ghana, sometimes where chemical mercury readings were undetectably low, showing the gene test can be more sensitive. A resistant bacterium carried the gene on a transferable plasmid, ready to spread. Fecal gene screening is proposed as a practical gauge of population mercury exposure.
plos-pone-0358076: Balanta Martínez and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the ecological worth of palm wetlands in the Amazon foothills. The wetlands, called Cananguchales, center on the buriti palm, Mauritia flexuosa. The team used an emergy method, which counts the energy nature spent to build a system. Putting a number on nature's work can argue for protection in terms planners respect.
plos-pone-0358176:
Abbas Ahmad and coauthors published a 2026 computational study in PLOS ONE on rheumatoid arthritis, the autoimmune disease that inflames and destroys joints. Recent work implicates two metal-driven forms of cell death, one powered by iron and one by copper, but their shared controls were unclear. The team combined several gene-data techniques on blood immune cells from patients and healthy controls, seeking genes that differed and moved together in networks.

Three genes sat at the crossing point of both death pathways and were switched on more strongly in patients. One stores iron, one disarms damaging oxygen molecules, and one puts the brakes on cell division. These genes also lined up with a shift in immune cell mix, toward inflammatory types and away from calming regulatory cells. The trio is proposed as candidate regulators worth lab testing, possibly opening treatments aimed at metal-driven cell death.
plos-pone-0358476:
Jin-Hyang Park and three colleagues show how to measure muscle fibers on ordinary archived slides with a browser based tool, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fiber cross sectional area is the standard yardstick for muscle wasting and regrowth, but the usual workflow needs frozen tissue and fluorescent stains, so old paraffin blocks in hospital archives go unused. Their pipeline runs an artificial intelligence segmentation program through a public web interface, then tidies regions and measures fibers in free image software.

Validated in mouse muscle, the method's area distributions from routine pink stained paraffin sections matched those from a comparison stain and from frozen sections. In a nerve injury model it correctly registered the shrinkage of fibers cut off from their nerve. The payoff is access: decades of stored slides become measurable, and small laboratories without specialist kit can join neuromuscular research on equal terms.
plos-pone-0358576: Zuo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diet, sleep, and lung cancer in southwest China. They compared patients with lung cancer against people without it, in a case-control design. The focus was on polyunsaturated fats in food and on sleep patterns. Links found in such studies can shape diet and sleep advice, though they need care before being read as causes.
plos-pone-0358776: Shimagaki and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on outlook after liver cancer surgery. They tested a blood-based index, built from C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte counts, measured before surgery. The question was whether that index predicts how patients fare after part of the liver is removed. A cheap score from routine blood tests could help surgeons judge risk before operating.
plos-pone-0359776:
Joshua Vo and six colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a scoping review of how medical students and residents around the world are taught telemedicine. Telemedicine, care delivered by video or phone, became a core skill during recent years, yet training in it varies wildly between schools.

A scoping review will map what is taught, where, and how it is evaluated, across countries. Medical schools building telemedicine teaching need that world map before writing their own courses. Educators and accreditation bodies are the audience for a review designed to show the gaps in training.
plos-pone-0359976:
Lei Zhu and colleagues built in 2026 a mosquito recognition system that runs on a mobile device. Identifying mosquito species matters because only some kinds spread diseases such as dengue and malaria, and control efforts differ by species. Their system uses a convolutional neural network, the image recognizing form of deep learning, trained to judge mosquitoes by two kinds of shape evidence at once, which the authors call dual morphology.

Putting the trained model on a phone moves identification out of the laboratory and into the field, where health workers and citizens actually encounter the insects. Fast, accurate identification can sharpen surveillance maps and help target spraying and breeding site removal. The study joins a growing set of phone based tools for tracking disease carrying insects.
plos-pone-0360076:
Andrew Tusubira and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how people living with HIV manage their own care when they also live with high blood pressure or diabetes. Their systematic review gathers studies from low and middle income countries, where clinics are stretched and patients carry much of the daily work of staying well. Self-care covers taking medicines faithfully, watching diet and symptoms, and knowing when to seek help.

Having three long term conditions at once multiplies that work, and health systems built around single diseases can leave such patients unsupported. By mapping what self-care looks like and what helps or hinders it, the review gives program designers a view from the patient's side of the clinic door.
plos-pone-0360376:
Jhon Zabaleta-Santisteban and a large team of collaborators mapped in 2026 where cacao could grow well in the Amazonas region of Peru. Their approach is an ensemble of predictive models, combined through a platform called BIOMOD2, that weighs many data sources at once. The maps fold in territorial management and plant health alongside climate and soil, so the result speaks to farming decisions rather than to climate alone.

Cacao is a valuable export crop and an alternative livelihood in regions pressed by deforestation. Knowing which land suits it, and which land should be left alone, helps planners steer planting toward success and away from forest clearing. The study gives regional authorities a planning tool grounded in the region's own conditions.
plos-pone-0360476:
Amine Ben Safta and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 on the pressure used during a common gallbladder operation. In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, surgeons inflate the abdomen with gas, a pneumoperitoneum, to see and work, and the operation is usually done at standard pressure. Some surgeons argued that a lower pressure, eight millimeters of mercury, would leave patients in less pain afterward.

Patients were assigned by chance to the low pressure or the standard approach, and their pain was scored on a visual analog scale after surgery. The trial's headline result is plainly stated: the lower pressure did not significantly reduce those pain scores. A clear negative answer is useful, since it tells surgical teams that this particular adjustment is not where pain relief will be found.
pmc-13155776:
Larissa Bianchini is first author on a 2026 review offering practical guidance for surveys in clinical research. Surveys capture what patients and other stakeholders know, believe, and do, and can measure how treatments are put into practice. They are versatile and cheap, but weak design ruins their value.

The review walks through each decision, from setting aims and choosing a sample to writing clear questions and picking how to deliver them. Knowledge, attitude, and practice frameworks can structure questionnaires. Online platforms widen reach and ease data handling. Low response rates and uneven engagement are named as key practical risks, with planning strategies offered to lift participation without harming data quality.
pmc-13196176:
Mustafa Al-jarshawi and colleagues offer a 2026 projection for oral semaglutide in the United States. Semaglutide is a drug for type 2 diabetes that also protects the heart. The team applied results from the SOUL trial to national survey data to estimate broad impact.

They estimate about six point one million adults would qualify for the drug. Over four and a half years, wide use could prevent about 118,664 major heart events. Those events include heart-related death, heart attack, and stroke. Gains held across sex and race groups. Even at half uptake, tens of thousands of events could be avoided. The authors argue that better access could bring large public gains.
pmc-13197376:
Albrecht Lindemann and colleagues report a 2026 case series on stopping leukemia therapy after remission. Older patients with acute myeloid leukemia often get two drugs long term until the disease returns. Past work hints that stopping in deep remission may not hurt survival, so the team offered a fixed six-month course.

Seven patients reached full remission and chose to stop therapy. Five cleared their mutation traces to very low levels. Six of the seven stay in remission, from seven to fifty months so far. One patient relapsed after fourteen months and regained remission once therapy resumed. The authors suggest time-limited therapy may suit select patients, though the group is tiny.
pmc-13197476: Xiaoming Wang and colleagues issued a 2026 author correction to a study on forecasting the strength of permeable cement road base. The original source data file was an older, less complete version. The notice explains how one figure's results were built, adding nine outside strength values to three lab values for one mix design. It gives the full value list, the mean and spread used, and why a population formula was chosen for that larger set.
pmc-13202076:
Dementia care research rarely asks which questions matter most to affected families, and a 2026 plan by Elena Michel sets up a partnership to do exactly that. The plan presents GenderDem, a priority setting study on diversity-sensitive psychosocial programs for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia.

Following the James Lind Alliance approach, people with dementia, caregivers, and health professionals will serve together on a steering group as co-researchers. Two rounds of online surveys will gather and rank candidate research questions from wider participants, supported by a literature review. A final workshop will settle a top ten list meant to guide future dementia care research funding.
pmc-13202676:
One molecule hitting two cancer targets is the design goal of a 2026 study by Joydeep Chatterjee, which synthesizes eighteen new imidazoquinoxaline compounds. The research article uses a Pictet-Spengler route to build carboxamide-bearing molecules aimed at both the EGFR growth signal and the tubulin skeleton of cells.

Two compounds beat the approved drug erlotinib against breast cancer cells in culture and blocked EGFR enzyme activity at low concentrations. One of them also stabilized microtubules much like paclitaxel, raised reactive oxygen species, and arrested cells before division. Docking and dynamics simulations showed both compounds sitting stably in the two target pockets, supporting the dual-action design.
pmc-13209476:
Evidence favors cemented hip implants for broken femoral necks, yet surgeons rarely use them, and a 2026 study authored by Hamed Tayyebi quantifies the gap. The retrospective cohort covers 4,407 patients over fifty who received partial hip replacement for intracapsular fractures across a hospital system between 2009 and 2018.

Only about one patient in nine received a cemented implant, despite cemented cases showing significantly fewer fractures around the implant during and after surgery. Surgeon background predicted the choice: trauma specialists used cement far more often than arthroplasty specialists in the data. The authors call the mismatch a stubborn evidence-practice gap needing stronger guideline uptake.
pmc-13210176:
HIV infections among people who inject drugs in Kyrgyzstan have fallen sharply, and a 2026 modeling study authored by Ainura Moldokmatova asks what really drove the drop. The research article runs a deterministic compartmental model under three scenarios, switching needle programs, substitution therapy, prevention, and antiretroviral treatment on and off.

The simulations point to a shrinking population of people who inject drugs as the main engine of the decline. Prevention programs and treatment still reduced the overall burden meaningfully, the model suggests, even if they were not the primary trend drivers. Reported case patterns, meanwhile, likely mirror changing testing behavior more than true swings in new infections.
pmc-13237576:
Mehrabian and colleagues report a hard case of Hailey-Hailey disease eased by an unexpected drug. The patient, a man of sixty-five, had endured three years of burning, itching, and splitting skin in the groin area. Creams, steroids, antifungals, and repeated antibiotics had all given little relief before a biopsy confirmed the inherited blistering disease.

Treatment with naltrexone, a drug better known for blocking opioids, brought success where standard care failed. Why it helps this skin disease is still debated, but case reports build the record doctors consult when usual options run out. For a painful, embarrassing condition, one well-documented success can open a new path.
pmc-13237976:
Brusco and colleagues cost out a new infection-tracking programme for Australian aged care homes. The programme, NISPAC, gives homes a standard, streamlined way to log infections and antibiotic use. Outbreaks in aged care can turn deadly fast, yet until now nobody knew what rolling the system out would cost.

The team tracked implementation costs prospectively, as the work happened, from the aged care sector's own viewpoint. Three coordinating bodies share the running of the programme, and their costs count too. A clear price tag lets funders judge the programme fairly, and lets other regions copy it with eyes open about staff time and money.
pmc-13240876:
Wu's team at Jining exposed autism-model brain organoids to two gut fatty acids and read the gene readout. Short-chain fatty acids are thought to stir inflammation and metabolic trouble in autism. Organoids received sodium acetate, sodium butyrate, or no treatment for seven days. Three repeats per group went through RNA reads.

The two pushed gene activity opposite ways. Acetate mainly shifted genes tied to gene-switch control, enzyme work, and membrane leakiness. Butyrate instead switched on immune processes, with the TGF-beta pathway standing out in the scan. The split suggests each fatty acid nudges the growing autistic brain through its own route.
pmc-13241376:
Feng's team at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan reviewed how rewired metabolism drives fibrosis across the body's organs. Scar-forming cells switch their glucose, amino acid, and fat handling in Warburg-like fashion. The review walks through core pathways before turning organ by organ. Heart, lung, liver, kidney, skin, and peritoneum each get a section.

Tags on metabolic enzymes, including the newly recognized lactylation, recur as control knobs. Some enzymes push fibrosis through side jobs unrelated to their chemistry. The authors close with therapies already aiming at glycolysis and lipid pathways. Targeting metabolism, they argue, could sit beside current anti-scar care.
pmc-13243876:
Alberte Aspaas Lundquist and colleagues add two patients to the tiny known group with disease caused by faulty MRPS34, a mitochondrial protein. Their report appeared in JIMD Reports in 2026. The gene builds part of the mitochondria's own protein factory, and damaging variants on both copies cause a Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder. One new patient died in infancy carrying two severe variants. The other, with two copies of a gentler splice variant, survived into mid-childhood.

The team then reviewed all eleven reported individuals to hunt for patterns. Developmental delay appeared in every case, and lactic acid buildup and brainstem lesions in nearly all. Carrying two copies of the milder variant tracked with longer survival, the clearest genotype-phenotype link so far. The disorder strikes many systems beyond the brain. With so few cases worldwide, the authors argue each new report materially sharpens counseling for families.
pmc-13244076:
Zhicheng Lai and colleagues ran a randomized phase two trial of two liver-directed combinations for advanced liver cancer. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. Seventy-two patients with advanced tumors received chemotherapy infused into the liver's artery, paired either with the immunotherapy toripalimab or with the targeted drug sorafenib. The main measure was how many patients remained progression-free at six months.

The two arms finished close on that measure, at just under two-thirds of patients each. Survival leaned toward the immunotherapy pairing, with a median of 20.9 months against 16.4 months for sorafenib, and time without progression also ran longer. Serious side effects were fewer with toripalimab: a third of its group had severe events against well over two-fifths on sorafenib. The trial was not designed to crown a winner between the arms. The authors call the immunotherapy combination favorable and ready for a phase three test.
pmc-13245076:
Harry Magunia and colleagues surveyed how the world performs right-heart ultrasound, and found a specialty speaking many dialects. Their RVNet survey appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Guidelines have tried to standardize right heart checks, yet practice anecdotes suggested wide variation. The anonymous sixty-eight-question survey drew 588 replies from many countries in late 2024 and early 2025.

Most were certified and experienced, yet their methods diverged at nearly every step. Views captured, timing of measures, image orientation, and what gets reported all varied, in both exam types. The authors organize the chaos with a six-part framework covering views, phase, orientation, interface, timing, and scaling. They propose it as a simple shared checklist, V-POINTS, to make measurements comparable between labs. The message: the right heart deserves the discipline the left received years ago.
pmc-13246876:
Norman, Conduit, and Laycock asked what mental abilities make some people better at spotting changes in a scene, in this 2026 Psychonomic Bulletin and Review study. Missing changes, called change blindness, matters for drivers and radiologists alike. Two hundred sixty participants took a naturalistic flicker task, where two versions of a scene alternate until the change is found, plus nine cognitive tests.

The strongest links to spotting accuracy were top-down visual search control, visuospatial ability and memory, and basic visual inspection speed. Factor analysis grouped the test battery into flexibility, visuospatial working memory, and attention-speed factors, and the visuospatial memory factor was the main predictor of change detection. The authors conclude that holding a scene in spatial memory is central to noticing what changed.
pmc-13246976:
Yang, Huang, and Wei systematically reviewed how football boot design affects injury risk, in this 2026 Sports Medicine - Open article. Boots are the player's interface with the ground, and their studs and soles shape the forces reaching knees and ankles. The team searched two decades of literature and kept thirty-two studies, checking each one's quality with a standard scale.

Several patterns stood out. Screw-in and bladed studs grip so hard in rotation that the foot can lock, raising the risk of ligament tears, ankle sprains, and stress fractures. Sole stiffness showed a U-shaped risk curve, with both very stiff and very soft plates creating problems. Mismatches between boot, foot shape, and surface added further risk. The authors call for standardized boot testing.
pmc-13248376:
Farlie and an international group of colleagues argue for a better way to dose balance training, in this 2026 comment. Falls threaten older adults, and balance exercise helps, yet prescriptions rarely state how hard the exercise should feel. The authors say that missing measure, balance intensity, holds back both research and clinical advice.

They call for one standard yardstick of balance intensity and practical ways to sample it during training. With a shared measure, studies could pin down the level that best prevents falls and protects independence. The piece is a position statement, meant to steer future trials and guidelines rather than report new data.
pmc-13248876:
Khatatbeh and colleagues surveyed adolescents in Jordan in 2026 about online gaming habits and how they view its health effects. They used the Health Belief Model, a frame that links behavior to felt risk and prompts to act. Four hundred three students aged 10 to 17 answered an online form covering daily play time, game types, and views on body and mind.

Students played about three hours a day on average. More than a quarter saw no harm to physical or mental health, a sign of low felt risk. Over a third had never been counseled on gaming harms, with parents the main source when guidance came. Older age and longer daily play tracked with poorer self-rated physical and mental health, and beliefs about mental harm also shaped ratings. The authors urge awareness efforts aimed at adolescents, parents, teachers, and school health staff.
pmc-13248976:
Liu and co-authors studied rehearsal training for heart attack teams, in a 2026 report from a Chinese chest pain center. For the deadliest heart attacks, minutes spent reopening the blocked artery shape survival. The center introduced simulation-based team training, then compared two hundred sixty patients treated before and after the program began.

After training, the median time from hospital door to balloon treatment fell from ninety-two to sixty-eight minutes. Arrival-to-treatment times improved as well, and the authors link the drills to smoother teamwork under pressure. Because the study looked backward at one center, they ask for prospective multicenter trials before declaring the training a proven cause.
pmc-13250176:
Prestedge, El-Murr, and Williamson interview Australian health workers about testing done right beside the patient. Their 2026 BMJ Open study concerns point-of-care testing, where results come during the visit instead of from a distant laboratory. Eighteen participants took part, drawn from hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, emergency care, and pathology services.

Three themes ran through the interviews: care centered on communities, connected records, and sound quality control. Workers praised programs that improved fairness of access, but they named weak funding and poor information systems as major barriers. Clearer training guidance for staff outside laboratories was seen as a practical fix. The authors call for funding that covers testing, quality checks, and staff training together.
pmc-13250876:
Wang and co-authors measure how well heart and vessel nurses lead teams in China and what drives it. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine survey covers four hundred eleven such nurses at three large hospitals, surveyed in early 2025. Nurses rated their own leading, their workplace, and their confidence in their own abilities.

Scores ran above average, strongest for urging others on and setting an example, weakest for questioning the status quo. Job title, department, training in leading, workplace quality, and self-belief each lifted the scores. Workplace and self-belief linked most strongly with the ratings. The authors advise focused training, healthier work settings, and self-belief building to grow nurse leaders in practice.
pmc-13251076:
Haiyan Pan and co-authors are the subject of this 2026 retraction notice from the journal Cancer Cell International. It withdraws their earlier paper, published in 2020, which claimed a long non-coding RNA drives stomach cancer cell growth and spread through a partner RNA chain.

After publication, concerns were raised about the Western blot and flow cytometry data in three of the paper's figures. The authors could not provide the raw data when asked to back it up. The editors state they have lost confidence in the results and conclusions. The notice adds that none of the authors replied to letters about the retraction.
pmc-13252976:
Meijun Jiang, Shaoyun Zhang, and Cong Xiao review electrical stimulation around flap surgery in this 2026 article. Skin flaps moved to cover wounds from cancer or injury can partly or wholly die, and no drug has reliably prevented that loss.

Drawing on more than 120 studies, the review sorts benefits by timing. Stimulation before surgery encourages new blood vessel growth into the flap. After surgery, it helps fight infection, drain swelling, and speed wound healing, while also guiding cells to move and multiply. Because one drug usually hits only one part of the failure process, the authors argue that a physical method touching many steps at once holds real promise.
pmc-13256176:
Jessica Appleton and colleagues report a 2026 study of SleepWellBaby, a phone app that gives parents a seven-day program on infant sleep. The program can be repeated and mixes facts with interactive features on helping babies sleep in a responsive way. Parents of infants under six months joined online and filled in surveys at the start, after seven days, and after thirty days.

Seven hundred parents started the study, with 339 still responding at seven days and 220 at thirty days. Most said the app was easy to use and that they trusted its content, though most had stopped using it by one month. Parents who used it more, or found it most helpful, showed the greatest drop in fatigue. Some also said it kept them on their phones too long.
pmc-13257876:
Xiaoqi Zhang and colleagues study a welding problem that arises when stainless steel meets ordinary carbon steel. Rail vehicle bodies join these metals with resistance spot welding, but mismatched properties shift the weld nugget off center. Their 2026 analysis inserts a thin nickel layer between the sheets.

Computer models tracked force and heat fields through the welding process with the nickel layer in place. Physical welds then confirmed what the models predicted. The nickel insert curbed nugget drift and evened out the metal's internal structure. Hardness varied more smoothly across the joint, and the finished spot welds came out stronger.
pmc-13257976:
Elizabeth A Cook leads a 2026 animal study of two drugs that block chemokine receptors, proteins that guide immune cells, during treatment for hemorrhagic shock. Hemorrhagic shock is a life-threatening state after heavy blood loss. In rats, the team compared the drugs BX471 and INCB3284, given alone or together, against a control fluid. They measured how much fluid was needed to restore blood pressure over six hours.

With control treatment, fluid needs rose sharply and averaged 108 units per kilogram of body weight. With BX471 the average was 31, with INCB3284 it was 51, and with both drugs it was 36.5. Death rates differed between groups but not significantly, and survival time in a second test did not change. Both drugs also shifted markers of body-wide inflammation, which the authors link to their fluid-saving effect.
pmc-13259576: CMAJ's June 2026 obituaries column records the deaths of Canadian physicians in short, uniform notices. Each entry names the doctor, home city, medical school and graduation year, and specialty, from family medicine and surgery to neurosurgery and radiology. Ages at death stretch from the thirties to past one hundred, and every notice links to a fuller published obituary. The column serves as the journal's running roll of the profession's losses.
pmc-13260976:
Neil Ming leads a 2026 case report of subcutaneous emphysema, air trapped under the skin, following postoperative nausea after dental extraction. An 18-year-old female had four wisdom teeth removed in a routine procedure without air-driven instruments, which are the usual source of such air. After multiple episodes of retching and vomiting she developed progressive facial swelling and was transferred to a tertiary care center for evaluation and treatment.

Imaging showed widespread air tracking through the chewing muscle and under-jaw spaces, with no abscess present. She was managed conservatively with intravenous antibiotics, sinus precautions, and supportive care, and the swelling gradually resolved. The authors warn that this complication can spread toward the chest and threaten the airway. They argue that vomiting may force air into unhealed extraction sites, so early recognition matters even without an air source.
pmc-13261976:
Jarosław Kopko and colleagues report a hard-won birth in a woman with Swyer syndrome. In this rare condition, a person with XY chromosomes develops as female but without working ovaries. Donor egg IVF can still work when the uterus is intact, as this 2026 case shows.

The twenty-nine-year-old patient, whose ovaries had been removed earlier, conceived after a frozen embryo transfer. That first pregnancy lodged dangerously in the uterine wall and was dissolved with methotrexate. Six months later a second transfer grew normally, ending in a healthy boy delivered by cesarean at thirty-nine weeks. Early ultrasound for every IVF pregnancy is their firm lesson.
pmc-13262176:
Wenjie Sun and colleagues sew a medicated patch that cooks tumors with light while leaking chemotherapy on cue. Inoperable abdominal tumors need options gentler than surgery and systemic drugs. Their 2026 electrospun patch embeds copper sulfide and polydopamine, which heat under near-infrared light.

Acidic tumor surroundings and light-triggered warmth both unlock the drug stored inside. In animals, the combined patch killed far more tumor cells than heat-only or drug-only versions. Every treated mouse survived the ninety-day watch, with little body-wide toxicity. The authors pitch the implant as a surgical alternative for selected patients.
pmc-13262276:
Franziska Ulrich and colleagues take a famous diabetes drug duel out of the trial clinic and into British general practice. Once-weekly semaglutide beat dulaglutide in a controlled trial, but strict trial entry rules left real-world patients untested. Their 2026 cohort follows over six thousand new users in UK primary care records.

After one year, semaglutide users lost more weight and trimmed blood sugar further than dulaglutide users. The edge survived in the large majority who would never have qualified for the original trial. Trial-eligible patients, though, improved most on either drug. Safety events were tracked while treatment continued, completing the real-world picture.
pmc-13262676:
Tian-Tian Liu and colleagues find obese children need less sedative per kilogram than lean peers, a counterintuitive dosing result. Remimazolam, a new ultra-short benzodiazepine, is spreading into pediatric procedure rooms with thin data on obesity. Their 2026 trial enrolls sixty children, half obese, alongside a fixed pain-drug partner.

A staircase design adjusted each dose by the last child's response until the midpoint dose emerged. In obese children that midpoint sat roughly a quarter lower than in normal-weight children. Dosing strictly by the scale would therefore overshoot in heavier patients. The authors urge weight-band care when sedating obese children for procedures.
pmc-13263276:
Sota Ihara and Akihiro Okamoto propose a new bacterial species from an electricity-linked growth culture in a 2026 journal article. The rod-shaped bacterium was isolated from filtered liquid of an electrochemical enrichment culture, a setup that grows microbes able to move electrons to solid surfaces. They named it Cellulomonas electrica and compared it with its closest relatives by genes and chemistry.

Whole-genome similarity values fell well below the thresholds that define a species, while broader measures kept it inside the Cellulomonas genus. Its main cell fat and its chief quinone, a molecule used in energy handling, set it apart from relatives. It grew best at around 30 degrees and mildly acidic conditions. The strain is deposited in two public culture collections.
pmc-13263376:
Yichen Li and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on an electronic skin inspired by the pitcher plant Nepenthes, whose rim channels liquid in one direction. Their Janus e-skin moves sweat away from the body actively while staying breathable and waterproof. It aims to keep skin dry during long wear.

The material stretches to more than six times its length and senses in several modes, including touch-free signals and Morse code taps. It records brain, muscle, heart, and eye signals cleanly. Paired with machine learning, muscle signals from the skin steered a four-legged robot, and the system recognized letters with over ninety-five percent accuracy.
pmc-13264276:
Nidhal Ben Abdlekrim led a 2026 study of match demands in elite under-19 female basketball players from North Africa. Most past profiles came from men or adults, so youth data were thin. The team compared guards, forwards, and centers, and national against world-level play.

Thirty Tunisian players were tracked through eight playoff games with video, heart-rate bands, and blood tests. World-level players did more hard efforts and spent more time at near-max heart rate. Guards did the most hard side-to-side moves, while centers did more still, hard work and had higher blood lactate, a fatigue marker. Hard effort fell from the first to the last quarter in both groups, less so for world-level players.
pmc-13266276:
Ruth-Ann Yaa Frimpong and colleagues published a 2026 food study on plant-based mayonnaise made by swapping egg yolk for protein from sprouted moringa seeds. Egg yolk stabilizes the sauce's oil droplets, so a plant swap must match its texture. They extracted the seed protein three ways: with ultrasound, with enzymes, or with both together.

Swaps from five to fifty percent were tested. Texture improved over the all-egg control up to a twenty percent swap, then declined. At twenty percent, the combined-extraction version matched a commercial benchmark in firmness, consistency, and stickiness. Several mixes also gave finer oil droplets than the control. Yellowness faded as swap levels rose, and acidity stayed in the low-acid food range. The authors back sprouted moringa protein as a working partial egg replacer.
pmc-13267276:
Marie Oosterlynck and a large team report a 2026 study of tiny particles that may spread tau damage in the brain. In Alzheimer's disease, the tau protein clumps and seems to pass from cell to cell. Small sacs released by brain cells, called extracellular vesicles, carry tau seeds, but which tau forms drive the spread was unknown.

The team took these sacs from frozen brain tissue of patients with three tau diseases and from healthy controls. Protein profiling showed that each disease left a distinct tau pattern in the sacs. Alzheimer's sacs were rich in tau pieces from one key region. A short piece named PHF6 did most of the seeding work. The authors name PHF6 as a possible drug target.
pmc-13267976:
Cristina Kontogiannis, Sami Asif, and Amit Kharod present a 2026 case report on a rare artery squeeze after major weight loss. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome occurs when the gut's third section is pinched between two large vessels. Their patient was a 28-year-old woman with lasting nausea and vomiting after losing 110 pounds. She also had a heart-rhythm condition and slow stomach emptying, which muddied the picture.

Standard scope and ultrasound checks found nothing. A CT scan showed the tight vessel angle and short gap that mark the syndrome. Surgeons used a robot to join the pinched gut section to the next part of the small bowel, bypassing the squeeze. Her symptoms resolved. The authors present the robotic route as a workable fix for this rare problem.
pmc-13268076:
T D Barry and a large team report a 2026 evaluation of Wales' national TB cohort review program. Cohort review is a structured team audit of every TB case, checking care quality and public health data. Wales started its national program in 2012. The team analyzed all notified TB cases from 2012 to 2022 in this low-incidence country.

Of 1,175 cases, 985, about 83 percent, were presented at cohort review. Many care outcomes reached near their targets. Support to finish treatment was aimed more and more at patients with social complexity and higher spread risk. The completeness of surveillance data improved substantially. Weak spots persisted in finding and assessing contacts of cases. The authors offer the program as an efficient model for other low-incidence countries nearing TB elimination.
pmc-13268176:
The editors of PLOS One published a 2026 editorial note on a greenhouse tomato study. The original paper tested a micro-fog system that cools and humidifies greenhouse air, improving tomato growth in summer. After publication, concerns arose about where some of the data came from. The first author admitted that a figure's environmental data came from a different institution and was included by mistake.

The note prints a corrected figure and fixes several results sentences, including midday temperature and humidity readings for the fogged and control sections. The greenhouse's reported dimensions were also wrong and are corrected. Raw data behind the figures and tables, missing from the original submission, are now supplied. The editors state they cannot verify the data's origin because the institutions involved gave conflicting advice.
pmc-13269876: An author correction from 2026, for a paper led by Zicong Huang on a protein that organizes sperm maturation, fixes swapped labels in one table and one sentence. In Table 2, the column headings for two patient groups, labeled NOA and OA, had been exchanged. The correction also reverses the group counts in the results text, which now reads 30 OA samples and 25 NOA samples. Both changes were made in the online and PDF versions.
pmc-13270876:
Yangyang Zhang is lead author of a 2026 review article on the HOXA gene cluster and bone disorders. Bone stays healthy through a balance of building and breakdown, and losing that balance drives diseases such as osteoporosis, where bones thin. HOXA genes help direct early body patterning and cell fate.

The review gathers recent work on how HOXA family members act in bone disease, finding wide, uneven roles across the family. It groups their effects into three shared patterns: setting regional pattern in the skeleton, adjusting signalling pathways, and joining gene-control networks with non-coding RNAs. The authors argue these roles offer possible targets for new bone treatments.
pmc-13271476:
Rui Sun and Zhihao Chen report a 2026 journal article designing a syllabus for Architectural Art English, an English for Academic Purposes course for undergraduate architecture students. The design draws on needs analysis, asking what students must do in English, and genre analysis, studying the text types architects actually read and write.

A university-wide questionnaire gathered 650 students and faculty. It found a sharp gap between students' aims, such as joining international projects, studying abroad, and following foreign lectures, and their current weak listening skills and subject vocabulary. The proposed syllabus teaches seven genres, from textbooks and research papers to design statements and presentation scripts, through themed units using real cases and task-based projects.
pmc-13272276:

pmc-13277276:

pmc-13279276:

pmc-13279576:

pmc-13279876:

pmc-13281776:

pmc-13282876:

pmc-13285676:

pmc-13286076:

pmc-13287576:

pmc-13288976:

pmc-13290876:

pmc-13290976:

pmc-13291776:

pmc-13292376:

Group differences peaked at day two after hatching, then communities converged, with the sprayed mixture staying distinct longest and richest early on. The authors call coarse spraying a practical, industry-ready delivery route.
pmc-13293476:
Mary Kamillah Grace Reyes and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how artificial intelligence tools help people manage stress on their own, outside clinics. Stress is widespread, yet therapist-led care is limited by capacity, cost, and stigma.

Following standard review steps, the team searched six databases for English studies from 2000 to 2025 and kept 35 of 3008 records found. Quality was checked with a mixed methods tool. Five core roles emerged: direct therapy support, behavior support, teaching, companionship with emotional support, and stress tracking with triage. Early proof looks promising, though the authors stress that evidence is still taking shape.
pmc-13293576:
Mingyue Fan and Binbin Gu build, in a 2026 study, a chart tool to predict when hands-on realignment of a broken wrist will fail. Wrist breaks are very common, and knowing failure risk early can steer patients to the right first treatment.

Records covered 822 patients whose breaks were classed by whether manual realignment worked or failed. Eight factors entered the final model, from break type and swelling to drinking history and time since injury. The tool sorted risk well in internal checks and matched observed outcomes closely. The authors suggest it can support personal treatment choices, though outside testing is still needed to confirm its worth.
pmc-13293776:
Masamitsu Eitoku and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, Japan's notebook health record system for retired workers once exposed to hazardous agents, including migrant workers. Japan's aging population draws more migrant labor, and past exposure can sicken workers long after jobs end.

The scheme, set in law, gives former workers a personal record book and free checkups for 15 named agents or jobs. New books issued for major agents have slowly fallen in recent years. Over two decades, three more agent types joined the scheme, and asbestos rules widened. Public hospitals may serve as checkup sites in workers' home countries, the authors suggest.
pmc-13293876:
Yuan-Hao Mao and coauthors describe a 2026 advance in ring laser gyroscopes, devices that sense rotation from tiny frequency shifts between two beams. At very slow rotation the beams lock together, a flaw that blocks precise sensing. Past fixes add moving parts or extra optics, which hinder small designs. The new approach needs no inserted elements.

Inside a helium-neon device, chiral symmetry breaking and nonlinear pulling bias the system on its own. Experiments showed beam direction switching that followed rotation direction, with a linear response near zero rate. Bias instability reached 2.2 × 10−2 degrees per hour at a 10 s integration time, pointing toward compact high-precision sensors.
pmc-13294276:
Zhenyue Qin and colleagues test a uterus-sparing plan for severe adenomyosis in a 2026 retrospective case series. Care choices hinge on fertility wishes and disease pattern, and the Kishi scan classes sort cases by where growth sits. Their patients wanted no future pregnancy but wished to keep the uterus. Partial removal of diseased tissue was paired with hormone device and drug steps afterward.

All 34 patients treated from December 2017 to October 2022 completed surgery. Pain scores, bleeding scores, hemoglobin, a blood marker, and uterine size all improved clearly after treatment in the reported comparisons. One hormone device slipped downward. Longer follow-up will judge lasting relief.
pmc-13294376:
Niousha Sadjadi and coauthors test how far a species' word-pattern fingerprint stretches across its genome in a 2026 study. Short DNA word frequencies form chaos game pictures that identify species without alignment. Complete chromosome sets from humans and three other eukaryotes from distinct kingdoms were scanned, hunting spots where the local fingerprint strays from the genome-wide one.

Most regions matched the home fingerprint closely. In humans, 80% of half-million-letter segments sat within 0.24 of the chosen reference on a zero-to-one scale in the reported metric. Stray segments clustered where short and long repeat runs pile up. One short reference stretch can thus stand in for most of a genome in sorting tasks.
pmc-13295376:
Laura Franziska Flach, Emilio Sabia, and Thomas Zanon study dairy goat farms in South Tyrol in a 2026 article. Mountain goat keeping supports rural income, old landscapes, and farm diversity under hard conditions. How profits and environmental costs interact on such farms was little documented.

Ten alpine farms shared interview answers and accounting records for the analysis. Full-cost accounts measured money performance, while life cycle methods scored impacts per litre of corrected milk and per hectare. Joining the two views exposes trade-offs that single scores would hide. The framework aims to guide support that lifts both earnings and environmental care in mountain systems.
pmc-13295776:
Katarina Ulfsdotter Gunnarsson, Martin Henriksson, and Marcus Bendtsen simulate lifelong gains from a digital alcohol programme in a 2026 study. Online help for risky drinking can shift behaviour, but whether shifts pay off in health and costs over decades was unclear. A person-level model followed two virtual groups through life.

One group received the digital programme and the other usual care, with ten alcohol-linked diseases tracked. Lasting effects gave the programme group fewer illnesses, slightly more quality-adjusted life years, and lower healthcare costs per person. Gains shrank as the assumed effect faded faster, and vanished when fading ran quickest, stressing proof of lasting change.
pmc-13297076:
Anamaria Violeta Țuțuianu and colleagues examine, in 2026, the home lives behind 333 Romanian children treated for dental neglect between 2020 and 2024. Records from a city hospital and a private practice profile caregivers' age, schooling, income, substance use and family stability.

Most caregivers were young adults, many with little schooling, and nearly half used alcohol. Low income, present in most families, tied closely to dropping out of the treatment plan. Children of drug-using caregivers arrived years later than others, and over half lived in disrupted homes. The authors stress neglect's many-sided roots.
pmc-13298776:
Bone density can be read from ordinary chest scans if the calibration holds up, and Yizhang Tong with colleagues validated an automated phantom-less system in a 2026 prospective study. Among 252 people having routine chest CT, the system measured spinal density at T11 to L1 without a physical reference phantom.

Against phantom-based measurement, results correlated strongly, with r = 0.867, and the system detected osteoporosis with an AUC of 0.962. Manually chosen visceral fat calibration beat the automatic subcutaneous fat choice for spotting early bone loss. Readings stayed consistent across five different scanners. The authors endorse the approach for opportunistic screening during scans done for other reasons.
pmc-13299476:
Cell-shed specks are the skin trade's new hope, and Candelaria Contreras and Amin Ariza-Donado grade that hope in a 2026 review. The specks, sold as exosomes, pass proteins and gene bits from cell to cell.

Trials hint at gains for skin youth, hair growth, wound mend, and dark spot care. Gains may flow through fresh skin frame, new blood paths, and calmer immune fire. The team also asked twelve skin doctors in Colombia how the tools feel in real work. Their word is care: goods swing wide in source and make, hard trials are few, harm has come from goods with no stamp of law, and rules are far from set.
pmc-13299576:
Women may break down one common mood drug through a liver path more fast than men. Janina Eiberger and her team hint at that in a 2026 blood-level study. They mined past blood checks from sick people on one of three mood drugs and set drug break pace by sex, grouped by gene type.

For two drugs worked by the CYP2D6 path, no sex gap showed in 117 and 73 blood sets. For the third drug, escitalopram, worked by CYP2C19, men with the plain gene type held more drug per dose in the blood than women. That hints women clear it more fast. With just 51 sets for that drug, the team call the find a first hint, not a fact, and ask for a big check.
pmc-13300276:
How stem cells guard their glutathione supply changes as they turn toward neurons, Nobuko Matsumura and colleagues show in a 2026 cell study. Working with mouse bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells and neuron-like cells derived from them, the team tracked the cysteine transporter EAAC1 and its brake protein, GTRAP3-18.

Undifferentiated stem cells held more glutathione yet kept EAAC1 mostly off the cell surface, while the derived neuron-like cells relied on it more directly. Removing GTRAP3-18 lowered glutathione in stem cells but raised both EAAC1 and glutathione in neuron-like cells. The split shows redox control is rewired by lineage, a point that matters for stem-cell therapies aimed at nerve repair.
pmc-13300576:
Carbon dioxide calms bees for handling, yet its inner effects vary with age, Ying Wang and two colleagues show in a 2026 proteomics study. They exposed honey bee workers at three life stages, newly emerged, nurse, and forager, then compared protein patterns in hemolymph and brain tissue.

Newly emerged bees proved the hardiest, leaning on chemical defense pathways in both blood and brain. Nurse bees mounted weaker blood responses but guarded the brain first. Foragers instead favored blood detoxification paired with brain energy control. Across all ages, bees shifted energy use to ride out the stress, a finding with practical value for transport and colony care.
pmc-13300876:
In a 2026 retrospective study, Zeynel Mert Asfuroğlu and colleagues find that rebuilt web spaces between fused fingers generally serve patients well for decades. They assessed fifty-three people and ninety reconstructed web spaces after congenital syndactyly surgery. Appearance, hand function, and psychosocial state were scored with the Withey scale, QuickDASH, and a purpose-built survey.

Median follow-up reached ten years, and the typical scores, Withey 2, QuickDASH 14, and psychosocial 29, all sat in the favorable band. Complicated syndactyly fared worse on every measure, and girls reported weaker function and psychosocial results. Surgery between ages one and five and repeat operations also tracked with poorer appearance, guiding family counseling.
pmc-13301176:
Should every aortic repair patient get a heart artery check first? Marwan Hamiko and colleagues examine that habit in a 2026 study of 177 elective thoracic aortic repair patients treated between 2015 and 2025. Half the group received coronary angiography before surgery; survival was tracked for a median of 4.9 years.

The test uncovered new or worsening coronary disease in 44.7 percent of those tested, and 13.6 percent of all patients had their heart arteries treated before repair. Yet hospital deaths and major cardiac events matched the untested group, and long-term survival did not separate either. Coronary disease itself looked deadlier before adjustment, a gap the authors trace to wider artery disease across the body.
pmc-13301376:
As grassland turns to desert, the fungi nursing plant roots swap identity, Xue Wang and colleagues show in a 2026 field study. Along a drying gradient, they sampled rhizosphere soil around Stipa breviflora and Artemisia frigida, sequencing fungi and scoring root colonization. Network analysis and path modeling traced how the community rebuilt itself.

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, the classic root partners, lost diversity and root foothold as dryness deepened. Dark septate endophytes moved the other way, gaining ground in roots and inferred abundance. Fungal networks broke into looser fragments, a shift the models tie to the guild swap itself. Soil usefulness fell too, marking wider decline beneath the visible plants.
pmc-13305176:
Mei An and co-authors review sulfur movement in coal chemical looping combustion in a 2026 synthesis. The clean coal method captures concentrated carbon dioxide with low nitrogen oxide output, but sulfur in coal poisons the oxygen carriers and dirties the gas stream.

Sulfur release during coal heating and gas steps is mapped for two looping styles, and paths that spread sulfur through the system are traced. Rather than merely tolerating sulfur, the authors urge carriers designed to grab it on site. Multi-job oxygen carriers could protect themselves while cleaning the stream, speeding real-world use.
pmc-13306576:
Faouzia Tayari reviewed greener sound-absorbing materials and shapes in a 2026 critical survey. Standard mineral wool and foams soak up sound well but cost heavy energy and rely on non-renewable inputs to produce.

Pore layout, airflow resistance, thickness and layered or resonant shapes all shape performance in the gathered work. Printed structures now allow precise geometry control alongside bio-based and recycled fillings. Weak low-frequency capture, durability and fire safety still limit wider use, so the authors favour hybrid designs that join material and shape gains. The team sees hybrid builds as the best path to green quiet rooms.
pmc-13306976:
Yang Pu searched for signs of heart recovery after drug therapy in newly found dilated cardiomyopathy in a 2026 cohort study. A total of 198 patients began with pumping fraction at or below 35% and received standard guided drug care for three to six months.

Recovery meant pumping fraction climbing back above 35% after treatment in the study definition. Baseline and follow-up scans, heart tracings, clinical notes and lab values fed a prediction model built with a bias-aware regression method. Later heart death and heart failure readmission were also tracked, aiming to flag patients needing closer watch and device review.
pmc-13308676:
Xin Li and co-authors chart in 2026 the load carried by patients in China who start triple inhaler therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Records from Tianjin for 2019 to mid 2023 held 7871 starters, split between one inhaler and many inhaler forms of the triple mix.

Mean age was 65.8 years, and most patients were men who had first gone to a top tier hospital for care. High blood pressure and asthma led the list of side ills at the start date for this group. Use of clinics and hospitals stayed high, and drug cover days sat low at a mean share of 0.35 overall. Better adherence could cut the heavy cost and visit load.
pmc-13309376:
Sandra Furlan Nogueira and colleagues offer a 2026 analysis of nitrous oxide released from farm fertilizer in Brazil. Nitrous oxide is a strong greenhouse gas, and mineral fertilizer accounts for a large share of farm emissions there. Older national counts used broad default factors that may miss local conditions.

The team reviewed 56 papers covering 325 field trials in sugarcane, grain, and pasture systems. They compared climate, biome, soil, and fertilizer type to build sharper emission factors for each system. Pasture and some warm-climate grain and cane fields showed higher factors. The authors argue that local factors give Brazil a fairer and more accurate emissions count.
pmc-13310676:
Hongzhan Cui and co-authors assess hole closure between the heart atria as migraine care in China in a 2026 study. A patent foramen ovale is a flap-like opening left from birth that links to migraine in many patients. Closing it with a catheter device is offered as treatment, yet large real-world Chinese data were scarce.

Records covered 974 migraine patients aged 15 to 65 who had the closure at one hospital between 2020 and 2024, all with sizable right-to-left shunting and high headache impact scores. The responder rate, set at halving headache impact or migraine days, reached 83.98 percent at follow-up in the cohort, with 59.90 percent gaining complete or near-complete relief. Younger age predicted better response. Safety and operator learning effects were also tracked.
pmc-13310776:
Rula Odeh Alsawalqa and co-authors study feelings at work among social workers in Jordan in a 2026 survey. Social work is close and draining, and staff must manage their own feelings while helping others. How the effort to manage feelings links to trouble calming them was little known outside Western settings.

A poll of 132 social workers in Amman found low use of feeling management skills and high trouble with calming feelings. Greater skill use linked to less trouble overall. Women and master degree holders scored higher on skill use, while men reported more calming trouble. Training in these skills may support staff health and service quality.
pmc-13310876:
Xiaoyu Liao and co-authors study a tryptophan byproduct that eases liver swelling and insulin resistance in mice in a 2026 paper. Levels of the compound, called 5MT, fell in obese and diabetic mice and rose after a diabetes drug, which hinted at a guard role. The team tested direct dosing in two mouse models.

Dosed mice showed better insulin response and less liver fat. Blocking a cell sensor removed much of the gain. Gene tests showed the compound raised a signal protein in liver immune cells, and mice lacking that protein in those cells lost the benefit. The path may seed new metabolic drugs.
pmc-13310976:
Hui Li led a 2026 trial of a low dose lung artery scan for suspected lung clots. Standard scans use high radiation and iodine doses, which raise cancer and kidney concerns. A spectral scan with tiny iodine dose and blended injection was tested against standard care.

Patients totaled 160 in number, split evenly between the new and standard scans. Expert readers rated the new scans higher in quality, and key contrast scores stayed above the needed bar. Radiation fell by over two fifths and iodine by two thirds compared with standard care. Clot finding rates were alike. Iodine maps showed flow gaps clearly.
pmc-13311176:
Allison L. Harris and co-authors build whole brain imaging for spreading depolarization in fruit flies in a 2026 study. The wave of nerve shutdown links to migraine, stroke, and brain injury, yet its start and spread rules are hard to watch in large brains. Fly brains allow fast, whole organ views with rich gene tools.

Waves began at many shifting sites across and within flies and spread through the whole nervous system in adults and larvae alike. After one wave, tissue resisted a second wave for a time through a raised threshold that did not depend on shutdown itself. Home balance shifts may explain the pause.
pmc-13311676:
Takahito Miyake, Hideshi Okada, and Norihide Kanda review fat embolism syndrome in a 2026 article. Fat drops entering the blood after injury can harm lungs, brain, and skin, sometimes with fatal results.

The review sums up diagnosis, care, and prevention from English-language work found in PubMed and Scopus up to 2025. Classic sign triads exist, but the illness varies widely and old scoring rules lack solid proof. Chest and brain scans plus new blood markers may sharpen diagnosis, though none is specific. Care stays supportive, early bone fixing within 24 hours prevents best, and steroid use remains in dispute.
pmc-13311976:
Elham Khoori and Tayebe Ziaei write a 2026 commentary on a qualitative study of maternal grief after stillbirth in China, faulting paternalistic medical culture for deepening that grief. A baby born sleeping brings losses across identity and family life.

The discussed study by Zheng and colleagues traced how culture and spirituality shape grief after stillbirth. The commentators urge providers to weigh cultural and spiritual beliefs when designing support for bereaved mothers. They call for studies comparing grief across diverse populations. Their title makes the charge plain: ignoring how staff power and habits affect grieving mothers compounds the harm.
pmc-13312176:
Han Xiao and colleagues report a 2026 study on the receptor RAGE in lung adenocarcinoma growing under low oxygen. Tumors of this common lung cancer type showed reduced RAGE levels, and lower amounts tracked with poorer patient survival, even as hypoxia markers rose inside the tumors.

Experiments gave a split picture. Blocking RAGE slowed cancer cell growth and migration in cell culture, yet inhibiting it sped tumor growth in living animals, where tumors switched on alternative routes to keep progressing. The authors trace the harm to damage-associated molecular pattern signaling, the alarm molecules stressed and dying cells release in oxygen-starved tissue. Their account warns that a target can look protective in a dish yet act differently in a whole tumor, which matters for drug design.
pmc-13313376:
Abida Sanjana Shemonti and a large team present CARGO, a new way to draw and study flow cytometry data, in work published in 2026. Standard plots and maps such as PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP often flatten the rich data from these tests and give weak grounds for firm number work.

CARGO builds a graph where each node is a cell group set by its marker pattern. The gap between groups is gauged by an optimal transport measure called the Sinkhorn distance, and the layout uses a phenotype-aware Hamming distance. The graphs stay true to biology in two dimensions and support direct measurement of how samples differ. The frame gives labs a clearer, more principled view of high-parameter cell data than the usual scatter maps.
pmc-13313476:
Peter Dimitrion and colleagues report in 2026 that the tunnels formed in hidradenitis suppurativa, a painful skin disease, carry a mucosal-like gene pattern. These tunnels grow from burst hair follicles, and odd keratin staining had hinted that their lining cells are reprogrammed by inflammation, but their gene profile was not mapped.

The team used STEREOseq, a spatial method that reads genes at single-cell detail, on sore and healthy skin from one patient with advanced disease. They compared tunnel lining with sore and non-sore outer skin. The tunnel cells showed a gene signature like mucosal surfaces rather than normal skin, a trait that may feed the ongoing inflammation. The finding reframes tunnels as active, mucosa-like tissue and points to new targets for calming this hard disease.
pmc-13314476:
Caitlin Fountain and co-workers test how self-chosen music lifts mood after stress in a 2026 study. Music is more and more used as a low-cost aid for well-being and calm, yet how song type shapes emotion repair after a blow was not well mapped.

The study began with a screen of 795 undergraduate students in the United States, counted in the report, who rated their music tastes. Those ratings built personal playlists of two kinds: upbeat and fast songs meant to empower, and upbeat but slow songs meant to calm. After a social rejection stress task, students heard their music while the team tracked gains in positive feelings and drops in negative ones. The design shows whether picking your own songs, and their tempo, changes how fast mood recovers.
pmc-13316076:
Mengjiao Wang and colleagues propose in 2026 an integrated sustainability hierarchy that crosses topic silos, to close the gap between global pledges and real action. Single-issue fixes stay fragmented and often treat damage downstream instead of preventing it upstream, the authors argue.

Reviewing existing hierarchies for waste, climate, biodiversity, and more, they build a cross-domain compass for policy agendas, finance portfolios, and judging interventions. The ongoing Global Plastics Treaty talks serve as a worked example. The frame offers a practical, theory-based tool for systemic action amid rising social and ecological risk and political backsliding.
pmc-13316276:
Sandro Tiziano Stoffel, Helene Seaward, and Aksha Balakrishnan held focus groups in 2026 with patients to understand why Swiss cancer trials struggle to recruit. Cancer ranks second among causes of death in Switzerland, and about a quarter of randomized trials there stop early, often for low enrollment, wasting resources.

Known barriers include fear of randomization, side effect worry, travel and time load, cost, low awareness, and distrust, while hope of benefit draws others in. Patient voices add lived detail on those trade-offs, pointing to changes in information, logistics, and trust building that could raise participation.
pmc-13316576:
Jin Zhang and Hao Feng report a 2026 case of blood clots found just after a kinked PICC line was straightened in a 78-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy. The line, placed for long-term drug delivery, first blocked, then ran freely after adjustment, then blocked again the next day.

Ultrasound imaging revealed several deep vein clots, a known cause of unplanned line removal that can grow silently. The authors review current guidance and suggest ultrasound checks within the first one to two weeks after placement, plus follow-up scans for high-risk patients. Relying on nurse checks at weekly care visits, they argue, misses early clots that imaging would catch while treatment can still help.
pmc-13316676:
Mitsuru Mizuno and co-authors surveyed, in a 2026 study, how cleanroom monitoring is actually done across regulated factories in Japan, with a focus on regenerative medicine plants. Cell therapy making leans heavily on hand work, so watching air and surfaces for germs is central, yet practice varies.

Fifty-five monitoring staff from six sectors answered a 55-item questionnaire. Statistical grouping showed wide gaps: how often surfaces are checked in mid-grade clean areas, how growth media are tested, and when air particles are counted. Regenerative sites mixed frequent media tests with uneven coverage. The authors say naming the high-impact gaps gives these plants a base for sharper, risk-based monitoring, cleaner records, and better training.
pmc-13317776:
Chungang Zhang, Deyu Fang, and Lin Zhang reframe, in a 2026 review, the blood-brain barrier in Alzheimer's disease around its sugar-rich skin. That layer, the endothelial glycocalyx, faces the blood and decides what passes. Leakiness alone, they argue, is too crude a lens for this interface.

They sort the evidence, strong in mice and thin in humans, and propose grading the interface on four axes: structure, sugar pattern, transport, and inflammation. Damage looks patchy, with early loss of one domain rather than wholesale shedding. A repair window may stay open in APOE4 carriers and early memory loss, then close when vessel amyloid joins. Their order of attack: repair first, engineer transport second, exploit last.
pmc-13318076:
Katlin T Wilson, Areeba H Rizvi, and Kevin O Turner describe a 2026 case of collagenous gastroduodenitis in a previously healthy 13-year-old girl who arrived with severe tiredness and breathlessness on effort. The rare stomach disorder lays down a thick collagen band under the gut lining alongside chronic inflammation.

Tissue samples from stomach and duodenum matched not one but three overlapping patterns at once: collagenous sprue, collagenous gastritis, and chronic atrophic gastritis. The authors say such a triple meeting is highly uncommon in children. Because causes remain unknown and care is limited to watching and easing symptoms, each well-documented case sharpens ideas about how the disease starts and what targeted treatment might one day do.
pmc-13318576:
Ampuan Shazani bin Ampuan Haji Sadikin and Heru Susanto offer a 2026 security study. It is set in Brunei's instant payment system. They test a two-layer shield for payment data. The shield pairs AES-128 encryption with hiding data inside audio. Interviews with national cyber and payment bodies fed into the work.

Human mistakes drove 47 percent of the security concerns identified in the study. One local bank also took part in the interviews. The audio hiding method survived most attack scenarios tried. It survived 87.5 percent of eight scenarios in the testing. Average processing time was 568.82 ms per task, with sound quality still acceptable. The method also worked inside a test payment flow. The authors argue inner protection can compensate where people remain the weak point.
pmc-13318676:
Siyu Zhou and colleagues review, in 2026, new inhaled drug platforms for lung diseases. Swallowed or injected drugs often lose strength before reaching the lungs. They can also cause harm elsewhere in the body. Breathing a drug in gives faster, more targeted delivery.

The review covers nanoparticles, liposomes, and microspheres for inhalation. It also covers platforms that mimic natural biological carriers. Uses span asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumonia, fibrosis, and lung cancer. Inhaled forms spread evenly and start working quickly. They also avoid the liver first-pass effect that weakens oral drugs. The authors see broad prospects for safer, stronger lung treatments built on nanotechnology and new materials.
pmc-13318876:
Antonella Mosca and colleagues present a 2026 case report with a narrative review on allergy arising after childhood liver transplant. New IgE-mediated food allergy and asthma are recognised problems in young recipients. Their patient was a 15-year-old boy transplanted at 28 days old for newborn liver failure. He later developed severe asthma and multiple food allergies.

Repeated anaphylaxis and strict food avoidance were harming his growth. At age ten, doctors started off-label omalizumab treatment. His asthma came under excellent control, and background medicines were stopped. His diet became far less restricted. Liver graft function stayed stable throughout, with no graft problems over more than five years of follow-up. The authors present the drug as safe and effective in this setting.
pmc-13320376:
Kai Li and Grit Walther present a cleaned data set on fast fashion clothes in a 2026 data article for reuse research. Sorting and recycling studies need item level facts on what each garment is made of, split by color, yet shop data is messy and audits cover few goods. Pages from two big chains selling in Britain and Australia were scraped and harmonized into one shared shape.

After cleaning and checks, the set holds 47522 color level garment records, each with source links, shop and region, item name, color, and fabric shares split by garment part. Fabric names and garment classes were mapped to shared terms for fair counts. Photos, raw page grabs, and shopper reviews were left out of the public set. The files may aid sorting, recycling, and green audits.
pmc-13321376:
Runrou Wong and Seo-Jin Chung set out to standardise how sweetness strength is measured in a 2026 sensory study. Tasters rated sweeteners across strengths, and the team compared serving methods, sample order, and two rating scales. One scale, the generalized Labeled Magnitude Scale, lets people rate against their strongest past sensations.

Protocols using that scale gave truer strength curves and resisted context bias far better than a 15 point category scale. The category scale overstated strength at low doses, above all for intense sweeteners. Mixing sucrose into serving added little once the magnitude scale was used, and serving order did not move its readings. A shared protocol could make sweetener claims comparable across labs.
pmc-13322076:
Colin J Shew and co-authors study gene control switches in human specific duplicated DNA in a 2026 report. Segmental duplications hold millions of letters found only in humans, including genes shaping brain growth. Though under six million years old, duplicated genes already show wide differences in activity between copies.

Using long read data, the team found human specific copies tend to run quieter than ancestral ones. A mass reporter test of 7760 duplicated and chimpanzee matching stretches found 14 to 24 percent with differing activity, mostly by small amounts. Predicted switch activity tracked gene output in nerve cells, and checks on three genes supported copy specific expression patterns.
pmc-13322876:
Jianting Wen and Jian Liu review Tripterygium wilfordii and Xinfeng capsule for rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2026 article weighing benefit against harm. The plant has a long history in traditional use for this joint disease, and its tablets and capsule forms are widely studied in China.

Lab work links its compounds to signals such as NF-kB and PI3K/AKT/mTOR, to inflammasome activity, joint lining growth, blood vessel growth and immune cell faults. Clinical reports suggest gains in disease activity, joint symptoms and inflammation markers, alone or with standard drugs. Wider multi-part action in the capsule may raise benefit and lower toxicity, yet safety worries, weak large trials and poor standard dosing still limit use.
pmc-13325376:
Anand U. Kyatanwar and Bala R. Prabhakar test whether blended polymers can match single-grade polymers in peptide microspheres in a 2026 study. Peptide drugs need carriers that shield them and release them slowly, but top-grade polymers are scarce and pricey.

Two shelf polymers, R202H and RG502H, were mixed in varied ratios to mimic custom grades. Microspheres loaded with the heart drug eptifibatide were made from blends and from plain shelf polymers. Both sets performed the same on structure and release in side-by-side checks. The match matters because blending stocked grades skips costly custom synthesis. Peptide delivery projects gain a cheaper formulation path without giving up quality.
pmc-13327876:
Wan Qin and co-authors probe why students grow bored in AI-assisted English learning in a 2026 survey study. Boredom can drain drive and results, and a growth mindset is thought to soften it, but the path in AI settings was untested. The team followed 536 first-year university students in eastern China across three waves, two months apart.

Mindset was measured first, then AI literacy and confidence in using AI, and finally boredom. A growth mindset predicted stronger AI literacy and confidence, and both of those predicted less boredom, while mindset alone showed no direct link to boredom. AI literacy also fed confidence, forming a chain that teachers can build on by training skills, not just attitudes.
pmc-13328176:
Yi Zhao and co-authors trace how a mother's low iron may slow a newborn's hearing development in a 2026 study. Data from 696 mother-infant pairs were joined with pregnant mouse models and cochlear tissue experiments. Iron shortage without anemia is common in pregnancy, and its hearing effects were unclear.

Higher maternal ferritin and hemoglobin went with faster auditory brain responses in newborns, and newborn ferritin carried part of that link, with mediation shares from 28.57 to 76.32 percent across the measures reported. Iron-short mouse pups showed weaker, slower responses, fewer ribbon synapses in inner ear hair cells, and damaged mitochondria, while added pyruvate partly restored synapse function. Energy failure in support cells is the proposed chain.
pmc-13329376:
Philipp Schenk and a large study group report in 2026 on bone drug care for inpatients with spine breaks from weak bones. Such drugs help prevent further breaks but are often missed. Data came from the prospective EOFTT study, with 518 patients in 17 clinics who had breaks in the chest or lower spine area.

Hospital stay raised treatment a lot: among women the share rose from 36 percent at entry to 83 percent in the reported results, with a smaller rise in men. Months later, shares fell sharply again for both sexes. Calcium and vitamin D use followed the same rise and fall. Proven bone drugs stayed rare. The authors flag long-term follow-up as the weak point in care.
pmc-13331176:
Ali Hammed and colleagues pool trials on surgery for bleeding inside the brain in a 2026 meta-analysis. Whether removing the clot beats drug care alone has long been debated. The pool held 29 randomised trials with 5,531 patients, comparing surgery with standard medical care on function and death.

Surgery linked to better function and lower death overall in the pooled odds given. Turned into plain terms, gains ran near 6 to 7 extra good outcomes per 100 patients in the authors' worked examples. Surgery inside 24 hours gave the largest gains, with a clear timing interaction for function but not for death. Site, size, and technique showed no firm modifying effect in their checks.
pmc-13332476:
AE Carolus and colleagues describe GripAgain, a 2026 mobile app project supporting hand training after nerve surgery. Recovery of grip and fine movement shapes quality of life after such operations, and the team's earlier work showed intense targeted training speeds recovery.

Built with FlutterFlow for the interface and Firebase behind it, with data security addressed throughout, the app packages 21 exercise videos with progress tracking meant to keep patients engaged between clinic visits. The team compared it with current therapy apps on friendliness and content and gathered feedback from varied users. Judged competitive on usability and function, it still needs better tailoring of plans and stronger long-term motivation features. The authors conclude the app can carry current treatment pathways into patients' homes.
pmc-13333376:
Ke Wang and colleagues packaged a protective drug into clay-like nanoparticles in 2026 to stop acute kidney injury from hardening into chronic kidney disease. Butylphthalide guards organs in principle, but the body clears it fast and absorbs it poorly, so little reaches injured kidneys.

Their layered double hydroxide carrier released the drug faster in mild acidity, matching the sour conditions inside damaged, scarring kidney tubules. In rats with one kidney injured by a blocked-then-restored blood supply, the loaded particles eased kidney dysfunction, curbed scar tissue, and restored mitochondrial health. Human kidney cells provoked with a scarring signal answered the same way. Blocking mitophagy, the cell's mitochondrial cleanup program, erased every benefit, proving that route central.
