Gene signals pointed to the PINK1-Parkin pathway as the switch the treatment turns on. The authors present the system as a translatable strategy against the injury-to-chronic slide.
pmc-13333476:
Yue Li and co-authors document a bladder cancer mistaken for a bowel one in a 2026 case report with a review of cases. Primary mucinous adenocarcinoma of the bladder is rare and aggressive. Because it looks glandular, proving it did not spread from the gut is the diagnostic battle.

Their patient, a 70-year-old woman, had difficulty urinating but no blood in the urine. A marker panel pointed away from a colorectal origin: CK7 negative, CK20 and CDX-2 positive, beta-catenin staining confined to the membrane, and SATB2 and GATA3 negative. Endoscopy found no gut tumor. She had a transurethral resection, then robot-assisted removal of the bladder, staged pT4aN0M0, and declined treatment. Six months on she remained free of recurrence or spread. The authors use the case to show how a marker panel secures the diagnosis, and how treatment choices get made without guidelines.
pmc-13333676:
Jianpeng Liu and co-authors translated an AI literacy questionnaire for China's pre-service teachers and validated the adapted scale in a 2026 study. The work tests whether the scale measures what it should and whether teacher profiles differ in useful ways.

The sample held 341 pre-service teachers from Guangdong Province, most of them women in their third year. Factor analyses supported a 24-item scale with five parts: AI ethics, behavioral commitment, self-efficacy, cognitive application, and intrinsic motivation. Reliability and validity checks were supportive, and three parts of the scale correlated with how much teachers integrated AI into teaching. A profile analysis sorted respondents into four groups, from overall high to overall low, giving teacher educators a basis for tailored support.
pmc-13333776:
Tim Ho and Mark Ryan propose a new model of chronic pain in a 2026 narrative review, treating it as a state-constrained disorder of brain networks. Imaging reliably shows altered salience, default mode, and central executive networks in persistent pain, yet older models explain its stubbornness poorly.

Their triple-network account adds body-level regulation to the picture. Sleep organization, autonomic balance, and interoceptive signals continually shape how the three networks interact. When regulation falters, salience processing tilts toward bodily threat and the networks settle into a stable pattern that keeps self-focused pain processing going. Viewed through dynamical systems, chronic pain becomes a locked-in attractor state. The framing suggests treatments, including brain stimulation, should aim to loosen that state rather than silence one region.
pmc-13335076:
Alexandra Lecours and co-authors studied telework used as a health accommodation in a 2026 qualitative study, centered on the relationship between employee and manager. Workers with chronic illness or caregiving duties often need changes to stay employed, and remote work became a common one after the pandemic.

Two focus groups brought 12 people together, eight workers with chronic illness and four caregivers, in an interpretive descriptive design. Four themes named friction points with managers: negotiating the accommodation itself, day-to-day running of telework, honoring boundaries, and keeping social ties alive. The findings argue that telework succeeds as an accommodation mainly when the manager relationship is strong, since flexibility and trust are worked out there.
pmc-13335676:
Qiannan Jia and co-authors characterized cutaneous mastocytosis in Chinese patients in a 2026 ten-year pathology study. The disease, driven by mast cell buildup in skin, varies widely in form, and its detailed features in Chinese patients were poorly mapped.

The cohort held 88 patients diagnosed by skin biopsy in a dermatology department between 2015 and 2024. Mast cell burden tracked with subtype: lowest in telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans, higher in urticaria pigmentosa, and highest in diffuse disease and mastocytoma. Heavy burden also went with raised lesions and earlier onset. Staining patterns for CD2, CD25, and CD30 differed by subtype and clustered with high-burden disease, offering diagnostic clues. The authors highlight easily neglected features that pathologists should watch for.
pmc-13336676:
Chen Wang and a large team investigate a receptor called GPR124 after traumatic brain injury in a 2026 study. Brain injury is a top cause of death among young adults, and damage to the blood-brain barrier worsens outcomes. The team mapped where GPR124 appears using single-cell data and a controlled impact model in mice.

Mice lacking GPR124 in vessel-lining cells recovered worse, and stretched cells without it worked poorly in lab tests. Tight seals between vessel cells broke down when the receptor was reduced. The receptor partners with a binding protein to switch on the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway. Supporting this receptor could help protect the barrier and improve recovery after head injury.
pmc-13336876:
Xiaolin Li and a large team pack six health sensors onto one tiny photonic chip in a 2026 study. Light-based sensors can track glucose, pressure, temperature, and heart signals, but separate devices are hard to combine. Their polymer chip, about 1 cm by 0.5 cm in footprint in the prototype, merges grating sensors with an on-chip unit that reads them all.

Tests showed stable ranges for blood glucose from 0 to 2.3 mg/mL, pressure from 0 to 12 kPa, and temperature from 35 to 41°C in bench checks. A sweat glucose sensor covered 0–0.2 mg/mL with strong linearity in tests. The heart-signal sensor matched commercial gear. All-in-one chips could anchor future wearable health monitors.
pmc-13336976:
Sihao Wu and a large team build artificial skin from display transistor technology in a 2026 study. Their active skin uses thin-film transistors, a mass-production process on large sheets, as its base. Each touch pixel mixes light and electric-field sensing to extract richer contact features than either mode alone.

A 10×10 sample fitted within 1 cm2 read Braille patterns in validation tests. It kept 81.7% accuracy on hard fingerprint tasks even with 45% of information lost in stress tests. A fully wrapped robot hand with varied pixel density recognized objects by texture and shape while moving 80% less data and cutting computing cost by 76.6% in the reported system. Transistor skin could cover whole robot bodies.
pmc-13338676:
David M Huebner leads a 2026 trial protocol for a web program helping parents support gay and bisexual teen sons. Most teen HIV infections in the United States follow male-to-male contact, yet few proven programs target this group. Talking with parents about sex can lower risk, but no parent program for these teens had been trialed.

The PATHS program teaches parents to discuss sexuality and HIV and to support their sons' health. A total of 350 parents recruited online will be assigned at random to PATHS or a control path. Teen health outcomes at 6 and 12 months are the test, with parent behavior changes checked as the pathway.
pmc-13339876:
Cheng-Ta Li and colleagues use brainwave patterns plus machine learning to sort depression features in a 2026 exploratory study. Depression varies in severity, treatment resistance, and suicide risk, usually judged by subjective scales. Frontal brain networks are implicated, so EEG offered an objective angle.

Resting and task-based EEG from 209 patients fed several classifiers after a frontal-engaging thinking task. Random forest models led, reaching about 83 percent accuracy for severity and 87 percent for treatment resistance in the reported results. Suicide risk classification used balanced training to handle rare cases. Brain signatures may one day support, not replace, clinical judgment.
pmc-13340676:
Dental implants placed decades after a childhood jaw disorder settled down are described by Mergime P. Loxha and colleagues in a 2026 case report with 23 years of follow-up. The patient had cherubism, a rare condition that expands both jaws in childhood and often eases after puberty.

Long monitoring confirmed the disease had stabilized before guided implant surgery was done without bone grafting. The implants integrated well, and the prosthetic result stayed stable, restoring chewing and facial appearance. The authors argue that waiting for skeletal maturity and disease quiet, then planning treatment case by case, can make implant rehabilitation work for chosen patients.
pmc-13340776:
Spotting drug-resistant tumor cells by imaging an enzyme inside them is the aim of a 2026 study by Xin-Yu Luo and colleagues. The enzyme, MGMT, repairs chemotherapy damage and helps explain why resistance drives roughly 90% of cancer deaths.

The team built a tetrahedral DNA framework carrying four identical probes. Each probe senses MGMT, switches on a DNAzyme, and releases a fluorescent signal once the enzyme removes a methyl lesion. The scaffold's tight spacing made signals in resistant cells over three times stronger than in sensitive ones. Such a platform could support earlier detection of resistance and closer study of how it develops.
pmc-13341476:
Sorting stroke from other causes of lasting vertigo is the aim of a 2026 prediction model by Yue Ba and colleagues. The retrospective study covered 689 patients whose vertigo lasted over 24 hours, of whom 165 (23.9%) had clinically diagnosed strokes.

Regularized regression picked predictors including older age, smoking, hypertension, high lipids, and diabetes, with hypertension carrying an odds ratio of 5.452. Internal validation used cross-validation and bootstrapping, and the model was benchmarked against the ABCD2, CNS, and Triage-Plus scores. A bedside tool like this could speed imaging decisions when vertigo might hide a stroke.
pmc-13342876:
I Andriot and a large team present a 2026 dataset on how aroma compounds escape from food-like systems over time. Flavor release shapes taste perception, and lab models let researchers vary heat or container size in ways real eating does not allow, so the team tracked release under controlled settings.

Across 84 experiments, two aroma compounds, isoamyl acetate and diacetyl, were measured in water or gelatin discs with a proton transfer reaction mass spectrometer. Conditions varied in temperature, starting amount, and settling time before measurement. Files pair raw time-series readings with full details on products, compounds, and instrument settings, giving modelers clean data for linking signal strength to real concentration.
pmc-13345376:
Steven L Zeng and co-authors compare wound dressings after breast reduction surgery in a 2026 review of 250 patients covering 439 breasts. Dressing choice varies with little shared evidence, so the team tallied skin reactions, wound splitting, reoperations, and scarring across six dressing types used at one institution.

Groups started uneven, largely because Prineo patients carried more risk, and removing that group cleared most baseline gaps. Sylke tape predicted lower skin reaction and wound splitting in adjusted models, with odds roughly halved or better. Prineo tracked with more reoperations and poor scarring, though patient selection clouds that signal. The authors call for prospective trials before dressings get ranked firmly.
pmc-13347076:
Chengcheng Yu and co-authors test whether adding a large language model helps peer teaching in orthopaedic training, in a cohort study from 2026. Two student groups at a Hangzhou teaching hospital were compared. One group held 96 students taught the usual way in 2024. The other held 94 students given access to DeepSeek-V3 as support in 2025.

Outcomes covered a 50-item knowledge test, a four-station skills exam, engagement and satisfaction ratings, and retention after three months, all scored with shared rubrics. Peer teaching is praised for closeness but faulted for uneven quality, so the study asks whether on-demand model help can steady knowledge support without replacing student teachers. Full comparative results follow the setup described here.
pmc-13347776:
Hussein N Yassine and a large team test high-dose fish oil in older adults at risk for dementia, in a randomised trial published in 2026. The 24-month study at the University of Southern California enrolled adults aged 55 to 80 years without dementia who ate little DHA, giving 2 g per day of DHA or placebo. A willing subgroup also gave spinal fluid checks.

Of 739 people screened, 365 were randomised, and DHA raised the spinal fluid DHA ratio by a clear margin at six months against placebo in the reported result. Brain size and thinking scores showed no treatment gap over two years, dropout reached 38 percent. Side effects looked alike across arms, so brain entry is proven while benefit stays open.
pmc-13348076:
Ting Lin and colleagues follow pulse pressure and the march of heart-metabolic disease in UK Biobank, in a cohort study from 2026. A total of 403,851 adults free of such disease at entry were tracked for first illness, spread to two or more of diabetes, heart disease. Stroke, and death, with pulse width scored per standard step and by quarters.

Each step up in pulse pressure raised the hazard of first illness and of spread in the reported models. The top quarter carried 36 percent higher risks than the bottom quarter for both steps. The spread link ran strongest after stroke and in younger, female, and leaner groups, arguing for early pulse checks.
pmc-13350476:
Soetkin D'Haens and co-authors reviewed real-world use of a strong chemotherapy combination before surgery for pancreatic cancer in a 2026 single-centre study. Eighty-one patients with borderline removable or locally advanced tumours received FOLFIRINOX or a softened version between 2020 and 2023.

The median number of cycles delivered was six, and most patients had good fitness scores at entry. The team recorded doses, serious side effects, and why treatment stopped; surgery was the commonest reason, accounting for 45 patients. Pre-surgery chemotherapy is spreading, but its toxicity and delays are real, and honest completion numbers help design fair trials of the strategy.
pmc-13350676:
Yao Peng and colleagues built a risk model in 2026 for predicting newborn breathing distress from mid-pregnancy placenta scans. They studied 362 women scanned at a Xiangyang hospital between 2021 and 2024. Fifty-eight of their babies developed the syndrome.

Three-dimensional Doppler measures of placental vessel density and flow were gathered. Standard artery readings and mothers' clinical details were added. Together they fed a scoring chart for personal risk. Current antenatal checks guess this risk only crudely, with little basis in body function. A better forecast lets delivery teams prepare breathing support in advance. It also helps choose where a baby should be born.
pmc-13351276:
Bonnie Alberry and colleagues studied how poor metabolic conditions before birth rewire insulin responses in the brain's reward centre in a 2026 rodent study. Growth-restricted fetuses are known to carry lifelong changes in body and brain insulin sensitivity, but effects on reward circuits were unclear.

In their model, food reward triggered a blunted dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, a deficit that insulin specifically reversed, and the animals also ate palatable food faster at first. Gene activity in the reward centre was profiled at birth, weaning, and adulthood, with and without insulin. Early metabolic stress appears to programme how the brain values food, with lasting taste for quick reward.
pmc-13351476:
Rogerson and colleagues speak with shift workers who make food in United Kingdom plants. The study asks what helps or blocks healthy eating at work. Eleven workers took part in online talks. Most were men with long shift records. Eight themes came out. Workers knew what healthy food was. What they ate still bent toward what was fast and close at hand. Breaks were short and not safe to use in full.

Plant rules on hygiene and safety shut off some food choices. Night shifts made fresh food hard to find. The team says plants must first fix access and breaks. Only then can coaching on food choices help staff.
pmc-13351876:
Hua Sun and co-authors compare two ways of clearing older patients for lung surgery in a 2026 cohort study. Many patients are turned down because breathing tests look poor. From 2022 to 2024, patients first had standard breathing tests, and those with weak results went on to exercise testing before a decision.

In total, 130 older patients had surgery, with 71 in the breathing-test group and 59 in the exercise-test group. Complication rates were close, at 23.94 percent versus 25.42 percent, with no clear difference. Hospital stay and chest tube time did differ between groups. Results suggest exercise testing can safely widen access to surgery for patients with weak breathing tests.
pmc-13352176:
Ding-Tian Yu, Si-Si Xie, and Cheng-Guo Duan study how chromatin changes steer immune gene switching in Arabidopsis in 2026. Plant defence depends on fast rewriting of gene activity, but the chromatin controls behind it stay unclear. The team combined RNA, chromatin, and access profiling after treatment with salicylic acid or the peptide flg22.

Each signal reshaped chromatin and gene activity in its own broad pattern. Salicylic acid raised two activating histone marks together at defence sites, while flg22 worked mainly through one mark. Open chromatin tracked closely with active defence genes. Network checks highlighted NPR1, ICS1, and PR1 as hubs. Results show two signals can reach defence through partly separate chromatin routes.
pmc-13352376:
Hongqiang Li and co-authors profile the chemistry of eggs from five poultry species in 2026. Eggs are a rich nutrient source, and knowing species differences can guide production and new products. Chicken, duck, goose, quail, and pigeon eggs were split into yolk and white and screened with untargeted metabolomics.

Analysis found 519 differing compounds in yolks and 312 in whites across species, spanning lipids, ring compounds, and benzenoids. Yolk networks showed tighter grouping than white networks. Transport and amino acid pathways stood out as enriched routes. Machine learning picked 9 candidate markers that may separate species, though the authors say outside validation with targeted tests is still required.
pmc-13352476:
Jingnan Xue and colleagues report a 2026 surgical case of thyroid tissue found beside the bile duct. Misplaced thyroid tissue is uncommon, and spots near the gallbladder are extremely rare, yet such lumps can mimic bile or gallbladder tumours. A 50-year-old woman had 2 years of on-and-off pain in the upper right belly.

Scans showed a dense lump of 22 by 14 mm at the liver hilum next to the gallbladder neck. She declined further imaging for cost reasons and asked for surgery. Keyhole removal took the gallbladder and lump together, and tissue study showed benign mature thyroid follicles. Her own thyroid gland was normal, and she stayed symptom-free after surgery.
pmc-13353876:
Ayako Ijuin and colleagues test a multi-constriction nanopore called Epx4 for single-molecule protein reading in 2026. Nanopores sense molecules label-free as they pass through, and extra narrow points can sharpen signals. Epx4 is a pore-forming toxin with two separate barrels and up to four constrictions along its path.

In single-molecule runs, Epx4 caught positively charged polypeptides more often than the standard alpha-hemolysin pore. Machine learning on its signals reached an area under the curve of 0.82 and an F1 score of 0.72, both above the standard pore. Geometry checks confirmed the multi-grip layout. The authors propose Epx4 as a strong base for accurate protein sensors.
pmc-13354576:
Nidal H Abu-Hamdeh and co-authors used computer models in 2026 to test ways to speed up cold storage freezing. Their design used a ring-shaped tank, metal foam, a fluid with tiny mixed particles, and heat rays to move cold through the space. A math model tracked the line between liquid and solid as freezing went on.

Metal foam gave the biggest gain, cutting freezing time by about 79 percent in the model. Heat rays cut the time by about 23 percent, and the special fluid added a smaller gain. The work points to foam as a strong tool for fridges, air cooling, and other cold storage uses.
pmc-13355276:
Avinav Bharati and co-authors tested three AI chatbots in 2026 on questions about medical physics in cancer care. Experts wrote 11 questions and put each to ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, asking each one twice. Three experts then scored the answers for correctness, completeness, ease of reading, trust, and fit for local practice.

DeepSeek scored highest on correctness and gave the most complete answers, at ten of eleven questions. Still, no chatbot matched human skill on any measure, and scores for real-world use did not differ much. The authors argue that chatbots should support medical staff, not replace them, in a paired way of working.
pmc-13357076:
Ming Yan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how targeted drugs perform when bowel cancer spreads to the liver, a leading cause of death in these patients. Such targeted therapy is now common, but its exact gains in survival, shrinkage, and surgery chances were unclear. They pooled randomized trials and cohort studies found in four databases through July 2025.

Thirty-four studies with 12,084 patients showed targeted therapy lengthened overall and progression-free survival and raised response rates. It also increased the chance of surgery to remove liver tumors, most clearly in first-line and marker-selected patients. Severe side effects were more common but manageable. The authors support targeted drugs within team-based, precision care.
pmc-13358476:
Ya Wang and co-authors present a 2026 review of breathing support for acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe lung failure. Machines that breathe for patients can also harm the lungs if each breath is too big. Doctors already use small breaths; the team asked if even smaller breaths help more.

They combined six studies with 1,102 patients that compared ultra-low with low breath sizes. Most patients on the smallest breaths also used life-support machines that take over gas exchange for the lungs. The review weighs the gain in lower lung stress against the risks of extra machines, to guide care in intensive care units.
pmc-13358576:
Xuanyu Zhu and co-authors present a 2026 study on a warning sign in early lung cancer. Some tumors shed cells into nearby air spaces, a pattern called spread through air spaces. It raises the risk of the cancer coming back, yet doctors can only confirm it after surgery. The team built computer models to predict it before the operation.

They used records and CT scans from 445 patients with the earliest stage of non-small cell lung cancer. Machine learning models weighed scan traits and patient facts to sort likely cases. A good forecast matters because it can steer the choice between a small, lung-saving cut and a larger, safer one.
pmc-13362776:
Maryam Choulli and a large team report a 2026 study of throat cancer patients at three Barcelona hospitals, asking whether nutrition at diagnosis forecasts early response to curative treatment. The virus HPV splits this cancer into types with different outlooks. The team measured body size, muscle from scans, fitness tests, blood markers, and a standard nutrition score in 101 patients before therapy began.

Among virus-positive patients, the nutrition score split outcomes clearly: about three quarters with good scores cleared the cancer early, versus a third with poor scores. Among virus-negative patients, fitness level and age split outcomes instead. Muscle scans and blood markers added nothing once nutrition and fitness counted. Diet care at diagnosis may thus help, the authors suggest.
pmc-13363576:
Xiangjun Kong, Xia Wang, and Wulan Zeng present a 2026 review of nanostructured catalysts for clean energy conversion, covering both electric and light-driven reactions. These tiny engineered materials sit at the heart of water splitting, fuel cells, and carbon dioxide reuse. The review follows five catalyst families, from single metals to single-atom designs, and the recipes that shape them with care.

Five levers for better performance get close treatment: shape, doping, layered junctions, defects, and supports. For each key reaction, the authors name the measures that best predict success. Their verdict is pointed: raw activity is rarely the bottleneck now; holding performance under harsh, factory-grade loads is. Earth-abundant stand-ins for precious metals get special attention.
pmc-13365476:
Udomsak Saengow and co-workers set in 2026 how folks with long ills in south Thailand smoke, by zone: leaf grow zones and plain zones. They ask 879 patients face to face from care lists in both zone types. Hand rolled leaf rolls rule use, more so in grow zones.

Near one in five had smoked at some point, and all but a few past smokers were men. Smokers show high lung ill rates and more care stays per year. Grow zone life and more house cash lift smoke odds, while women smoke far less. Rules must face cheap leaf reach in farm towns.
pmc-13371876:
Amaya Daniels and co-authors tell of a huge gallstone that moved in an odd way in a 2026 case report. An 82-year-old woman had a drain tube path from her gallbladder to her skin. Such paths are used when surgery is too risky for a sick patient.

A stone about 65 mm long moved through the path and got stuck just under the skin. Scans can miss how much hard stone sits in such a lump, the team warns. They cut the path open and took the stone out, and her symptoms eased fast. The case is said to be the first of its kind with a stone this large.
pmc-13372376:
Eanna Johnston and co-authors built a fine eye scan to track burns in a 2026 study. Alkali burns are a harsh type of eye harm and can blind. Plain scans see shape well but miss tiny shifts in the clear front window of the eye.

The new scan reads light in a way that picks up shifts far below the plain scan's limit. The team used it on a burn model and on care with cell-based drops. Scan shifts tracked harm and heal steps as they changed. A tool that watches heal steps without touch could help eye teams time care and test new drops in trials.
pmc-13373676:
Shuroog Nabhan and co-authors summed up switch data for a gut drug and its copies in a 2026 review. The drug calms bowel swelling, and cheaper copies are now in wide use. Doubts stay on what switch steps do to health in daily care.

The search found seven studies with 5,721 adults in all. Three were planned ahead, three looked back, and one took a one-time snapshot. Watch time ran from six months to just over two years. The sum-up weighs if health held firm after a switch, and in which ways. Such proof helps clinics and patients trust a switch made to cut costs.
pmc-13374176:
Li Zhang and co-authors mapped a view-sort method in long ill work in a 2026 review. The method asks people to sort views into piles, which shows how groups truly see a point. It suits the mix of tales that long ills bring, where one fixed plan fits few.

The team used firm review steps and searched four data banks to late 2025. Each past use was logged for its ask, its craft twists, and its gains. Use has spread across many long ills, from pain to heart and mind care. The map shows where the method shines and where reports are thin, to guide new work.
pmc-13374276:
Caiping Liu and co-authors linked long calm-drug use to thought skill in a 2026 study in China. The drugs in view calm nerves and aid sleep, and are often used long in mind care. The group came from a large watch study of a grave mind ill.

Fifty-seven long users were matched to 57 non-users by age, sex, ill span, and main drugs. A set test scored thought, and scales scored signs, weight of ill, and daily life skill. Long users scored worse on thought tests in the match. The team says long use should be weighed with care, and thought should be checked in this group.
pmc-13379376:
Noel George, Usha Arcot, and Bruntha Devi Palanisamy published a 2026 mathematics paper on six common plastics, treated as chains of repeating units. They use a formula called the M-polynomial, which captures the structure of a molecular graph in algebraic form. From that single formula, many numerical measures of structure can be derived.

The plastics covered are polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon-6,6, and PET. For each chain the authors work out the formula as a function of chain length, then compute eleven standard measures, including the Zagreb and Randic indices. Graphs comparing the plastics show how the measures grow and differ, which can help predict material properties from structure alone.
pmc-13379976:
Yecheng Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study of blood sugar stress measures in critically ill patients with heart failure. Illness can push blood sugar up sharply, and that rise is linked with worse outcomes. One measure corrects the rise for a patient's usual sugar level, but people differ in how their blood sugar marks long-term control.

Records for 2,488 patients came from three intensive care databases. The team grouped patients by a glycation index, which captures that personal difference, and tracked how the stress measure changed over time against death rates. The link between the stress measure and death differed across the groups, so the same reading may not mean the same risk for every patient.
pmc-13382776:
Eric N. Enyong and co-authors examine caveolin-1 outside its usual membrane pockets in retinal support cells in 2026 work. In Müller glia, the main support cells of the retina, caveolin-1 is plentiful while its pocket-forming partner is scarce. Microscopy confirmed that the flask-shaped pockets themselves are almost absent in these cells.

Without pockets, caveolin-1 boosted signals from a bacterial sensor and raised levels of the messenger IL-6 after stimulation. Silencing the protein, or forcing pockets to form, calmed that response. In vessel cells where pockets are normal, silencing had the opposite effect, a contrast that may guide care for inflamed eye disease.
pmc-13386876:
Benjamin Hafey and Liangqi Xie review hybrid viral-human DNA circles in HPV-driven cancers in a 2026 article. When human papillomavirus integrates into host DNA, it can spawn circular elements mixing viral and human stretches. Such hybrids appear in roughly 30 percent of HPV-linked throat cancers, with parallels in cervical cancer models.

The circles amplify viral drivers together with captured human genes and build new enhancer hubs from scratch. They also drive very high gene output and can act as roaming activators elsewhere in the genome. The authors discuss how these traits may open treatment angles tailored to hybrid-carrying tumors.
pmc-13386976:
Erasmus N. Kotey and a large team build a glowing, traceable version of a monkey virus related to Epstein-Barr in 2026 work. Rhesus lymphocryptovirus mirrors human EBV infection in macaques, making it a prized vaccine test model. Until now it lacked the green fluorescent tag that speeds EBV cell tracking in the lab.

The engineered virus kept its full genome intact and infected blood cells from several primate species. A mutant missing the entry protein gp350 infected B cells and surface cells far less well in their tests. That result confirms gp350 as the key to entry, matching its human counterpart.
pmc-13391476:
Nadja Deflorin and colleagues run, in 2026, a randomised crossover trial on whether a short trip to low altitude improves night breathing for people who live higher up. Sleep-disordered breathing is common at moderate altitude, where thinner air lowers blood oxygen overnight.

Forty-four healthy residents living above one thousand metres had sleep studies in random order. Each person spent two nights at home and two nights at a laboratory in Chur at 590 metres. A two-week washout sat between the blocks. The main outcome was time spent below ninety percent oxygen saturation, with overall saturation and apnoea counts as secondary measures. Altitude medicine readers gain controlled evidence on descent as a simple remedy.
pmc-13392676:
Qianru Jiang leads a large structural study showing that ketamine and its older cousin phencyclidine, better known as PCP, can plug directly into human opioid receptors and switch them on. Both drugs are famous for blocking a different brain receptor, yet their mix of helpful and harmful effects hinted at more targets. The team froze receptors with each drug bound and imaged them at near-atomic detail.

The pictures, backed by targeted mutations and chemical variants, pinpoint the grips each drug uses inside the receptor's binding pocket. A drug-free view of the kappa opioid receptor shows the pocket before any guest arrives. Ketamine shifted around more inside the pocket than PCP did, a looseness that may explain its distinct clinical behaviour. The authors argue opioid receptors belong in any full account of ketamine.
pmc-13393276:
Xiaoyun Wu and five colleagues review how re-engineering the flanking groups around diketopyrrolopyrrole, a workhorse pigment-turned-semiconductor, unlocks functions far beyond its classic roles in transistors and solar cells. Standard synthesis fixes aromatic rings on both sides of the core, and those rings dictate energy levels, packing, and charge flow. Decades of swapping them delivered steady gains but boxed in the possible shapes.

Newer work breaks the mould with naphthalene motifs, vinyl links, and fused backbones that reshape how molecules couple and stack. Those moves stretch the material family toward flexible electronics, intelligent skins, and biological sensors that demand softness and responsiveness classic designs lack. The review organises the field into a structure-property-application map, presenting flanking-group design as the unifying lever for next-generation multifunctional organic electronics.
pmc-13394776:
Feldman and co-authors assess, in 2026, whether the seizure drug cenobamate can be restarted at full dose after a short break without triggering hypersensitivity reactions such as rash. Slow dose escalation is normally required when starting the drug, leaving restart rules unclear. They exploited a natural experiment: epilepsy patients whose medicines were paused during intracranial EEG monitoring at a tertiary center, then restarted before discharge.

Thirty-two patients, median age 29 years, had cenobamate withheld for a median of seven days and restarted at a median of 200 milligrams per day. A quarter resumed at 300 milligrams or more, and 44 percent had a prior history of rash from some cause. Even so, no hypersensitivity reactions or rashes attributable to the drug appeared during hospitalization or two weeks of follow-up. The authors suggest previously tolerant patients may skip retitration after brief interruptions, easing management of missed doses.
pmc-13395276:
Vendhan and Mysore survey, in 2026, how Indian dermatologists use narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for vitiligo, the skin condition that destroys pigment in patches. The light treatment is standard care, but real-world dosing, upkeep schedules, and pre-treatment dose testing vary widely. Their survey, checked by three senior dermatologists with over 15 years of phototherapy experience each, drew 80 replies from doctors in practice.

The response rate was only 5 percent, itself a finding about survey fatigue among clinicians. Among respondents, 65 percent had more than ten years of experience with the treatment. Just over half, 52.5 percent, used whole-body phototherapy units exclusively, while the rest combined whole-body cabinets with targeted devices for limited areas. The authors use the snapshot to argue for more standardized practice, since inconsistent dosing strategies and upkeep plans can change outcomes for vitiligo patients receiving the same nominal therapy.
pmc-13395376:
Lawrence Ejike Ugwu and co-authors expose, in 2026, an age penalty in blood pressure and diabetes care across Africa. Data came from a world risk factor pool built on 2,309 studies and 245 million people. Country-year figures ran from 1990 to 2022. Care steps, from diagnosis to control, were compared across age bands.

Older adults had more hypertension yet less control of it than fifty-year-olds. Diabetes treatment coverage fell after age seventy, dropping further past eighty-five. Severe untreated hypertension was most common in Central and West Africa. The authors say health systems built for infections and acute care miss older needs. They urge age-split tracking in coverage goals.
pmc-13395476:
Joachim P. Sturmberg and Carmel M. Martin argue, in 2026, that generative AI fits poorly with the heart of family medicine. Many patients now ask AI first when ill. The editorial grants that AI spots patterns and sums records fast. Good primary care, though, rests on knowing a patient over years and judging through doubt across visits.

Much illness arrives vague, and time itself is a diagnostic tool in this setting. No data set can supply moral judgement or healing ties, the authors say. Tests of AI should weigh continuity, skill loss, patient feel, and fairness, not accuracy alone. Family doctors must steer AI use, not just adopt it, they urge.
pmc-13395976:
Damian Lewis and colleagues set out to put number values on life with open wounds in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition where skin blisters and tears easily. Their 2026 study fills a gap, since such values are needed when new wound treatments are judged for cost and benefit.

The team wrote short health descriptions, called vignettes, that varied in wound number and size, pain, itch, and hours spent on wound care. A United Kingdom public sample of 1,139 people and 44 people with the condition rated these states with a standard quality-of-life tool. Patients rated their own states, while the public rated states as if caring for someone affected.
pmc-13396176:
Wang and team report, in 2026, evidence that microwaves can push electrons in a semiconductor into superballistic flow, a regime where a viscous electron fluid conducts better than free flight allows. Working with point contacts carved from ultrahigh-mobility two-dimensional electron gas, they used photoconductivity, the change in conduction under microwaves. That let them probe how edge magnetoplasmons, waves running along the sample edge, stir the electron fluid.

Weak microwaves at low magnetic fields produced photoconductivity matching superballistic flow, while strong fields flipped the signal negative as phonon scattering took over. The key evidence was geometric: photoconductance scaled with the square of the point contact width, the fingerprint of viscous flow. Edge waves that reinforced each other sharply enhanced the signal, while waves that cancelled were strongly suppressed. A conductance plateau near 35.6 units of e-squared over h implied an effective channel width of 0.44 micrometers, measured with error below 1.5 percent.
pmc-13396576:
Georg Evers and co-authors gathered records from 12 German lung cancer centers on what happens after a common modern treatment path fails. Their 2026 study follows patients with locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer whose disease returned after chemotherapy with radiation and a follow-on year of the immunotherapy drug durvalumab.

Charts for 145 such patients were reviewed for tumor traits, later treatments, and survival. No standard approach exists for this relapse point, since the drug sequence is recent and trials have not settled the next move. Real-world series like this one show what doctors actually choose and what those choices deliver.
pmc-13396676:
Tiankai Di and co-authors restored the blood-vessel-growing power of aging dental pulp stem cells by delivering two gene messages into them, in a 2026 study. Older pulp cells lose their ability to support new vessels, which stalls attempts to regrow living tooth pulp instead of filling dead teeth.

The team traced the loss to weak sugar metabolism, with low levels of a glucose transporter and an enzyme called HK2. A branched polymer carrier delivered the instructions for both proteins, entering over 90 percent of cells without harm. Fluid from the treated cells doubled the length of vessel tubes grown in the lab and brought branch points back to youthful levels.
pmc-13397576:
Sajni Parikh and co-authors compare short and extended blood-thinner cover after breast rebuilding with the patient's own belly tissue. Their 2026 chart review covers DIEP flap cases at one centre from January 2017 to June 2025. Blood clots in veins kill many patients each year, yet national guidance on longer cover never covered this operation.

Patients went home on enoxaparin, sold as Lovenox, for either two weeks or a longer course after a practice change. Anyone with past clots, clotting disorders or regular anticoagulant use was left out. Rates of lung and leg clots, plus procedure problems, were compared across the switch to judge whether longer cover helps or harms.
pmc-13398476:
Ziyin Huang and colleagues map the gene-activity states inside metastatic melanoma and test which states forecast survival. Their 2026 study profiles tumour samples from 111 patients with in-transit metastases diagnosed between 1990 and 2020, using digital spatial RNA profiling. Melanomas fall into distinct internal states, but how those states track with how long patients live was unsettled.

Clean profiles emerged for 105 patients, including 30 who received checkpoint immunotherapy and 20 with acral melanoma in the set described. Four main axes separated the states, from undifferentiated to melanocytic patterns, with immune and stromal signals on other axes. The melanocytic state tied to poorer overall survival on its own, a warning sign pathologists may add to staging.
pmc-13399576:
Michal Zielinski and Kamila Dziemianowicz report a fatal case of re-expansion pulmonary edema in 2026, a rare complication that can follow the draining of a collapsed lung. Scans showed a complete left-sided pneumothorax with the left lung nearly fully collapsed. On arrival he was walking, stable, and holding 95 percent oxygen saturation on room air.

A large chest tube was placed and connected at once to active suction at minus 20 centimeters of water pressure. Roughly thirty minutes after decompression he crashed into fast-worsening oxygen failure. A new chest X-ray showed dense, one-sided clouding filling the re-expanded left lung, with blood-tinged frothy secretions in his airway. The authors present the timing and one-sided picture as strong evidence for fulminant re-expansion edema. They urge especially close monitoring after drainage when a lung has been down for a long time in diseased tissue.
pmc-13400476:
Anastasia Kolesnikova, Andrew Armitage, Klara Hajdu and Helen Cockerton review, in 2026, how the recombination pathway could help breed better crops. During sexual reproduction, matching chromosomes swap segments, mixing parental genes into new combinations. Breeders depend on that mixing, yet crossover events are few and tightly controlled in most plants.

The authors assemble an up-to-date network of the plant proteins that run recombination, covering how crossovers form and how chromosomes separate cleanly. They assess how far breeders already alter the process, survey new tools that could raise or redirect crossover rates, and weigh the gains on offer. More crossovers, in theory, mean more new trait combinations to select from.
pmc-13400576:
Caviglia Marta and an international group reflect, in 2026, on trauma stabilization points, small forward clinics set up in war zones to treat the wounded near where injuries happen. Moving care forward matters when normal evacuation breaks down. The World Health Organization convened experts to draft guidance drawing on deployments including Gaza.

Between February and July 2024, three such points in Gaza handled over 4,000 consultations. Though built for trauma, they soon treated minor injuries and everyday illness too, reflecting what people could actually reach. Referral success varied with hospital distance, ambulances and shifting front lines, and insecurity forced mobility. Lessons echoed other conflicts: stay near injury points, link into a working referral chain and keep clear staffing and records.
pmc-13400876:
Sagaidac Irina, Cemortan Maria and Cernetchi Olga review, in 2026, the World Health Organization Labor Care Guide for monitoring childbirth, with a focus on adoption in Moldova. The older partograph chart, used for decades, relied on rigid thresholds for how fast the cervix should open. Newer evidence favors care tailored to each woman.

The guide, launched in 2020, supports monitoring tailored to the woman. It cuts needless interventions and promotes respectful care without harming safety, according to global experience. Moldova approved a new national guideline on care in labor in 2025, aligned with the guide. The authors trace the science behind it, its global uptake and the Moldovan policy steps.
pmc-13401576:
Svatava Kubickova, Halina Cernohorska, Hana Hradska, and Miluse Vozdova developed a 2026 rapid molecular method for sexing primates, aimed at managing captive populations of endangered species where males and females look alike. Knowing a newborn's sex early helps zoos plan breeding and group composition.

Their PCR test targets the male-specific SRY gene with a c-myc control gene found in both sexes. It was validated on blood DNA from adult Sumatran orangutans, western lowland gorillas. Silvery gibbons, then applied to non-invasive samples from four newborns, two orangutans, a gorilla, and a gibbon, using umbilical cord material collected after birth and hair. The method also worked in adult chimpanzees and pig-tailed macaques. Non-invasive sampling means infants need no handling for an early, reliable sex result.
pmc-13401676:
Fardina Rahman Omi, Farhana Zaman, and SM Saidur Rahman Mashreky wrote a 2026 systematic review of how chronic diseases affect health-related quality of life in South and Southeast Asia. Chronic illness in the region imposes a double burden of sickness and economic hardship on patients and health systems alike.

The search covered studies from 2014 to 2024 measuring quality of life in chronic disease patients, spanning cross-sectional, observational, cohort, and economic designs. Conditions ranged across lung disease, kidney disease, diabetes, sarcopenia, cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and hepatitis C. Twenty-five studies from multiple Asian countries were included. For each, the reviewers charted the population, disease, methods, sample size. Which validated quality-of-life instruments were used, exposing both the weight of the burden and the variety of tools used to measure it.
pmc-13401876:
Herong Wang and colleagues ran a large survey of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Tianjin, China, reported in 2026, measuring prevalence, associated factors, and public awareness of the disease. Smoking is the best-known driver, but biomass fuel smoke and other exposures matter too, and big surveys guide prevention.

Between January 2023 and December 2024, a cluster-sampled cross-section enrolled 65,680 adults aged 35 to 75. Diagnosis rested on breathing tests after a bronchodilator, with the standard ratio threshold defining obstruction. The team assessed age, sex, body mass, smoking history, biomass fuel use for cooking and heating, and chronic cough, then used multivariable regression to isolate independent associations. Awareness questions probed how much the public knows about a disease many carry undiagnosed, rounding out a prevention-oriented snapshot of one Chinese city.
pmc-13402576:
Debojyoti Chowdhury and colleagues built ACSCeND, a deep learning framework that reads cancer stem-like cell states from gene activity data, in both single-cell and bulk tumor samples. Stem-like cells drive tumor variety, drug resistance, and relapse, yet profiling them evenly across data types has been hard. One part of the tool sorts single cells into pluripotent-like, multipotent-like, or unipotent-like states; a second part, guided by attention, unmixes bulk samples into those same shares.

Put to work on more than 25,000 tumor profiles from atlas and outcome datasets, the tool linked higher stem-like shares to shorter disease-free survival and weaker response to checkpoint immunotherapy. It also recovered known growth hierarchies in healthy tissue, supporting wider relevance. The authors offer the package freely in Python and pitch stem-like state as a pan-cancer marker that could guide stemness-aware treatment choices.
pmc-13402676:
Tian and co-authors name, in 2026, the protein LRP4 as an entry receptor shared by several encephalitic alphaviruses, including Eastern equine encephalitis virus, whose human case fatality rate approaches 40 percent. Known receptors from the lipoprotein receptor family left some infection unexplained. The team ran a CRISPR activation screen in cells stripped of several attachment factors to find what else the virus uses.

LRP4 handled viral attachment and entry directly, its binding domain gripping the virions, and it served Western equine encephalitis, Semliki Forest, and Sindbis viruses as well. Soluble LRP4 decoy proteins strongly blocked Eastern equine encephalitis virus in primary mouse neurons, in live male mice, and in human brain organoids, a possible treatment route. Mammalian and avian versions of LRP4 both promoted infection, fitting the virus's bird-mosquito-human cycle. The authors say the shared receptor reshapes understanding of alphavirus tissue targeting and defense design.
pmc-13402776:
Kazuki Ohashi and colleagues map who actually used telemedicine in Hokkaido, Japan, from 2022 to 2024, as pandemic rules relaxed. Claims data followed more than 1.48 million people with regular outpatient care, and only 0.4 percent, or 5965 people, ever had a remote visit. The analysis stacked 34 personal and municipal factors under Andersen behavioral model of health service use.

Where a person lived mattered hugely: 39 percent of the variation sat at municipal level, rising to 54 percent among people aged 75 and older. Sicker patients, women, prior telemedicine users, and those with opioid or psycholeptic prescriptions used remote care more; older age itself pulled use down. Towns with more single-parent households and stronger finances saw higher uptake. The authors call for infrastructure and caregiver-friendly policy to reach older, digitally left-behind patients.
pmc-13403376:
Yanguang Mao led a 2026 study on a protein part called LMP2 and its role after a stroke blocks and then restores blood flow. Star-shaped support cells in the brain shape the swelling and repair that follow. The team used mice that lacked LMP2 in all cells or only in those support cells.

Mice without LMP2 had smaller damaged areas and better movement and thinking after the event. LMP2 seemed to push one alarm pathway up while holding a repair pathway down. Blocking it shifted support cells toward help and growth support. The work points to LMP2 as a drug target for stroke care.
pmc-13403476:
Kenan Sabuncu headed a 2026 rat study on whether syringic acid can limit harm when a twisted testicle is untwisted. Untwisting restores blood flow, yet the return flow itself can injure tissue. Forty-eight male rats were split into six groups, with treatment given half an hour before untwisting.

Groups were checked four or twenty-four hours after flow returned. Treated rats kept higher levels of protective chemicals and showed lower swelling and cell-death signals. Tissue scores also looked better, with more sperm-making structure kept intact. One damage marker showed no clear change, so the benefit rests on the wider set of measures.
pmc-13403576: Chun-Chia Cheng and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 for their 2016 study on blocking an enzyme to cut tumor blood vessel growth in bowel cancer. The notice is a correction only, adding a missing reference for a reused photograph. That photo, showing high levels of a vessel growth signal in patient serum, had already run in a separate paper from the same team. Both papers drew on the same batch of patient samples, the authors explain, and the added citation now makes that reuse clear to readers.
pmc-13403976:
Alexander P Ligocki and a large team asked in 2026 whether aging changes how gene-silencing drugs spread when given into spinal fluid. Such delivery is the most advanced route for this drug class, yet age is rarely built into trials. Their test drug pairs a fat tag with a short silencer RNA.

Age had little effect on where the drug went or how well it hushed its target gene. Safety signs also stayed steady across ages in their checks. A rival fat-tag design worked best only when matched with the RNA shape it was tuned for. Mixing parts across designs hurt results. The findings ease fears about using such drugs in older patients.
pmc-13404176:
Fadhilah Zulfa and co-authors presented two fertility cases in 2026 involving a rare hormone fault that leaves ovaries dormant. Women with this fault make too little of the brain hormones that wake the ovaries. Standard egg-growth plans often fail, so doses and timing must be tuned by hand.

The first woman also had low egg reserve and a partner factor, yet reached pregnancy with a mixed drug plan plus growth hormone help. The second woman had better reserve and normal partner results, but a simpler plan did not yield pregnancy. Tailored dosing can work for picked patients, the team concludes, while growth hormone value needs bigger studies.
pmc-13406176:
Andres Prieto Trujillo and colleagues present a ring-shaped clot test that watches clot breakdown in real time, in a 2026 methods paper. Standard viscoelastic machines summarise clotting and breakdown together but cannot isolate breakdown of a ready-made clot. A sensitive standard test could sharpen care for bleeding disorders.

Their plasma annular clot assay adapts a tagged fibrin ring method to plasma from healthy donors. Plasmin, the body's clot-dissolving enzyme, was added at rising doses and the digestion curve tracked over time. Breakdown sped in a straight-line relation with dose in the reported experiments. Results were compared with thromboelastography readings, and the drug pentamidine tested the system's response to interference.
pmc-13407476:
Peter G. Kennedy and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether underground truffle fungi can also travel by air. Textbook ecology splits fungi into two camps. Mushroom-formers spread spores on the wind. Truffles supposedly move only when animals dig and eat them. The team sequenced DNA from spore traps and soil at eight United States sites.

Truffle-forming species made up about 17 percent of the fungal types and 19 percent of the DNA reads caught in air traps. Their airborne appearances came in bursts rather than steadily, and the truffle species caught aloft had smaller spores than those found only in soil. Matching types turned up in traps and soils tens of kilometres apart, hinting at real wind journeys. The authors argue the two dispersal worlds overlap more than assumed.
pmc-13407876:
Jakub Kopal and co-authors map, in 2026, the shared genetics linking brain shape, mental illness, and metabolic disease. People with psychiatric disorders often develop heart and metabolic illnesses. Both illness groups track with brain structure changes. The team combined huge genome-wide data sets. They covered mental disorders, heart-metabolic diseases, and brain-surface anatomy. Most people studied had European ancestry.

Patterns split by disorder. Schizophrenia shared many genes with cortical thickness and type 2 diabetes. Its overall correlation stayed weak, though. ADHD correlated more strongly with heart-metabolic disease but barely shared genes with brain shape. Surface area of the cortex partly carried the genetic link between ADHD and diabetes. Pathway analysis highlighted metabolic stress in ADHD against brain-development and immune processes in schizophrenia. Comorbidity, the authors conclude, runs through both shared and private genetic routes.
pmc-13408076:
David T. Rubin and co-authors report, in 2026, subgroup results testing a once-daily pill as the first advanced therapy for ulcerative colitis. Etrasimod tunes immune-cell trafficking receptors, and the phase III ELEVATE UC trials randomised patients two-to-one against placebo. This analysis isolates patients whose prior treatment stopped at conventional drugs. It uses three nested scenarios, from simple acid-suppressant-class failure up through steroid and thiopurine exposure.

Among patients who had failed only the mildest conventional therapy, etrasimod beat placebo on clinical, endoscopic, and tissue endpoints at both twelve weeks and one year. Pooled analyses of the broader conventional-failure groups showed the same direction, strongly significant at week twelve and mostly numerical by week fifty-two in the most pre-treated group. Safety matched the overall trial population. Early positioning of the drug is supported.
pmc-13408176:
Cong-Hui Gao and co-authors report a 2026 advance in making twisted, mirror-sensitive indole compounds. Indoles appear in many drugs and natural products, and chemists usually modify them by electrophilic attack because the ring is electron rich. Forcing the opposite, nucleophilic, pattern at the ring's second carbon has remained difficult.

Shining visible light on a chiral acid catalyst flipped the reactivity of specially prepared indoles, letting them couple with a second indole partner. The products were axially chiral paired indoles, obtained in good yields with excellent selectivity for one mirror form. Readers in synthetic chemistry gain both a first-of-its-kind substitution method and a practical route to a hard-to-build family of chiral structures.
pmc-13408676:
Seunghyun Oh and a large Korean team build in 2026 a single light sensor that sees visible light or short-wave infrared on demand. It needs none of the stacked filter layers that usually separate the two. Such dual-mode detectors serve imaging and diagnostics, yet interlayers add noise and manufacturing complexity. Their device merges an organic layer with lead sulfide quantum dots in one monolithic stack.

Controlled phase separation inside the organic layer, running both vertically and sideways, steers charge flow so cleanly that no auxiliary interlayer is needed. The result is high detectivity with little crosstalk between bands. Single-pixel imaging reconstructed sharp pictures in both bands even with the light dimmed. The dual view also let the team align silicon parts by registering front and back features. The design strategy transfers to other photoactive pairings.
pmc-13409976:
Potjana Jitjamnong and colleagues describe in 2026 a Thai program that uses games and smart software to curb risky drinking among trade-school students. Heavy drinking at that age can harm health, study, and later work life. The program builds skill in finding, judging, and using health facts rather than just handing out warnings.

Students took part online, working through tasks that mixed game rewards with tailored feedback. The study design compared groups over time without random assignment, so care is needed when reading gains. Early results favor the program for safer drinking habits. The authors propose it as a model schools and health services could scale up, since it runs on tools students already use daily.
pmc-13410376:
Harikumar Suma and colleagues report in 2026 that social amoebae grow tiny tubes to talk to each other. These single-celled organisms act together like a many-celled body at times, which takes close coordination. Known signals were mostly chemicals released into the surroundings, not direct cell-to-cell links.

Using glowing labels and fine microscopy, the team watched the tubes form fresh between cells of the amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum. Live imaging showed the actin-rich tubes keep membranes continuous, letting cargo pass directly across. Similar tubes turned up in other amoeba species, hinting at a shared tool in natural communities. Links held even when cell scaffolding was disturbed, which suggests an early, sturdy route to multicellular life.
pmc-13410576:
Soobon Ko and colleagues benchmark in 2026 computer tools that predict where a peptide sits in an immune display molecule. Those molecules show peptide pieces to T cells, and the grip point, called the binding core, shapes the immune answer. Getting the core right matters for vaccine and therapy design.

Four tools were tested on 72 known complexes plus shuffled and known non-binding peptides. Two structure-based tools built on AlphaFold caught most true binders yet often called non-binders positive. A sequence-based tool, NetMHCIIpan, proved best at spotting non-binders while missing more weak positives. Blending tools into agreed calls balanced those strengths, and the authors map when each blend suits best.
pmc-13411776:
Paola Maroni and co-authors' 2016 study of cell self-eating in human bone metastasis is retracted by the journal in 2026. The paper had claimed the autophagy process unfolds in bone spread of cancer, with one protein playing different roles at early and late stages. Doubts about its figures reached the editorial office and triggered a formal investigation.

Editors confirmed that parts of a key figure duplicated elements from a figure in another paper by a similar author group, despite showing different experimental conditions. The board states it lost confidence in the findings and withdrew the paper under publisher policy, with the editor-in-chief approving. Two authors agreed to the retraction when informed; the rest gave no comment.
pmc-13413176:
Rui-Bin Huang and co-authors ask in 2026 whether separating tiny capillaries from large vessels in eye scans forecasts who will see better after treatment for diabetic macular edema. Swelling at the retina's centre blurs vision in diabetes, and anti-VEGF injections are the standard fix. Forty-two untreated eyes received three monthly injections while a custom analysis measured vessel density for the full network, large vessels, and capillaries alone from baseline scans.

Vision improved and retinal thickness fell markedly after the loading course, and 73.8 percent of patients reached a good visual outcome as defined. Baseline thickness predicted nothing about later sight in their models. Capillary density alone did: eyes starting with a healthier fine network ended with better acuity and better odds of a good outcome.
pmc-13413476:
Vytautas Kiudelis and colleagues test in 2026 whether three blood molecules can flag microscopic colitis, a cause of chronic watery diarrhoea that today needs colon biopsies to diagnose. No dependable blood marker exists for its two forms, collagenous and lymphocytic colitis. Plasma from 45 collagenous patients, 16 lymphocytic patients, healthy controls, and ulcerative colitis patients was assayed for a gut-leak protein, an anti-inflammatory signal, and bacterial wall fragments.

The gut-leak protein, FABP2, ran highest in collagenous colitis yet overlapped too much with healthy levels to separate the groups. The anti-inflammatory signal IL-10 differed mainly between ulcerative colitis and other groups, not for microscopic colitis itself. Bacterial fragments showed no group differences at all. None of the three markers identified the lymphocytic form, leaving biopsy unchallenged for now.
pmc-13413976:
Akhil Chandrakanth Komaram and co-authors turn a phone camera into a lab reader in 2026 for interleukin-8, a signal of swelling tied to infection and cancer. Their card prints catcher antibodies in a two-by-five grid on glass. A drop of fluid lands on the card. Gold flecks tagged with a second antibody latch on where the target binds. The flecks tint the spot, and a phone photo plus free software scores the tint.

A drop of eight microlitres was all the test needed on the bench. It could find as little as 0.23 picograms per millilitre of fluid. Repeat reads varied by less than one percent. Spiked blood serum gave back 99.5 and 106.1 percent at the two levels tried. The authors offer the card as a cheap stand-in for plate tests.
pmc-13415376:
Eduarda Nabinger and co-authors ask whether genes of cellular senescence, the state where cells stop dividing, relate to repeated pregnancy loss, in 2026. More than half of such cases lack a clear cause. The team first checked six gene activity levels in placenta and womb lining datasets from public sources.

Gene activity did not differ between patients and controls in those datasets. Variant testing in 107 patients and 118 fertile controls told a subtler story. One variant in the CDKN1A gene appeared more often in patients. Certain variant pairings also split unevenly between groups, in directions suggesting higher or lower susceptibility. The authors treat the senescence link as a preliminary hypothesis.
pmc-13415476:
B. Eser and a multicenter team chart how lymph node surgery for endometrial cancer changed in German academic centers, in the 2026 E-PEC analysis. Records covered 644 patients treated surgically between 2018 and 2022 at six university hospitals. Patients who started with drug or radiation therapy were excluded.

About 62 percent received some lymph node surgery. Sentinel node procedures, which sample only the first draining nodes, grew to about 61 percent of all staging operations. Full systematic node removal fell from about 30 percent in 2018 to about 18 percent in 2022. Practice moved toward gentler staging alongside shifting guidelines.
pmc-13418276:
Toshihiko Mandai and co-authors report a failed pairing in magnesium battery electrolytes and explain why, in a 2026 study. Magnesium metal batteries promise cheap large scale storage. Two fashionable ingredients, a weakly coordinating salt and an amine ether solvent, were expected to combine well, yet performance came out poor while the same solvent suited a strongly coordinating salt.

Analysis traced failure to trace water in the solvent, which partly converts the fancy anion and builds unstable oxygen rich surface layers during cycling. The strongly coordinating salt instead forms a protective fluorine and nitrogen rich layer with the solvent. Even that system has limits for real use, the authors note.
pmc-13418476:
Chuanwang Yao and co-authors test a common nutrient as a weapon against a devastating plant bacterium, in a 2026 study. Ralstonia solanacearum wilts many crops, coordinating attack through chemical quorum sensing. The compound 4-aminobenzoic acid resembles the bacterium's own signal and was tested for jamming that system without killing the microbe outright.

Treated bacteria made less slime, formed weaker biofilms, and moved less, while signal molecule output dropped. The compound binds the signal receptor and blocks it from switching on virulence genes. Two contact points on the receptor proved essential. Signal jamming offers a non antibiotic route to soften plant disease.
pmc-13419176:
Gladys Estheysi Elías Solís and colleagues pool trial evidence on whether friendly gut bacteria and their food sources can lift blood levels in children. Prebiotics, probiotics, and combined synbiotic products are often pitched as gentle help against childhood anemia. The team searched three major databases through August 2025 for randomized trials in children.

Nineteen trials with 4188 children met the bar for the pooled analysis. Set against placebo or standard care, the products showed no important effect on hemoglobin, red cell share, or iron stores, alone or paired with iron. Certainty in those pooled results ranged from high down to very low across outcomes. The sober findings suggest clinics should not count on these products as an anemia fix for children.
pmc-13419476:
Yuming Zhang and colleagues trace how loss of a gene called ARID1A helps colorectal cancer spread, following a known signaling chain inside the cells. Colorectal cancer ranks as the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and spread drives most of that toll. ARID1A sits in a complex that opens packed DNA, and its loss was already tied to invasion, yet the route stayed unclear.

The team mined public cancer genome collections, including the national atlas program, for mutation and outcome data. Survival analysis set gene activity against patient features to test forecast value. Their work points along the AKT and mTOR chain, a growth circuit that ends in a protein-building switch. Naming the route gives drug developers a line of targets to test against tumors missing this gene.
pmc-13420176:
Iftikhar Ahmed Charan and colleagues follow children in rural Pakistan to see how early hardship shapes behavior into the teen years. Harmful childhood experiences steer emotional development, yet long-run proof from lower-income countries stays scarce. Their data come from the Bachpan Cohort, with 1,791 observations across three waves spanning ages 4 to 15 years.

Behavior was scored on a standard strengths and difficulties survey at each wave, covering inward distress, outward behavior, and kindness to others. Emotional neglect was the most common hardship, touching 83.7 percent of children in the reported share. Dose-response and network methods tested how hardships stack and interact. pmc-13425576:

pmc-13425876:

pmc-13427576:

pmc-13427876:

pmc-13428776:

pmc-13431176:

pmc-13437676:

pmc-13443876:

pmc-13445076:

pmc-13446176:

pmc-13447576:

pmc-13448876:

pmc-13448976:

pmc-13452176:

pmc-13452276:

pmc-13453576:

pmc-13471276:

pmc-13473276:
Nemcová and colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of people who use child sexual abuse material but have never been caught, a group rarely heard from directly. pmc-13473376:

pmc-13473976:
Naina Kumar and colleagues describe a 2026 case where bowel cancer spread hid behind signs of ovarian cancer. pmc-13474576:
Mary E Hackbarth and co-authors model a rare storage disease in mice in 2026 by copying its most common gene fault. pmc-13474676:
Zhenning Feng and colleagues probe blood antioxidants and thinking skills in 2026 in people with schizophrenia who had never taken antipsychotic drugs. pmc-13474776:

pmc-13474876:
Batuhan Aydın and co-authors test a dissolving membrane in 2026 for guiding bone regrowth in rat skull defects. pmc-13476076:

pmc-13476576:
Kinan El Husseini and co-authors chart research themes in 2026 for chronic lung transplant failure, the top cause of late death after transplant. pmc-13477076:
Harrison R Herrera and co-authors show in 2026 how follow-up quality warps reported harms after mechanical aortic valve surgery. A group of 558 patients from 2000 to 2023 split into local and referral patients by distance from the center. Bleeding and clot events were counted by chart review and by billing codes. Matched groups of local and distant patients were compared.

Local patients were followed far longer and showed higher raw event rates. Careful time-based math shrank but did not erase the gap. Billing codes stretched the gap wider than chart review did. Distant patients are not safer; they are simply watched less closely.
pmc-13477776:
Singh and co-workers in India reported in 2026 a rare appendix cancer that wore the mask of plain appendicitis. Their patient was a woman of 64 with right low belly pain for a week. Scans showed a plump appendix with small stones, a classic sign of a blocked, sore organ. The team took the organ out, as is standard for such a case.

The lens told a split tale. The wall held a signet ring cell cancer, named for cells that look like signet rings, spread through the full wall and into the fat pad. Stains for three marks came back plus, and a fourth came back minus, a code that points to the lower gut as the source. The cut edges still held tumor. The authors stress that each removed appendix needs a full tissue read, since this fast cancer needs more care than the first cut.
pmc-13479476:
Peng and co-workers in China sifted in 2026 what shapes a heart patient's full day of motion, rest, and sleep. They hunted wearable based studies of adults with coronary heart disease, the clogged artery ill. No study had yet traced all three day parts at once in this group. Twenty four studies fit, most of them on motion alone, and the team sorted each driver by scale, from the self out to home, streets, and state rules.

Age and rehab stood out at the self scale: older patients moved less, while rehab joiners moved more. At the home scale, a spouse's backing cut both sloth and seat time. Street traits, like how green or dense the home zone was, also tracked with day shape. No study tied state rules to the day at all. The authors urge plans that push rehab sign up and home backing first.
pmc-13479576:
Jun Liu, Jun Sun, Huanyu Li, and Jingyu Zhao published a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing physical activity programs for people with autism spectrum disorder. Exercise is a promising drug-free support, yet families face a confusing menu of types and doses. Seven databases were searched through December 2025 for controlled studies.

Forty-five studies covering 1,479 participants met the criteria. Outcomes were social communication, repetitive behaviors, and motor skills. Network methods let the authors rank programs that were never tested head-to-head, by borrowing strength across the whole evidence web. The ranking approach gives therapists and parents a comparative map for choosing activity type and dose, rather than another single-program verdict.
pmc-13479976:
Chenxi Jin and coauthors published a 2026 retrospective MRI study checking whether jaw disc positions after surgery are actually sensible. The operation, arthroscopic disc repositioning done on both sides, treats jaw joints where the cushioning disc has slipped forward and will not return. Ninety consecutive patients with scans were screened for the analysis.

After exclusions, fifty-nine surgical patients covering 101 joints were compared with thirty-one symptomatic patients whose discs were not displaced. Scans at one, three, and six months after surgery measured both disc position and joint mobility. The authors call their yardstick rationality: a disc can sit correctly yet still fail to move with the jaw. The graded follow-up shows whether early good positions hold or drift.
pmc-13480076:
Fumio Kurosaki and co-authors present a 2026 review of an inhaled drug used for stubborn lung infection with Mycobacterium avium complex. The drug, a liposomal form of amikacin breathed in through a nebulizer, serves patients whose infection resists standard care. The team read charts for 27 patients treated for at least six months at one centre between late 2021 and mid-2025.

Faulty use also mattered, covering stretched-out dosing gaps and late swaps of nebulizer parts. Voice hoarseness was the most common side effect and at times drove the dosing gaps. pmc-13482576:
Alshammari and colleagues show in 2026 that how you brew a medicinal plant changes what you get from it, comparing three methanol extraction methods for the herb Onosma rechingeri. The methods were sound-wave extraction, plain soaking, and heated Soxhlet extraction, Each yielded a different chemical mix. Plain soaking won elsewhere, carrying the most luteolin-7-glucoside of the three and blocking the brain enzyme and the starch enzyme most strongly of all. Computer docking backed the chemistry, flagging luteolin-7-glucoside as a strong binder of the starch enzyme, with rosmarinic acid favored for the brain targets.
pmc-13482876:
Gider and colleagues asked whether newer deep-learning tools beat a standard method at spotting the rare crashes that kill people. Their 2026 study used 5,676 crashes recorded in Batman province, Türkiye, from 2013 to 2022. Fatal crashes made up only 0.8 percent of records, so a lazy model could look accurate while missing every deadly case. The team compared XGBoost with two neural designs, TabNet and FT-Transformer.

FT-Transformer won, reaching the strongest discrimination scores and catching about 44 percent of fatal crashes among its top-ranked cases. Its precision-focused score ran nearly four times the random baseline the authors computed for comparison. XGBoost and TabNet trailed close behind each other. Gider warns that with so few fatal cases, scores that reward overall accuracy mislead, so rare-event measures should guide model choice for road safety work.
pmc-13483576:
Karen Redhead and co-authors separate the effects of sleep apnea and low mood on pregnancy outcomes in a 2026 observational study. One hundred twenty-two women late in pregnancy at a large maternity hospital completed overnight breathing and oxygen monitoring and reported depressive symptoms. Chart review then recorded outcomes for mothers and newborns.

Babies of mothers with sleep apnea had much higher odds of a low Apgar score five minutes after birth, even after mood and body size were accounted for. More frequent oxygen dips were linked to higher birthweight babies. Depressive symptoms, in contrast, were linked to preterm birth rather than to newborn condition at delivery. The authors argue that both breathing treatment and mental health care deserve attention in pregnancy.
pmc-13483676:
Hou and colleagues filmed pelvic organs in motion to map how prolapse actually unfolds inside the body. Pelvic organ prolapse means organs such as the bladder sink from their normal places, and doctors usually grade it while the patient lies still. Their 2026 study scanned 63 women with advanced prolapse using MRI while they strained, then tracked each organ's center point across three pushes.

Each organ followed its own segmented path rather than sliding straight down as textbooks imply. The bladder traced a reversed C shape, bending at three turning points as its angle shifted. The uterus traced a reversed S with four turning points. By the third strain, the uterus had traveled about 83 percent of the reference line's length, far beyond its first-push distance. Hou argues surgical planning should respect these organ-specific routes.
pmc-13484876:
Zheng Cao fabricates a conductive heart patch that copies the layered, aligned fiber architecture of natural heart muscle. Published in 2026, the patch weaves oriented nanofibers into a gel matrix laced with dopamine and polypyrrole for electrical conduction. Fiber direction gives each layer one-way electrical character and guides heart cells to line up along the fibers.

Cell layers stacked seamlessly in dishes, showing smooth transitions between strata.
