pmc-13484976:
Sangrim Lee coats traditional mulberry paper with a conductive nanomaterial to build a flexible pressure sensor for wearables. Published in 2026, the design stacks several coated sheets so their rough, porous fibers compress and change electrical contact under load. Paper type, stacking pattern, and coating amount are tuned systematically for best response.

Sensitivity exceeded 15 per kilopascal across an unusually wide span from gentle touch to a full megapascal of pressure. Response was fast, output stayed consistent, and the device survived more than a thousand loading cycles. Built into gloves and wristbands, prototypes tracked finger bends, wrist pulse, and touch strength in real time. Wireless links even carried Morse code taps and CPR training feedback. pmc-13485076:
Lasrado and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how eye doctors in India manage optic neuritis in children, a sudden inflammation of the optic nerve that harms vision. Care for this condition varies, and the team wanted to map current practice and spot gaps. They sent an online survey to ophthalmologists in late 2024, asking about training, case loads, tests, and treatments.

Blood tests were ordered by nearly all, while spinal fluid tests were rare, and only about a quarter advised full brain and spine scans with the preferred settings. Almost all used intravenous steroid treatment, but course length and dose split widely. Doctors with less experience more often repeated scans and treated regardless of vision in repeat cases. The authors call for shared practice guidelines.
pmc-13485676:
Thomas Brochhagen and co-authors test one principle behind word shape patterns across more than 1,900 languages. Published in 2026, the large-scale analysis asks why similar meanings often share forms, both as whole words and inside words at the subword level. Two pressures compete, since reuse aids learning while distinct forms prevent confusion.

Sharing of meanings proved highly systematic at both levels, even though the particular meanings involved differed between levels. Subword reuse emerges as a compromise where full word reuse would risk misunderstanding. pmc-13487276:

pmc-13487976:
Iversen and team studied how stroke patients travel through Norway's emergency call system, then tested an artificial intelligence assistant on recorded calls. The AI model caught about 81 percent of strokes while correctly clearing about 80 percent of non-strokes in internal testing. pmc-13490376:

The loaded particles proved gentle on cells while strongly suppressing viral genes and proteins in the dish experiments. Treated mice showed reduced inflammation and viral activity compared with untreated infected animals in the in vivo work reported. pmc-13490576:
Marlina and colleagues tested whether low blood albumin, a protein that leaks away in severe preeclampsia, can flag which pregnant patients will turn severe. pmc-13491676:

Narcissism linked to problematic use both directly and through those two outlooks, while sadism showed only a small overall link. Among women the narcissism path ran fully through competitive individualism, and among men psychopathy pulled in opposite directions along different paths. pmc-13491776:

Women with the syndrome carried more Lactobacillus, Roseburia, and Escherichia-Shigella, and less Akkermansia, a microbe often tied to metabolic health. pmc-13491876:

The sensor measured hCG across a wide range with a detection limit low enough for early pregnancy, and it ignored other hormones while distinguishing the pregnancy-specific subunit. Tests in urine worked directly without sample cleanup. The authors pitch the platform for quantitative point-of-care testing beyond pregnancy as well.
pmc-13493776:

pmc-13493976:

No deaths, fluid buildup, or visible damage to the abdominal lining followed, and microscopy showed the surface cell layer intact apart from mild flattening and slight scarring beneath. pmc-13494076:

Both groups lost a little bone over the twelve months, but the probiotic group unexpectedly lost slightly more at several sites rich in spongy bone, including the shin and spine. The main comparison reached statistical significance. The authors urge caution: the differences were modest and outside factors may have crept in despite randomisation. pmc-13495376:

Instruments led the top hundred, then fixation devices, healing biologics, implants, access tools, and computer-guided systems. Fixation patents drew the most citations and the fastest yearly citation rate. Across eras the mix shifted: instruments dominated the earliest years, then shrank in share, while implants and biologics climbed. Near half the patents had expired at the time of study. The authors read the map as a record of where shoulder scope invention has concentrated and where it is heading.
pmc-13495476:
Wajahat Mirza and colleagues pool, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, studies comparing single-port and multiport robot surgery to remove a cancerous prostate. Single-port surgery took about ten minutes longer, yet patients lost less blood and left hospital about seventeen hours sooner. Complication rates and bladder control at three months did not split. pmc-13499676:
Hamzah M Javed and colleagues describe in 2026 a delayed, whole-body collapse after a large overdose of a common HIV treatment tablet that combines four antiviral drugs. Published overdose reports had mostly described mild courses handled with supportive care alone. Their patient was a 35-year-old man with HIV, high blood pressure, and amphetamine use who intentionally swallowed about 90 tablets and arrived awake, alert, and stable.

Within the next day his course changed sharply. He developed shock needing drugs to support blood pressure and breathing failure needing high-flow oxygen. pmc-13500376:
Sugiyama, Morimoto, and Asai report finding drug-resistant bacteria in an Asian black bear in Japan, a worrying sign of human pollution in nature. The 2026 genome analysis showed the resistance genes were built into the bacterium's chromosome. The strain resisted five tested drugs, including ampicillin and tetracycline.

Its genes sat close to isolates from a pig farmer in Vietnam and from Japanese slaughterhouse wastewater. They sat within a few dozen DNA letter differences, hinting at recent shared ancestry across the human-animal boundary. Dropping DNA showed a mostly wild plant diet, so the bear likely picked the bacterium up from its surroundings. The authors warn wildlife can become a reservoir spreading such bacteria back toward people.
pmc-13501576:
Yazhou Li leads an eight-author team comparing two endoscopic operations for far lateral lumbar disc herniation, where a slipped disc pinches a nerve root at the spine's side. The study reviewed 122 patients treated between January 2022 and July 2024 by one surgical team. Of these, 62 received percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy through a single channel, and 60 received unilateral biportal endoscopy, which uses separate viewing and working channels. Everyone was followed for at least twelve months.

Both groups improved markedly in pain and disability. The biportal operations took longer, averaging about 132.77 minutes against 86.61 minutes in clock time, and involved more blood loss, near 270 millilitres against roughly 37 millilitres on average. Long-term pain scores, disability scores, and excellent-or-good outcome rates, 91.9 percent against 93.3 percent, were comparable. A cumulative sum analysis placed the learning curve turning point at 24 cases for the biportal method and 38 for the single-channel one.
pmc-13501776:
Tianlong Wang leads a twenty-three-author team reporting a 2026 multicentre validation of a transfusion risk score for heart surgery on bypass. The overall transfusion rate reached 40.1 percent, giving the test plenty of events to judge. Discrimination was good, with an area under the curve of 0.713, and calibration was excellent, meaning predicted rates matched observed ones closely. Every single ingredient of the score, from age to surgery type, predicted worse alone than the combined score did. Performance held across all nine centres, with each centre's area above 0.65 on that measure. The authors back its use for blood management planning.
pmc-13502576:

The team's yttrium and gadolinium dinitrogen complexes, sources of divalent reactivity, instead cleaved P4 into a series. First came a four-atom dianion, then a two-atom dianion, then a phosphorus atom carrying an electron.

Structures and spectra characterized each stop. The four-unit ligand adopts a bicyclobutane-like shape, the two-unit ligand binds side-on as a double bond of the element, and the atom behaves as an element-centred radical. Paramagnetic resonance confirmed coupling to the element and yttrium, while the gadolinium version showed antiferromagnetic exchange with the radical. Calculations placed the spin on the element, extending its multiply bonded chemistry into the rare earths.
pmc-13502776:
Wang and colleagues described a sixty-one-year-old woman with breast cancer that spread into the membranes around her spinal cord. Her tumor was triple-negative, lacking the drug targets, and had returned after two quiet years, paralyzing both legs.

Wang profiled her genes and found an mutation in PALB2, a DNA-repair gene that makes tumors vulnerable to a drug class called PARP inhibitors. After chemotherapy and a checkpoint immunotherapy drug had failed, they added the PARP inhibitor olaparib. Her leg strength improved from paralysis to partial movement, and scans showed shrinkage of the spinal-membrane and bone lesions. Progression-free survival reached forty months with side effects. The authors caution that one case cannot separate drug's contribution, but argue the strategy merits study in patients.
pmc-13503276:
Emma Elizabeth Sabu Kattuman leads an eight-author team with a 2026 melanoma study that unmasks an inflammation receptor as a self-fuelling tumour driver. pmc-13503476:
Basri and a large team review how bile acids, the detergents the liver makes to digest fat, may help or harm the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Beyond digestion, bile acids act as hormones, and gut bacteria constantly remodel them before they circulate to distant organs. Their 2026 narrative review pulls together biochemical, animal, and clinical findings on two bile acid receptors that sit at the crossroads of metabolism, inflammation, and brain health.

People with Alzheimer's or mild cognitive impairment show altered bile acid profiles. The review sorts the family into villains and protectors. Water-hating secondary bile acids are linked to blood-brain barrier leaks and direct nerve toxicity, while water-loving types appear anti-inflammatory and protective in the cited evidence. Bile acids also trigger gut hormones, including GLP-1, the target of blockbuster diabetes drugs, giving them indirect routes to the brain.
pmc-13503876:
Chao Ma leads a team that glued crystal sponges into gas-sorting sheets with a plastic-like bond, in a 2026 study. The crystals, called metal-organic frameworks, sort gases by pore size and chemistry. Sheets made from them leak through gaps where grains meet, which ruins the sorting.

Heat and a helper compound triggered a linking reaction right at the grain faces of one crystal type, UiO-66. The sheets ended up almost all crystal by weight, with few leak paths left. They passed carbon dioxide fast while holding back nitrogen, beating a known quality line for that pair. The sheets also shrugged off damp air and could be refreshed. The same trick worked for three more crystal types of the same family.
pmc-13505076:
Yaodong Zhang leads a team testing a newer anesthetic against propofol for preventing sickness after surgery, in a 2026 trial. Nausea and vomiting after operations strike about a third of patients and most high-risk ones. Propofol helps but can sting on injection and drop blood pressure.

The trial enrolled 334 women having keyhole gynecologic surgery, split between the two drugs for sleep induction and upkeep. Sickness rates in the first day were near equal, at about 58 percent in each group. The new drug did not prove itself no worse within the set margin. It did win on safety: far less injection pain, less early low pressure, and less slow heart rate during surgery. Pain scores and satisfaction matched. The authors offer it as a gentler option.
pmc-13505176:
Denzel L Q Drop leads an international team that tested a virtual reality video made to help intensive care survivors understand what happened to them. Many survivors develop stress symptoms, anxiety, or low mood after critical illness. Across eleven hospitals, 344 adults who had spent at least three days in intensive care were split among standard care, an early video viewing, and a late viewing.

Six months later, stress symptom scores did not differ between either video group and standard care. Anxiety, depression, and quality of life also showed no group differences. Patients still rated the video highly, giving it a median eight out of ten for improving understanding and for satisfaction. The authors warn that a single viewing should not be expected to work like longer, guided, or personalised programmes, and they suggest future trials focus on high-risk patients.
pmc-13506576:
Kanako Kasuya and colleagues review, in a 2026 study from Japan, how often older patients with womb lining cancer received care that matched national guidelines. Records covered 130 patients aged 70 or older treated between 2010 and 2019 at one hospital. Guideline care meant main surgery, node checks when needed, and added chemotherapy based on risk.

Patients aged 75 or older met the full standard far less often than those aged 70 to 74, mainly through fewer node checks and less added chemotherapy. Missing the standard linked to worse outcomes even after other factors were counted. The authors advise judging fitness by full assessment, not age alone.
pmc-13508276:
Asima Khan and six co-authors map how proven type 2 diabetes care gets put into practice at primary clinics in poorer countries, in a 2026 scoping review. Diabetes is rising fast in low- and middle-income nations, where tight budgets make clinic care uneven. The team searched eight databases for studies from 1996 to late 2024. Papers had to describe rolling out, adapting, or judging evidence-based diabetes care in primary settings. Ninety-two articles covering 85 studies in 27 countries qualified.

Rollout tactics clustered most often around engaging patients, changing clinic infrastructure, and using feedback to adjust course. Tactics tailored to local context appeared less often. The team also coded what helped and what blocked progress, using a standard framework. Readers get a map of which strategies clinics actually use, where the gaps lie, and which hurdles planners must clear before diabetes care can improve at scale in resource-poor settings.
pmc-13508376:
Sofia Kaloper and four co-authors study how accurately people report the places tied to HIV risk and care in Los Angeles, in 2026 work. Prevention programs lean on location data to find hotspots, yet self-reported places carry error. Data came from a long-running study of gay, bisexual, and other sexual minority men in the city. Mapping checks and statistical models then weighed which traits, activity types, and areas predict reporting accuracy.

Personal traits, the kind of activity reported, and geography each shaped accuracy in a meaningful way. Places inside a person's home region were reported more accurately than places outside it. That regional tilt could quietly bias hotspot maps built from surveys alone. The authors plan sharper models with confidence ranges around reported points. Their goal is fairer targeting of prevention work, so that areas with fuzzier reporting do not get overlooked in funding maps.
pmc-13510376:
S. Fouziya Sulthana, U. Mohammed Iqbal, B. S. Sreeja, and Rajesh Anbazhagan review flexible wearable sensors that track body chemistry and body signals at the same time, in 2026 work. Most wearables today cover one side only, either movement and electrical signals or chemical measures such as glucose and lactate in sweat. Joining both sides in one soft, skin-fitting patch could give a fuller picture of health between clinic visits.

The review covers new flexible materials and building methods, then weighs progress in physical sensing, chemical sensing, and ways to merge them on one platform. Gains include steady tracking of chronic conditions and earlier warning of changes. Hurdles remain in accuracy over time, power, data handling, and the step from lab demos to approved medical use. The authors close with directions for the next wave of combined wearables.
pmc-13510576:
Marinos Chatzikonstantinou, Kyriaki Michailidou, Marios Pantzaris, Gavriella Alexandrou, Charalambos C. Charalambous, and Dimitris Sokratous pilot a two-arm exercise program for people with progressive multiple sclerosis, in 2026 work. Five participants with primary or secondary progressive forms took part in a twelve-week program of in-phase movements, where both arms move in the same pattern together. Sessions ran thirty to sixty minutes, and the study used a single-case design with staggered starts.

The program proved safe, workable, and well tolerated across the group. Three of the five participants showed clear gains in the excitability of pathways from brain to muscle, plus gains in some clinical measures. Earlier work had shown similar gains in the relapsing form of the disease. The authors call the low-cost program a candidate for routine and group rehabilitation, while stressing that five cases can only point the way.
pmc-13512776:
Koraj and colleagues redesigned inhibitors of ST6GAL1 to fix their flaw: they could not cross cell membranes. ST6GAL1 is an enzyme that decorates cell surfaces with sialic acid and helps cancers spread and hide from immunity. Their 2026 medicinal chemistry study started from a known non-sugar inhibitor bearing a sulfonic acid group. They replaced that group with look-alike substitutes called bioisosteres.

Koraj found that sulfonylurea substitutes restored passive membrane crossing in an artificial membrane test while keeping enzyme inhibition. An expanded series improved potency, with the best compound reaching low micromolar strength. Binding measurements confirmed the new compounds engage the enzyme at similar strength to the parent. Magnetic resonance mapping showed which parts of the molecule touch the enzyme, with the strongest inhibitors making extra contacts through their aromatic arms. The work supplies a design framework for cell-permeable versions of this cancer target.
pmc-13514676:
Teresa Sinicropi and four co-authors present a 2026 case report of a giant desmoid tumour in the small bowel of a 27-year-old man. Desmoid fibromatosis is rare, grows invasively where it starts, and almost never spreads, yet its behaviour is unpredictable and no standard treatment pathway exists. The patient arrived with fever and worsening abdominal pain five years after sleeve gastrectomy weight-loss surgery, and a CT scan revealed a large abdominal mass arising near the small intestine.

Surgeons removed the mass along with the right colon and the end of the small intestine, and laboratory examination confirmed the desmoid diagnosis. The man left hospital on the fifth day after surgery in good condition, with no sign of the tumour returning at the time of writing. Sinicropi's team reviews the wider literature and finds their full-removal approach matches current thinking.
pmc-13515876:
Mikołaj Maga and six colleagues translate and validate a Polish version of the Walking Impairment Questionnaire in a 2026 study. The questionnaire scores walking distance, speed, and stair climbing for people with intermittent claudication, the leg pain of narrowed arteries that strikes during walking. One hundred patients lined up for vessel-opening treatment completed the Polish form, two quality-of-life surveys, and a six-minute walking test.

Scores on the Polish questionnaire lined up with both quality-of-life surveys across every domain. They also tracked the distance walked before pain began and the maximum distance reached. Repeating the test gave near-identical results, and the questions hung together strongly as a set. Maga's team concludes that the Polish version, built on metric units, is a reliable and clinically useful gauge of walking limits in this patient group.
pmc-13515976:
Gulnur Nakhanova leads a twenty-two-author team developing a quality-control test for a brucellosis vaccine candidate, in a 2026 study. The vaccine uses a lab-made protein, superoxide dismutase, as its antigen. Standard antibody tests can misread such proteins after the chemical steps used in vaccine making, so the team built an older-style diffusion assay instead. First they raised rich antibody serum in sheep, comparing two booster additives.

The aluminium-based additive produced far stronger antibody levels than the rival by day forty-two. With that serum, the diffusion assay formed rings whose size grew in a straight, predictable relation with antigen amount. It detected the protein down to a fraction of a microgram per millilitre, measured precisely, and ignored unrelated proteins. Nakhanova's team presents the assay as a sturdy tool for checking antigen strength in future vaccine batches.
pmc-13516676:
Rejoice Nyarku leads a ten-author team validating a rapid Salmonella test for poultry settings in a 2026 study. Salmonella in chickens is a top food-safety threat, and knowing which strain is present guides the response. The platform, GenoPATHX, runs two multiplex gene panels, one tuned to chickens and one to turkeys, each spotting priority strains plus a general Salmonella marker in a single same-day workflow.

Bench validation showed strong, straight-line readings and detection down to tens or hundreds of genome copies per reaction. The panels caught every target strain in the test set and excluded off-target germs cleanly. On naturally contaminated farm samples, the direct workflow reached about eighty-one percent sensitivity and ninety-one percent specificity against the reference culture method used by United States inspectors. Nyarku's team presents the assay as ready support for poultry surveillance and risk-based food safety action.
pmc-13518776:
Inka Romero-Ortells, Manuel Perea, Eva Gutierrez-Sigut, and Jon Andoni Duñabeitia report 2026 eye-tracking experiments on how subtitles steer attention in bilingual teaching videos. University students watched two-speaker lessons while researchers varied the spoken language and the subtitle language. The learners were Spanish speakers studying English, with native English speakers as a comparison group.

Dubbing the audio into Spanish shifted gaze from speakers' mouths toward their eyes, while comprehension rose compared with original English audio. Once subtitles appeared, viewers in both language groups spent most of their looking time on the text itself, whatever language it used. Comprehension stayed equally high with first- or second-language subtitles, a useful lesson for video designers.
pmc-13518876:
Yue Li and eight colleagues profile the immune landscape of high-grade serous ovarian cancer in 2026, a disease that recurs often and shrugs off checkpoint immunotherapy. Sequencing single cells from tumors of eight untreated patients, covering 84,065 cells, they mapped six major cell groups and traced how killer CD8 T cells wear out into exhausted states.

Exhausted T cells stood out for producing CCL3, a signal that talks to macrophages through the CCR1 receptor. Fluid from exhausted cells pushed macrophages toward the tumor-friendly M2 type far more strongly than fluid from active T cells, and added CCL3 boosted that shift further. Blocking this axis, the authors propose, might warm up cold ovarian tumors.
pmc-13518976:
Gaoyuan Fu proposes a 2026 network model, CT-GCN, that predicts how productive Chinese manufacturing firms will become while separating true causes from mere correlations. Total factor productivity gauges efficiency, yet older forecasters ignore links between firms and mistake correlation for causation. Fu's panel covers 12,847 enterprises from 2008 to 2022.

The framework estimates productivity with the Levinsohn-Petrin method, identifies causal effects with double machine learning, and maps firms into graphs built from supply chains, distance, and technology similarity. Prediction error fell by more than 19 percent versus baselines. Research spending, digital transformation, and human capital emerged as genuine drivers, with effects varying by sector, size, and region. Tailored strategy advice follows from those differences.
pmc-13520276:
Erenoğlu and Kılıç ask whether nursing students who cannot put their phones down also experience more abuse inside online dating relationships. Cyber dating abuse covers partners monitoring messages, controlling contacts, and attacking through digital channels. Their 2026 cross-sectional study surveyed 224 nursing students at a state university in southern Turkey, most of them women and nearly all single, using validated addiction and abuse questionnaires.

Every abuse dimension moved with phone addiction, always weakly but always significantly: students scoring higher on addiction reported more monitoring and control by partners, and more direct digital aggression. They also admitted doing more of each themselves. Nearly two thirds of the students said they felt lost without their phones, and a third reported low mood when not using them. The authors argue nurses are well placed to teach young people to spot digital abuse early.
pmc-13520376:
Bereket Yilma Beshah and colleagues map in 2026 where young children in East Africa miss their third diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccine dose, and which local factors track with missed doses. Survey data covered 14,200 children aged 12 to 23 months in seven countries from 2018 to 2023.

Missed doses clustered geographically rather than scattering evenly. The strongest cluster centred on central and northern Mozambique, where risk was nearly four times the background level. Having no maternal schooling and fewer than four antenatal visits tracked with missed doses, though strengths varied by place. Maps of this kind help outreach teams target cold spots first.
pmc-13521976:
Magdalena Benda and colleagues review in 2026 infection risk from T-cell redirecting cures for relapsed myeloma. The set held 123 studies, mostly early phase. Cures cover engineered CAR T cells and bispecific antibodies. These cures changed care, yet infection load stays high.

Any-grade infection rates ran from about 40 to 80 percent in most reports. Risk peaked early after cell dosing or in early antibody months. Severe infection topped half in some antibody groups. Fatal cases arose under both cure types. Viruses and bacteria led the germ lists. Fungal disease and one pneumonia type arose where preventive cover was absent.
pmc-13522276:
Yousef Hawas and colleagues present in 2026 a 54-year-old postmenopausal woman with lobular breast cancer in both breasts. Spread reached the stomach. An eye socket lump first feared as spread proved to be plain inflammation. Lobular cancers reach gut and orbit more often than other breast types do.

Biopsy showed hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative disease in both breasts. Scans found gut wall thickening and belly fluid. Lungs and liver stayed clear. Drug care then hormone upkeep held disease stable. Fresh eye checks after droop and vomiting named a steroid-responsive false tumour. Nerve harm from drug care needed plasma exchange. Bone scans showed no bone spread.
pmc-13522776:
Dongxu Li and colleagues build a membrane-based nanoplatform for painful tendon disease in a 2026 study. Tendinopathy causes long-term pain, driven by an inflamed environment that draws in pain-sensing nerves and weakens tendon stem cells. The platform fuses membranes from immune cells and sensory nerve cells and combines them with cleaned tendon matrix material.

The hybrid membranes soak up multiple inflammatory signals and pain-related molecules, calming the local environment and protecting stem cells from aging. The tendon matrix pushed those stem cells toward tendon identity and movement. In animals, treatment improved collagen alignment, eased pain, shifted immune cells toward healing, and restored tendon function. The authors present the design as a way to break the inflammation and aging cycle while rebuilding tendon.
pmc-13523376:
Ayse Sena Manzak Dursun and colleagues trial a home exercise program for women with asthma in a 2026 randomized study. Thirty women were assigned to a training group or a control group receiving a general activity booklet. The training group met a physiotherapist weekly for eight weeks and exercised at home three days a week, following a standardized, low-cost routine.

Compared with controls, the training group improved significantly on one breathing measure, walking distance in six minutes, an activity-related quality of life subscore, and leg strength measured by repeated standing. Other outcomes, including overall asthma control, did not separate clearly in the reported results. The authors present the program as an accessible alternative where advanced rehabilitation centers are out of reach, particularly for reducing sedentary behavior.
pmc-13523476:
Chunlan Yu and others assess, in a 2026 mixed-methods study, whether maternity care stakeholders in China would accept a midwifery continuity of care model. In that model, a known midwife or small team follows a woman through pregnancy, birth, and the postnatal period. Chinese maternity care remains largely led by obstetricians and split across many hands, so acceptance is a key test.

Surveys reached 896 maternity providers across China, and focus groups added views from providers and childbearing women. About 93 percent of them said they would accept and use the model, with midwives most willing and obstetricians least. Leadership backing was the strongest helper, followed by obstetrician endorsement and women's buy-in. Group discussions showed unmet needs for relational continuity alongside practical barriers the authors say planning must address.
pmc-13524676:
Kanita Mankan and others pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, how well standard kidney function equations perform in kidney transplant recipients. Knowing the filtration rate matters after transplant, and cystatin C depends less on muscle mass than creatinine. Guidelines endorse cystatin C for chronic kidney disease mostly, with little guidance for transplant care.

Twenty-six studies met the bar, and fourteen gave usable bias data on 4,041 adult recipients with repeat measures. An equation using both creatinine and cystatin C showed the smallest average bias against measured filtration. Rules using creatinine alone tended to underestimate true filtration, while rules using cystatin alone overshot it. Accuracy within set margins was also pooled. The authors support the joint equation for transplant follow-up while noting studies varied.
pmc-13524876:
Poirot, de Médina, and Silvente-Poirot propose in 2026 a new way to think about cholesterol production. The pathway that builds cholesterol runs more than twenty steps and makes many distinct intermediate molecules, called sterols, which seems wasteful if cholesterol is the only goal.

The authors argue that the intermediates are products in their own right, each with its own effects on membranes, signals, and oxidation chemistry. Their framework, sterol flux rewiring, says that what matters is how the flow through the pathway is redistributed. The redistribution creates whole sterol states rather than piles of single molecules. That view ties together findings long kept apart, from inherited pathway disorders to immune and brain biology. It also suggests treatments that reshape the sterol state instead of simply blocking cholesterol production.
pmc-13525176:
Andri Burger and colleagues survey, in a 2026 snapshot study, student wellbeing supports in medical schools across Australia and New Zealand after new guidance appeared. Medical students report more psychological distress than peers, with effects on learning and patient safety. National documents now urge safe learning environments and wellbeing-oriented curricula, and accreditation standards were revised.

All 24 accredited schools were invited to an online survey between February and May 2024, distributed through dean and wellbeing networks. Sixteen responses came from fourteen schools, representing 58 percent of the sector, after duplicate entries were merged. Respondents were educators and administrators working in student wellbeing or medical education. Their answers reflect personal institutional views, not formally endorsed positions, a caveat the authors state plainly while assessing alignment with the guidance.
pmc-13527576:
Son and colleagues test two plant compounds, alone and combined, as restorers of an immune system flattened by chemotherapy. Cyclophosphamide saves lives in cancer and autoimmune disease but leaves patients defenceless against infection. Their 2026 mouse study used extracts of two traditional medicinal sources, a bracket fungus and red sage root. It then tested their signature molecules: protocatechuic acid and tanshinone IIA, both known to prod immune pathways converging on the NF-kB switch.

In immunosuppressed mice the combined extract significantly eased weight loss and spleen shrinkage. It restored the proportions of T cells, natural killer cells, and macrophages that the drug had cut in the reported measures. Lymphocytes regained their ability to multiply, macrophages ate more aggressively, and killer cells destroyed tumour targets better. The two pure compounds each switched on the same immune pathways in cells, and together outperformed either alone.
pmc-13527676:
Leizhi Zheng, Mengyue Li, Bin He, Qiang Liu, and Chengbao Liu reconstruct, in a 2026 chemistry study, the surface of a crystalline carbon nitride polymer. Their aim is to hold ionic liquids in place for converting carbon dioxide into useful chemicals. Carbon nitride offers tunable structure and active sites but weak catalytic activity alone. Their design pairs organic superbases with hydrolyzed polymer as bonding partners.

The combined catalyst joins amino groups and hydrogen-bonding functions inside one framework, cooperatively activating epoxides for coupling with carbon dioxide. At mild pressure, ninety degrees, and six hours, the best version delivered a chlorinated cyclic carbonate in ninety-nine percent yield with ninety-nine percent selectivity. The solid catalyst was recovered by simple separation and reused. The authors present the platform as a sustainable route for green chemical transformations.
pmc-13528076:
Cristina A. Smith and four colleagues analyze COVID-19 vaccine willingness across fifteen developing countries in a 2026 study. Data came from a global survey run over six months. The design used repeated snapshots rather than following the same people. Models accounted for clustering and change over time. Culture was summed into three broad components.

People aged fifty-five and over were more willing to vaccinate. Women were more willing than men, with odds about one and a half times higher. Fear of side effects cut willingness in a curved pattern. Willingness also rose and dipped across months in a shallow arc. Culture pushed both ways, with no simple leaning. The authors say campaigns must work with local culture, not against it. Simple one-message drives are unlikely to fit all settings.
pmc-13529176:
Dai and colleagues reviewed nanomaterials engineered to deliver tumor vaccines in a 2026 survey of the field. Tumor vaccines train the immune system by giving it tumor antigens, the identifying markers of cancer cells, plus helper substances, so that antigen-presenting cells can activate killer T cells. Conventional vaccines underperform because their antigens are weak and often fail to reach those presenting cells in lymph nodes.

Dai organizes the new delivery materials into four families: polymer-based, fat-based, inorganic, and biomimetic, meaning modeled on natural cells or membranes. Tiny carriers can shield antigens, travel efficiently to lymph nodes, linger there, and be taken up by presenting cells. strengthens the anti-tumor response and may prevent spread and recurrence while reducing off-target effects. The authors map design choices across these families to guide construction of more effective vaccine platforms for clinical use.
pmc-13530076:
Yun Wang and Guohua Zhu introduce a 2026 method for finding long non-coding RNAs that shape tumor immunity across many cancers. These RNA molecules do not build proteins, yet they steer immune pathways and cell entry into tumors. Few such regulators had been pinned down before this work.

Their algorithm, named LncImmune, screens 32 cancer types and combines several tools to flag candidate regulators. Core molecules split lung adenocarcinoma into two groups with cold and hot immune character. The groups differed in mutations, immune cell levels, drug sensitivity, and outlook, pointing toward fresh markers for prognosis and treatment.
pmc-13531876:
Masaaki Yuki leads a 2026 study of a small protective protein, PRELP, that fades from scarred human lungs. Tissue staining placed the protein in support regions and some air sac cells of healthy lungs, with clear loss in fibrotic disease. Mouse experiments used a drug that scars lungs to test cause and treatment.

Mice lacking the protein scarred worse than normal mice. Giving the protein through the airway before injury suppressed scarring. Dish tests showed it kept surface cells in character, slowed scar-cell movement, and worked through two signaling routes, nominating it as an inhaled therapy candidate.
pmc-13532476:
Leah M Gober and colleagues report in 2026 on early stent care for a narrowed aorta in young pigs. A narrowed aorta, called coarctation, is a birth defect that can raise blood pressure and strain the heart. New stents can be widened over time as a child grows, yet long-term effects were not known.

Eighteen pigs were split into sham, untreated narrowed, and stented groups. Stents widened to adult size, removed the narrowing, and kept heart function close to normal. Four of six stented pigs formed small bulges near the stent that needed cover stents, a risk readers should note.
pmc-13534276:
Won Myung Lee and colleagues study in 2026 whether a sticky powder can prevent a pain and fever syndrome after scope removal of growths in the upper colon. The syndrome follows a scope procedure that cuts tissue under the lining and can lengthen hospital stays. Records covered high-risk cases treated from April 2023 to October 2024 across centres.

Nine patients developed the syndrome overall. Rates were much lower with the powder than without it, and all cases settled with rest and antibiotics and no surgery. Readers see early clinical proof that a simple barrier layer may prevent this problem.
pmc-13534476:
Weber and colleagues studied in 2026 a plant membrane protein called HIR2 in Arabidopsis, a small model plant. Plant cell membranes sort their proteins into zones, but the rules behind this order are murky. HIR2 belongs to a family of membrane-organising proteins and anchors to the inner face of the cell membrane.

HIR2 was found to bind several receptors, including partners of BAK1, a core receptor in growth and immunity signalling. Plants lacking HIR2 showed impaired growth and weaker immunity, tying the protein to those pathways. Advanced microscopy showed HIR2 changes how BAK1 moves and clusters in the membrane. Computer modelling predicted HIR2 assembles into a cup-like multi-protein complex, matching large complexes seen in lab gels. The authors propose HIR2 helps build membrane sub-zones that shape receptor behaviour.
pmc-13536276:
James DeWitt Crall and Marilia Palumbo Gaiarsa argue in 2026 that differences between individuals within a species shape how plant-pollinator communities respond to global change. Forecasts based on species averages may miss gradual shifts or sudden collapse risks. The authors draw on niche theory at the species level to frame the individual scale.

Individual variation may soften responses to stress in many cases, making change more gradual than average-based models predict. Outcomes hinge on how key traits, such as stress tolerance and pollination skill, vary and pair within individuals. A roadmap closes the piece for future field studies.
pmc-13536576:
Lei Wu and colleagues report in 2026 a simple new route to substituted 2-amino-1,3,4-oxadiazoles from hydrazides and isothiocyanates. These ring compounds matter widely in drug and farm chemical research, so easier synthesis has broad value. The method uses sodium hydroxide to drive a ring-closing step that removes sulfur under mild conditions.

The team reports wide substrate tolerance, strong yields, and easy handling across many variants. Such direct access could speed library building for biological screening in medicine and crop science. An alternative regioselective path to this valued scaffold is now open to chemists.
pmc-13536776:
Agata Olearczyk and co-authors survey workplace health promotion in Poland in a 2026 nationwide poll of 1,030 full-time workers aged 18 to 60 years. Online interviews in December 2025 asked whether employers offer health activities beyond required safety duties, how often workers use them, and what blocks use. Answers were compared across company size, ownership, job type, and satisfaction levels.

Fewer than half the workers said their employer offers health promotion, split between regular and occasional offers. About half of those with access used activities often. Lack of time was the leading barrier. Access clustered in large firms, foreign-owned private firms, big cities, and among highly satisfied staff and managers. Flexible hours and shift work also tracked with access. The authors highlight wide gaps by workplace traits.
pmc-13536876:
Jie Wen and colleagues analyze peroxisome-related genes across digestive cancers in a 2026 study combining data modeling with lab tests. Peroxisomes are small cell parts that handle fats and oxygen balance, yet their cancer roles stay unclear. Gene signatures for outlook were built for eight digestive cancers, immune surroundings were profiled, and focused tests in liver and bowel cancer cells probed treatment resistance and fat handling.

Signatures predicted outlook strongly across the cancers. High-risk tumors showed a more suppressed immune setting with more regulatory and repair-type cells. One gene, PEX13, ran high in treatment-resistant liver tumors, and silencing it or a partner gene eased resistance in lab models by reshaping fat use. The authors propose targeting peroxisome function in high-risk groups.
pmc-13538476:
Roxana Portieles and co-authors benchmark virus-derived wall-cutting proteins as antibacterials in a 2026 combined computing and lab study. Seven variants from Bacillus-infecting viruses were docked against a tiny wall fragment, simulated over long timescales, scored for binding strength, and tested against two bacterial species. The aim was to learn whether cheap fragment scores predict real killing power well enough to rank candidates.

Most variants recognized the fragment favorably, yet contact styles and stability differed widely. Lab tests crowned one variant as strongest against both species, while two others shone mainly in computing scores. Overall links between fragment scores and killing stayed modest. The authors nominate the lab winner and one runner-up for development, while warning that tiny fragments poorly stand in for whole walls.
pmc-13540876:
Chunfang Peng and colleagues present a new gene-picking method in 2026. The method serves single-cell and spatial gene-reading data. Analysts first pick the most variable genes. Only then can they group cells into types. Standard tools rescale the data first. That step can hide real biological differences.

Their method is called EMD-HVG. It skips rescaling entirely. It measures variation with earth mover's distance. That statistic makes no assumptions about the shape of the data. Tests on real and simulated datasets gave top scores in most scenarios. The count was twenty-six wins out of thirty. Gene sets from the method also gave cleaner cell clusters.
pmc-13541576:
Jose Carlos Pachon-M and colleagues discuss a rescue method in 2026. The method is cardioneuroablation. It can help when standard ablation blocks the heart's relay by accident. Slow-pathway ablation cures a common fast rhythm. The target sits millimetres from the AV node. Block still strikes two to three percent of cases. Block normally means a lifelong pacemaker.

The case involved a man in his early fifties. His final burn caused complete nodal block. He felt faint and breathless, with no reversal in thirty minutes. Operators skipped the pacemaker plan. They ablated a nearby nerve cluster instead. Normal conduction returned in the same session.
pmc-13542176:
Neha Chourasia and colleagues present a speech tool in 2026. The tool recognises emotion in spoken voices. Machines that answer human feelings need such a tool. Older systems lean on hand-crafted features. They crumble with new speakers or noisy rooms. The new design uses a one-dimensional convolutional network.

Three sound descriptors feed the network as one sequence. They cover tone texture, signal crossings, and energy. Training data pooled four public acted-speech collections. Extra training copies came from noise, shifts, and pitch changes. Stretching added still more variety. Seven emotion classes were tested at the end. Accuracy reached about ninety-five percent on test data.
pmc-13542276:
Agnieszka Gdowicz-Kłosok's team profiled the chemistry of fluid that collects where breast tissue was removed during surgery, in a 2026 study. One group of patients had breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy given during the procedure itself, while another group had full mastectomy. Fluid from 54 patients was taken on the first and fifth days after surgery and read with nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which found 42 small molecules.

The fluid's chemistry changed clearly between day one and day five in both groups, reflecting early wound healing. Levels of several amino acids fell while lactate and pyruvate rose in the breast-sparing group, a pattern suggesting more sugar-burning activity in the irradiated tissue bed. Ketone bodies declined across both groups. No firm chemical separation showed between the two surgery groups overall. The authors present the profiles as a baseline for future work on how wound fluid may influence leftover cancer cells.
pmc-13542376:
Pedro Acién and Maribel Acién published a 2026 review on how malformations of the female genital and urinary tracts present and get diagnosed. Because both systems develop from shared embryonic tissue, faults in one very often accompany faults in the other. The authors update their embryological-clinical classification, which sorts anomalies by their developmental origin, and discuss the mesonephric and Müllerian structures whose failed formation produces most cases.

One message runs through the review: a missing kidney on one side is the renal problem most often paired with obstructive genital anomalies. Some duct faults always come with that renal absence. Certain patterns, such as leaking urine between normal voiding in a girl, can point to the diagnosis early. Outcomes after surgery also depend on the anomaly's developmental type, so the classification is presented as a practical tool for choosing investigation and treatment.
pmc-13547376:
Muhammad Shazib Hameed and colleagues proposed in 2026 a way to judge AI storytelling systems, tools meant to carry family stories and cultural identity across generations. Rating such systems means weighing story coherence, personal connection, ethical trust, flexibility, and staying power under deep doubt, where expert judgments are partial and trust in each rating varies. Their model layers a flexible fuzzy number system over an established ranking method, so doubt and trust are carried through the math.

Applied to a set of storytelling system choices, every method tested agreed on the best option. Yet the new model kept more information and explained its verdict more clearly. The authors offer it as decision support for storytelling technology that is emotionally aware and ethically guided.
pmc-13548476:
Wen Zhao and co-authors surveyed in 2026 how safe intensive care nurses feel when moving critically ill patients inside the hospital, a journey full of risk. Six hundred fifty-three nurses from ten top-level hospitals in China's Hunan Province completed a transport safety scale and background questionnaire. Statistical profiling sorted the nurses into hidden groups rather than assuming one average attitude.

Three profiles emerged: about a fifth of nurses felt low safety during transports, well over half felt moderate safety, and just under a quarter felt high safety. Skipping the transport checklist sharply raised the odds of landing in the lower groups, while confidence in transport tasks protected against them. The authors suggest checklists and targeted training, while noting that perceived safety is not measured risk.
pmc-13548676:
Rigler and co-authors tested a 2026 pair of ways to read CT perfusion scans in stroke patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy, the clot removal procedure. Automated software rules scan reading, yet simple visual grading had already shown prognostic value. The study covered anterior circulation strokes with large vessel blockage at one centre.

Records of 579 consecutive patients were analysed with both methods applied to the same baseline scans. Agreement between visual and automated grading was only fair in Rigler's head-to-head test. Both predicted favourable ninety day outcome, with visual grading slightly the stronger of the two in the tests. In adjusted models visual grading stayed an independent predictor while automated grading lost its standing once collateral flow was added. The authors praise visual reading as simple and open to any centre.
pmc-13549976:
Raghavendra, Ghosh, and Nayak turn bottle gourd peel waste into a functional food ingredient. Their 2026 paper studies how particle size changes peel powder behavior. Bottle gourd peel is rich in fiber and bioactive compounds. Food makers discard it as processing waste today. Grinding size may decide how useful the powder becomes.

Water holding capacity rose as particles shrank from 600 to 425 micrometers. Grinding finer, down to 150 micrometers, reversed that gain. Swelling capacity fell steadily across the same range. It dropped from 16.4 to 11.2 milliliters per gram overall. Oil absorption peaked at the 500 micrometer size. The 425 micrometer powder absorbed the least oil. Taste panels picked favorite formulations for two products. A pancake mix called PM1 won among its group. A soup mix called SM3 won among soups. The pancake mix also showed higher antioxidant activity. Right-sizing the grind unlocks value from peel waste.
pmc-13551676:
David Thai, with six colleagues, published a 2026 case study of two siblings with TRAPS, an inherited autoinflammatory syndrome causing repeated flares. Standard steroid-sparing drugs need regular injections, a problem because the elder child, now 14, had developed needle phobia. Her 10-year-old brother's treatment also aimed to limit injections, reflecting family preference.

The sister started an oral JAK inhibitor, a drug blocking inflammation signaling, while her brother received tocilizumab. Over two years both children had almost no flares, their inflammatory markers normalized, and growth improved, with no adverse effects reported. The authors say this is the first report of a JAK inhibitor in TRAPS, and they add the tocilizumab case to limited published experience.
pmc-13551776:
Lingling Dai, with nine colleagues, published a 2026 brain scan study of vestibular migraine. In this condition, vertigo comes with migraine. Past work found odd links in the brain's balance cortex. The direction of those links was unknown. The team used resting scans and a method that infers direction. Groups held 56 patients with vestibular migraine, 58 with plain migraine, and 63 healthy people.

Vestibular migraine showed distinct flow patterns to and from one balance region. The patterns involved frontal and parietal areas tied to control and sense blending. A learning model built on the flows split the groups fairly well. It separated vestibular migraine from plain migraine best. The team suggests the flows could aid diagnosis where symptoms overlap.
pmc-13554476:
Adeviye Eda Somtaş and Aslı Gizem Çapar compare two diets for irritable bowel syndrome in a 2026 trial. Sixty-three adults with the condition were split evenly into three groups for four weeks. One group ate a low-FODMAP diet, cutting fermentable sugars that feed gut gas. Another cut out gluten entirely, while the third served as a control.

Both diet groups reported milder symptoms and better quality of life after four weeks. Once starting scores were weighed, only quality of life differed clearly between groups. Body measures such as weight, waist size, and carbohydrate intake also shifted between groups. Symptom severity itself did not separate the diets after adjustment. The authors back both diets as short-term options worth tailoring to the person.
pmc-13555176:
Pinar Dursun, Ayse Nur Saribas Yildirim, and Ayca Yazici compare skin mites in eczema patients on a modern drug versus untreated peers in a 2026 study. The drug dupilumab calms moderate-to-severe eczema, yet stubborn face and neck redness often persists on it. Tiny Demodex mites, normal skin residents, are one suspect. Sixty-one patients had skin surface samples checked for mite density.

Mites above the infestation line appeared in nearly half the drug group, but in very few controls. Every drug patient had already improved strongly on standard eczema scores. Mite-positive patients in the drug group were older than mite-negative ones. Most reported lasting face redness and itch, often with eye symptoms. The authors suggest checking for mites when faces stay red on treatment.
pmc-13556076:
Dauda Ishola Azeez and ten colleagues spent a year, reported in 2026, measuring blackfly biting around the Asejire dam on the border of Oyo and Osun states in southwest Nigeria. These flies swarm in huge numbers near the dam, and their bites are both a nuisance and a route for disease. Trained collectors caught flies landing on them from morning to evening at four community sites between December 2024 and November 2025.

Close to ten thousand flies were collected, with the Osun side yielding about two thirds of the catch. Biting peaked twice a day, numbers ran higher upstream of the dam, and every site passed a thousand bites per person each month. The authors call the biting pressure along the border intense and urge both state governments to fund control measures that keep flies away from people.
pmc-13558276:
Shota Nakamura and nine colleagues reported in 2026 five years of results from an online event that recruits students into surgery across eight departments at once. The event, GEKA-Navi, mixes plenary talks on surgical careers with departmental breakout sessions for medical students and junior residents. The team tracked who attended between 2021 and 2025, who later entered the departments, and how participants rated the experience.

Annual attendance ran from about eighty to one hundred fifty people. Of 151 new surgical residents entering over the period, roughly six in ten had attended the event first. Feedback was glowing: nearly all respondents said the event raised their interest in surgical departments, and more than eight in ten felt more motivated to become surgeons. The authors offer the shared-event model as a template for workforce recruitment.
pmc-13559576:
Chen and co-authors test a routine inflammation score as a survival marker in leukaemia, and find the opposite of the usual pattern. Their 2026 multicentre study analyses 609 patients, calculating the systemic immune-inflammation index from platelets, neutrophils, and lymphocytes before treatment. In solid tumours, higher values predict worse survival, but leukaemia distorts blood counts through marrow failure, so the meaning was unclear.

A threshold derived from the training cohort split survival sharply. Patients above it had less than half the death hazard of those below after adjustment, and curve analyses suggested a nonlinear inverse relationship. A prediction nomogram built on the model calibrated acceptably in both cohorts. The authors suggest a higher index may signal lower disease burden and better-preserved blood production in leukaemia, reversing the marker's usual interpretation.
pmc-13559676:
Sinuo Sun and colleagues study apolipoprotein E in papillary thyroid carcinoma, asking whether the protein pushes the cancer forward by switching on mitophagy, the cell's recycling of worn mitochondria. Their 2026 work combines cancer atlas and GEO dataset analysis with tissue staining, cell experiments, and a mouse xenograft model. APOE had already been tied to progression in this cancer, but the mechanism was missing.

APOE ran high in tumor tissue and cell lines. Raising it made cells proliferate more and die less, while lowering it flipped both effects. Extra APOE also activated the PINK1 and Parkin pathway that tags mitochondria for disposal, shifted energy-sensing signals, and increased autophagosome formation. Blocking mitophagy with drugs blunted the growth advantage, tying the behavior to the recycling pathway. Tumors in mice echoed the pattern. The authors suggest the APOE mitophagy axis as a lead for future preclinical work.
pmc-13560276:
Chanittha Niyomthammarat and colleagues chart ten years of invasive fungal disease in children at a Bangkok tertiary hospital. Their 2026 retrospective study reviews patients aged fifteen and under diagnosed between 2014 and 2023 under the 2020 global rules. One hundred fifty-six children had one hundred seventy-one infection episodes between them.

Invasive candidiasis and aspergillosis led the tally with about sixty episodes each, followed by Pneumocystis pneumonia. Aspergillosis and Pneumocystis cases swung year to year and bunched in later years, while candidiasis arrived evenly throughout. Some episodes broke through despite protective drugs, notably nearly a quarter of aspergillosis cases. Blood cancers underlay most aspergillosis, while candidiasis struck infants with lasting illness and central lines. Deaths by day ninety ranged from about thirteen to twenty-five percent by germ. The authors urge better testing and better ways to stop them before they start.
pmc-13562576:
Dongwei Yan and seven colleagues build a vision system that finds ripe ginkgo fruit on the tree so picking robots can harvest it. Ginkgo fruit blends with the leaves in colour and size, and shifting light, shadow, and overlap fool ordinary detectors. Their 2026 model, GinkgoSense-Net, extends a compact YOLO detector with two attention modules and a sharper box-fitting loss. Heat-map visualisation, part-removal tests, and head-to-head comparisons checked that each addition earned its place.

The finished model reached 95.0 percent precision and 92.1 percent recall, with an overall detection score of 93.6 percent. It also ran in real time, at about 75 frames per second. Accuracy, speed, and small size balanced well, the authors report. Reliable fruit spotting is a first step toward automated harvesting that protects freshness, and the team frames the work as a practical piece of smart farming.
pmc-13562676:
Ling Du and five colleagues spend three years testing how to wash salt out of reclaimed farmland in arid Xinjiang, China. Heavy salinisation chokes crops there, fed by evaporation and shallow groundwater. The 2026 field trial compared farming measures alone against combinations that added a salt barrier at root depth, drainage pipes, or chemical amendments, with an untreated control plot. Salt was tracked through the soil profile each season, alongside irrigation, evaporation, and groundwater depth.

Irrigation during the growing season pushed plough-layer salt down most strongly, with a correlation of minus 0.871. Farming alone let salt creep back to the surface. Pipes and chemicals shifted salt downward instead. Desalination peaked in year two and eased in year three. Root-zone separation and pipe drainage finished best, clearing 61.33 and 59.37 percent of salt from the top 80 centimetres. The authors recommend pairing engineering with good farming, weighed against build and upkeep costs.
pmc-13563876:
Ahmet Akmercan and five colleagues hunt for early warnings of the thyroid surgery complication patients fear most: parathyroid glands that never recover. Their 2026 review covered 498 people who had total or completion thyroidectomy between 2017 and 2024. Permanent hypoparathyroidism meant hormone levels still low and active vitamin D still needed six months on. Eighteen patients, 3.6 percent, met that bar. The team compared their surgery details, calcium readings, and day-one hormone levels against everyone who recovered.

One number stood out. A parathyroid hormone level of 7 picograms per millilitre or less on the first postoperative day predicted permanence with 86.7 percent sensitivity and 90.3 percent specificity, carrying an odds ratio of 16.60. Its real strength was reassurance: a value above the cut-off almost ruled the complication out, at 99.4 percent negative predictive value. Completion surgery also raised risk independently. The authors caution that eighteen events is a thin base, and ask for larger prospective checks.
pmc-13569576:
Claire Keenan and a large team map, in a 2026 scoping review, which patient health outcomes researchers use when judging pharmacist-led primary care in community settings. Searches of four databases and web sources from 1997 to early 2025 gathered 299 studies from more than ten thousand records.

Experimental designs made up about three fifths of the studies and grew more common over time. Outcomes were sorted by quality, effectiveness, and safety, then displayed as heat maps across diseases and services. As pharmacists take on fuller primary care roles, knowing which patient outcomes get measured, and which get skipped, helps funders demand better proof of benefit.
pmc-13569676:
J. Christian Virchow leads a 2026 EUFOREA consensus paper arguing that remission, not mere symptom control, should be the goal across chronic airway diseases. The diseases include severe asthma, sinus disease with nasal polyps, and allergic rhinitis. Specialists in lung, nose, and allergy medicine met in Rome in October 2025 to agree practical statements.

The panel held that remission is a target at any starting severity. Paired upper and lower airway diseases often form one condition. Each specialty should score remission separately while treating jointly. A four-week window for symptom recall and twelve months as the minimum remission span were recommended. Clinicians get shared language for aiming higher.
pmc-13572476:
Kerimali Akyildiz, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 rat study of liver harm from a 6 gigahertz field and a possible shield. Fields at this band serve new wireless gear, and their effects on tissue are under study. The shield tested is coenzyme Q10, a compound that helps cells handle oxidative stress.

Twenty-four male rats were split into three groups: a sham group, a field-only group, and a field group fed the compound at 10 milligrams per kilogram a day. Field sessions ran two hours a day for 30 days. The field raised damage markers, liver enzymes, and stress signals in liver tissue, and slides showed more harm. The compound group showed lower damage and calmer stress signals. The authors read this as the compound easing field-linked liver strain in rats.
pmc-13573376:
Jing Peng, with 11 colleagues, describes a 2026 study of low oxygen risk during repeat lung surgery. When a lung is operated on again, the other lung must do all the breathing for a time. Prior tissue loss makes oxygen drops more likely, and teams want warning signs before surgery starts.

The team reviewed 139 patients who had repeat lung removal at a Yunnan cancer hospital in 2022 and 2023. Oxygen drops hit just under a sixth of cases. Scan measures of working lung volume in the lung that stays down ranked among four solo risk factors. A past oxygen drop, strong pain two days after the first surgery, and a breathing test score completed the set. The scan measure comes from routine images, so clinics can add it to planning with no extra tests.
pmc-13573476:
Oliver da Costa Senior, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 review of three-dimensional checks on a split upper jaw surgery. Segmented Le Fort I surgery moves the upper jaw in pieces to fix width as well as height and tilt. Old two-dimensional reviews left doubts about its accuracy and stability, which 3D scans can now settle.

Four databases were searched to October 2024, and 22 studies passed the filters, three of them randomised. Methods varied too much for a pooled number. Overall, the surgery landed close to plan, yet some moves fell short: widening, forward shift, and pitch. During follow-up, width relapse ran larger at the teeth than at the bone. The authors urge one standard, voxel-based 3D method so future studies can be compared fairly.
pmc-13574776:
Cátia Silveiro, with five colleagues, led a 2026 study of two wall tweaks that shield the tuberculosis germ from penicillin-type drugs. TB kills heavily, and drug-resistant strains blunt the standard cures. The germ's wall sugar carries two odd chemical edits, and the team silenced the genes behind each one.

A gene-dimming tool cut output from the two edit pathways in turn. One edit proved vital for growth, the other less so. Both edits guarded the germ against beta-lactam drugs, since weakened versions fell to lower drug doses in mixed therapy. One edit also helped the germ thrive inside immune cells grown in dishes. Silencing shifted immune signals in opposite ways per edit. The authors flag both edits as fresh drug targets against resistant TB.
pmc-13575076:
Yuping Sun leads a 2026 early-phase trial in China testing two cancer drugs together. The pair are ceralasertib, a pill that blocks the ATR repair enzyme, and durvalumab, an immune therapy given by infusion. Patients had advanced solid tumours with few options left, many after prior immune therapy had stopped working.

Fourteen patients joined two dosing schedules. Most had some side effect, half had a severe one, yet no dose-limiting problems appeared. Drug levels in the body matched results from Western studies. Three of 13 patients checked for response saw their tumours shrink in a confirmed way, across lung and cervical cancers. The authors judge the pairing workable and active enough to study further.
pmc-13575176:
Jonathan Hunter and seven colleagues examine emergency department use by older adults with both physical and mental illness in a 2026 study. Having several long-term conditions is common in seniors, yet the added role of psychiatric illness in medical emergency visits was little studied. The cohort covered more than 2.5 million people.

At every level of physical illness burden, visits for non-psychiatric reasons rose as psychiatric severity grew. Statistical models confirmed separate effects for physical burden, psychiatric severity, and continuity of primary care. Seeing the same family doctor regularly did not soften the link between illness burden and frequent visits, a result the authors found unexpected. They call for more work on what regular primary care actually changes for this group.
pmc-13576276:
Petr Novak leads a 2026 study asking which thinking tests best separate mild cognitive impairment from dementia, using the first cohort from a Slovak memory clinic. The group enrolled 150 people over three years, with 84 classed as mild impairment and 55 as dementia in the main analysis. A wide battery of memory, fluency, attention, and daily-living tools was applied.

A verbal learning test and a questionnaire on complex daily activities separated the groups best. Two digit span tests, forward and backward, showed no difference between groups at all. People with dementia had more shrinkage in memory and outer brain regions, larger fluid spaces, and lower total brain volume. Schooling, vital signs, and body measures did not differ. The authors back daily-living assessment and call for sharper objective tools.
pmc-13578276:
Atefeh Zarei and colleagues ran a 2026 green wall trial in Mashhad, Iran, asking whether microbes and charred plant matter help plants grow on reused household wash water. Clean water is scarce, so the wall of Crassula plants was watered with city water or with greywater, the used water from sinks and showers. Three helpers were dosed at varied levels: blue green algae, root fungi, and biochar.

One mix more than doubled the green pigment in leaves. Another mix nearly tripled root and shoot weight next to the weakest plants. The best cleaning mix cut the waste load of the greywater by more than half. Which mix won depended on the goal, growth or cleaning, and the authors want tests in other cities before wide claims.
pmc-13579876:
Mohammad Basheer Alameer and colleagues link daily habits to sleep and mood among medical residents in Syria, in a 2026 survey across twenty two hospitals. Just over two thousand residents answered standard scales for sleep quality, depression, and anxiety, alongside questions on smoking, coffee, alcohol, and body weight. Residency is a draining stage, and the team asked which habits track with the strain.

Smoking tied to worse sleep and higher depression and anxiety scores across the board. Among women, coffee and alcohol each tied to higher anxiety, alcohol most sharply. Underweight women, against the grain, showed lower odds on all three problems. The authors urge programs that help residents quit smoking, guard sleep routines, and keep stimulant and alcohol use modest, for the sake of both doctors and patients.
pmc-13580676:
Sang and colleagues studied trichostatin A, a drug that blocks enzymes removing chemical tags from proteins, in a cell model of sepsis, the dangerous whole-body reaction to infection. Their 2026 experiments used human immune cells stimulated with a bacterial toxin to mimic severe inflammation. The team focused on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and on one protein that helps recycling compartments fuse with disposal compartments.

Sang found that trichostatin A quieted the targeted enzyme and reduced a modified form of the fusion protein. sped up the joining of recycling and disposal compartments inside the cells. Treated cells released less of the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha, a driver of sepsis damage, and cell recycling markers shifted in line with faster cleanup. Computer-based drug mapping also linked the target enzyme to sepsis pathways, together supporting this drug class as a candidate for sepsis-related disease.
pmc-13582176:
Leiane Mota Costa and colleagues validate a twelve question scale that sorts why older Brazilians skip regular exercise, in a 2026 study. Two hundred adults aged sixty and up, mostly women, took the scale plus a standard activity survey. The scale splits its questions into personal barriers, like pain or low drive, and environmental ones, like no safe place or no company.

The two part shape held up well under factor checks, with clean fit scores. Personal barrier scores split active from inactive elders as theory wants. Stability over repeat testing and internal consistency both ran strong. The authors offer the scale to clinics and researchers hunting fixable barriers, while warning their convenience sample limits how far the result travels beyond like groups.
pmc-13584276:
Xuanyu Meng and colleagues look at infection after surgery in babies with biliary atresia, a rare disease that blocks the bile ducts of newborns. The Kasai procedure builds a new drain for the liver, and keeping the child's own liver working is the main goal. Their 2026 study followed 404 children at one centre and asked how later infections lined up with liver outcomes.

Infections that began early were tied to slow clearing of bilirubin, the yellow pigment that builds up when bile cannot drain. Children whose first infection came later kept their own liver longer, with each month of delay linked to a lower risk of death or transplant. The authors warn that their design shows links, not causes, yet they argue that infection timing deserves close watch after this surgery.
pmc-13585876:
Akram Abushamma and colleagues run a follow-up drive for patients who tested positive on a stool-based bowel cancer screen at Cleveland Clinic. A positive stool test only helps if a colonoscopy follows, yet many patients never complete that step. Their 2026 quality project worked with Ohio patients aged 45 to 75 whose positive tests dated from the year before contact, using a patient navigator to call or message them.

Of more than 2,500 patients with positive tests, about a third had not finished a colonoscopy within a year. Among those the navigator reached directly, roughly one in six completed the scope within six months, against a far smaller share for message-only outreach. The main barriers named were gaps in knowledge and transport trouble, with fear and past bad experiences also cited. Overall completion still fell short of the team's goal.
pmc-13587276:
Farhad Heydari and colleagues put four bedside stroke scales head to head in an emergency department study. Brain scans settle a stroke diagnosis, but they are not always at hand in the first minutes, so short checklists of face, arm, and speech signs do the early work. The team scored 655 adults with suspected stroke between 2021 and 2023 and checked every score against MRI results.

Close to three quarters of the patients truly had an ischemic stroke, a blockage type. All four scales sorted patients well, with no firm winner overall. The Cincinnati scale caught the most true strokes, which suits roadside use, while the detailed NIH scale wrongly cleared the fewest healthy patients, which suits hospital confirmation. The authors advise picking the tool by setting, time pressure, and the user's training.
pmc-13587376:
Adekunle Ayomide Adegoke and colleagues compare two immune signals in Nigerians living with HIV on treatment. Antiretroviral therapy quiets the virus but often leaves the immune system partly stirred up. One signal, IL-6, marks inflammation, while IL-10 marks the calming side. Their 2026 study drew 81 people at a Port Harcourt teaching hospital: some on treatment under six months, some for two years or more, plus HIV-negative controls.

IL-6 ran highest in the short-term group, lower in the long-term group, and lowest in controls, with each step clearly apart. Years of treatment thus cool inflammation without fully matching the uninfected state. IL-10 ran higher in treated patients than controls but did not track time on treatment. Age and sex shifted neither signal. The authors back cytokine profiling as an extra gauge of immune health on therapy.
pmc-13592476:
Romain Bouet leads a 2026 study asking what magnetic brain imaging adds when surgeons hunt the seizure source in stubborn focal epilepsy. Their cohort followed 101 patients in a prospective imaging study; those who went on to implanted electrodes or surgery formed the test group. Magnetic source imaging was stacked against standard MRI and metabolic PET scans, with electrode findings and the removed zone as the truth standard.

Magnetic imaging flagged extra source regions beyond MRI in over half the cases, and beyond both older scans in a third. Using all three scans together gave the best detection rate, well above any single scan. Bouet and the team say the gain comes without extra false alarms, which matters most in complex or scan negative cases.
pmc-13592576:
Toshio Narimatsu and five colleagues measure low contrast vision in healthy adults to test whether ordinary short sight quietly dulls sight. Standard eye charts use bold black letters, which can miss subtle loss. Their records covered 43 healthy eyes from checkups at a Tokyo center, all with normal best corrected scores and no eye disease history. Grey chart acuity was tested under best correction.

Low contrast scores worsened with age and ran clearly worse in more short sighted eyes. Better low contrast scores tied to shorter eye length and milder prescriptions, among other factors. Narimatsu and the team conclude that even non diseased myopic eyes carry a real visual penalty, and they commend the grey chart test for clinic studies hunting subtle change.
pmc-13594076:
Xiao and colleagues published a 2026 study on forcing drug-resistant stomach cancer cells to self-destruct. Some stomach cancers survive platinum drugs by dodging a rust-like cell death called ferroptosis. A surface protein, EphA2, helps them keep that death route switched off. The team traced the full chain from EphA2 down to the cell's defenses.

EphA2 switches on a helper that shields a key antioxidant gate protein. With the gate steady, cells keep their chemical shields and survive drugs. Breaking the EphA2 link made the gate crumble in their experiments. Shields fell, damaging oxygen chemicals piled up, and cells died by ferroptosis. Drug sensitivity returned, pointing to a fresh target pairing for therapy. Platinum drug resistance is the clinical wall the work aims to breach.
pmc-13594476:
Elisa Hennings and a large group of investigators, including the Swiss-AF study team, examined how often the medicines taken alongside modern blood thinners could interact with them. They also asked whether those interactions actually harmed patients. Their 2026 analysis drew on a Swiss cohort of 1,732 people with atrial fibrillation followed for a median of six years.

Four in ten patients had at least one potential interaction recorded between their anticoagulant and another drug. Despite that high rate, adjusted analyses found no strong link between potential interactions and major bleeding. The same held for lesser bleeding and for stroke and embolism outcomes. The estimates hovered near no effect, with wide uncertainty for the rarest events. The authors read the results as reassuring but not definitive, since potential interactions flagged on paper may often be managed or harmless in practice.
pmc-13594676:
Pittman and colleagues report the first United States experience with a gentler breast augmentation technique in this 2026 case series. The minimally invasive method uses blunt tunneling and a balloon to create the implant pocket. It aims to preserve breast tissue. It also aims to ease fears about implant safety, oversized results, and general anesthesia. Those fears have held back demand. Five surgical centers collected outcomes prospectively over six months.

A total of 159 women were analyzed, and 13 percent also had fat transfer or a breast lift during the same operation.
